japanese-food:4.about:
Miso is a fermented food made from soybeans, salt and kōji. Depending on the area, there are many kinds, like red miso, white miso and barley miso.
The ingredients, like wakame seaweed, tofu and green onion, are different in every home.

japanese-food:5.fact: A food made by fermenting soybeans. It is known for being sticky.
japanese-food:5.about:
Boiled soybeans fermented with natto bacteria. The more you stir it, the more sticky strings it makes.
It is a traditional Japanese food that often surprises people from other countries.

japanese-food:6.fact: A traditional Japanese sweet eaten at moon-viewing and cherry-blossom viewing.
japanese-food:6.about:
A Japanese sweet made of rice-flour dumplings on a stick. The colours of tricolour dango are said to stand for spring.
At moon-viewing, people offer white dango to the moon.

japanese-food:7.fact: Born in India, it came to Japan through Britain and became Japan's national dish.
japanese-food:7.about:
It travelled from India through Britain and came to Japan in the Meiji period. It spread as a navy dish and became Japan's national dish.
It is a very popular school lunch too.

#japan-traditions: Can you play kendama? Here is some culture that has been treasured in Japan for a long time.

japan-traditions:0.fact: A game where you catch the ball on the cups or on the spike. There are even world championships.
japan-traditions:0.about:
Hatsukaichi in Hiroshima is the home of today's kendama. You catch the ball in 4 places: the big cup, the small cup, the middle cup and the spike.
Now it has fans all around the world as "KENDAMA."

japan-traditions:1.fact: You make a crane or a samurai helmet from one sheet of paper. "Origami" is a word people understand all over the world.
japan-traditions:1.about:
You make shapes by folding one square sheet of paper without cutting it.
Ideas from origami are even used in space, to fold solar panels small so they can be carried (the Miura fold).

japan-traditions:2.fact: Japan's traditional clothes. People wear them at New Year and Coming of Age Day.
japan-traditions:2.about:
A kimono is made by sewing together straight pieces of cloth. Even if your body size changes, you can wear it for a long time by changing how you put it on.
Many people wear a thin summer kimono called a "yukata" to summer festivals.

japan-traditions:3.fact: The art of writing beautifully with a brush and ink.
japan-traditions:3.about:
Children in Japan start learning shodō, writing with a brush and ink, in 3rd grade. At New Year, people do "kakizome," their first writing of the year.
The same character can look strong or gentle, depending on who writes it.

japan-traditions:4.fact: A way of making tea that values the spirit of welcoming guests.
japan-traditions:4.about:
The tea ceremony is said to have been perfected by Sen no Rikyū. Both the person making the tea and the person drinking it follow set manners to show care for each other.
The Japanese sweet you eat before the tea is part of the fun too.

japan-traditions:5.fact: Japan's national sport. You lose if you go out of the ring, or if any part of you except the soles of your feet touches the ground.
japan-traditions:5.about:
A Japanese sport with more than 1,500 years of history. The ring is a circle 4.55 m across.
Before a bout, wrestlers throw salt to purify the ring. The highest rank is "yokozuna."

japan-traditions:6.fact: Woodblock prints from the Edo period. Hokusai's "Great Wave" picture is famous all over the world.
japan-traditions:6.about:
Woodblock prints from the Edo period. Different people drew the picture, carved the woodblocks and printed the paper, so many copies could be made.
They went to Europe and had a big influence on painters like Monet and Van Gogh.

japan-traditions:7.fact: An event where everyone dances in a circle on summer nights.
japan-traditions:7.about:
A dance around the time of Obon to welcome and comfort the spirits of ancestors. People dance in a circle around a tower called a yagura.
Each area has its own songs and dances. "Tankō Bushi" and "Tokyo Ondo" are famous.

japan-traditions:8.fact: A New Year game. Whoever keeps their top spinning longest wins!
japan-traditions:8.about:
Spinning tops are very old toys found all over the world. Spinning helps them stay up without falling over (the gyroscopic effect).
In Japan they have long been a favourite New Year game.

#japan-inventions: Lots of inventions were born in Japan and are now used all over the world.

japan-inventions:0.fact: Invented by Andō Momofuku in 1958. Cup noodles were born in 1971.
japan-inventions:0.about:
At his home in Ikeda, Osaka, Andō Momofuku got an idea from tempura and found a way to dry noodles by frying them in oil.
Today, more than 100 billion servings are eaten around the world every year. They have even become space food.

japan-inventions:1.fact: Born in Japan in the 1970s. "Karaoke" became an English word too.
japan-inventions:1.about:
It is said to have started in the 1970s, when a band musician in Kobe, Inoue Daisuke, and others made a machine that played backing music for songs.
Now people around the world enjoy "karaoke."

japan-inventions:2.fact: Made for Japanese mobile phones in 1999, and now used all over the world.
japan-inventions:2.about:
It started with 176 emoji that Kurita Shigetaka made for mobile phones. Those emoji are now in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York.
Now there are more than 3,000 kinds of emoji.

japan-inventions:3.fact: Invented by a Japanese company in 1994.
japan-inventions:3.about:
Hara Masahiro of Denso Wave made it to keep track of car parts. The black and white stones of the game Go are said to have given him the idea.
The patent was made free to use, so it spread all over the world.

japan-inventions:4.fact: The world's first high-speed railway. It started running in 1964.
japan-inventions:4.about:
It opened between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka on October 1st, 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics.
The long nose at the front makes the loud boom smaller when it goes into a tunnel. One train's shape was inspired by the beak of a kingfisher.

japan-inventions:5.fact: Japanese scientists invented it and won the Nobel Prize in 2014.
japan-inventions:5.about:
Red and green LEDs already existed, but people said a blue one was "impossible in the 20th century."
Akasaki Isamu, Amano Hiroshi and Nakamura Shūji made it. With all 3 colours, white LED light and big colour screens became possible.

japan-inventions:6.fact: It was born in Osaka in 1958. The idea came from a conveyor belt at a beer factory.
japan-inventions:6.about:
Shiraishi Yoshiaki of Osaka got the idea when he saw a conveyor belt at a beer factory.
Now many shops let you order on a touch screen, and there are conveyor belt sushi restaurants all over the world.

#months1: When is your birthday? Let's learn the names of the months and the events in each one.

months1:0.fact: New Year. The month of osechi food, otoshidama money and the first shrine visit.
months1:0.about:
At New Year, people put up kadomatsu and shimekazari decorations to welcome the New Year god. Each osechi dish carries a wish too.
The English word January comes from Janus, the Roman god of doors.

months1:1.fact: Setsubun. People throw beans and say "Demons out, luck in!"
months1:1.about:
Setsubun, around February 3rd, marks the change of seasons. People throw beans to chase away demons and eat as many beans as their age.
February 14th is Valentine's Day. February has only 28 days (29 in a leap year), so it is the shortest month.

months1:2.fact: Hinamatsuri, a celebration of girls growing up. It is also the month of graduation ceremonies.
months1:2.about:
March 3rd is Hinamatsuri. People put out hina dolls and eat hishi-mochi and hina-arare.
In Japan it is the last month of the school year, with graduation ceremonies. The English word March comes from Mars, the Roman god of war.

months1:3.fact: Cherry blossom viewing and school entrance ceremonies. The new school year begins.
months1:3.about:
In Japan, the new school year starts this month. Many schools hold their entrance ceremony under the cherry blossoms.
April 1st is April Fools' Day. All over the world, it is a day when you can play small jokes.

months1:4.fact: May 5th is Children's Day. People fly carp streamers.
months1:4.about:
On Children's Day, May 5th, people put up carp streamers and eat kashiwa-mochi. They wish for children to grow up strong like carp.
There is a long holiday called Golden Week.

months1:5.fact: The rainy season. Hydrangeas bloom beautifully.
months1:5.about:
It is the rainy season, so there are lots of rainy days. Snails and hydrangeas love this month. The hydrangea is Nagasaki City's flower too.
June is the only month with no national holidays in Japan.

#months2: When is your birthday? Let's look at the events in the second half of the year.

months2:0.fact: Tanabata. People write wishes on strips of paper and hang them on bamboo.
months2:0.about:
July 7th is Tanabata. It comes from a Chinese legend that Orihime and Hikoboshi can meet only once a year.
The English word July comes from the name of Julius Caesar of Rome.

months2:1.fact: Summer holidays and fireworks festivals. Families get together for Obon.
months2:1.about:
The month of summer holidays. Lots of people go to fireworks festivals, summer festivals, the beach or the mountains.
At Obon, people hold events to welcome the spirits of their ancestors. The English word August comes from the Roman emperor Augustus.

months2:2.fact: Moon-viewing. People put out dango and pampas grass and look at the moon.
months2:2.about:
At the full moon viewing, people offer dango and pampas grass and look at the moon. In Japan, people see "a rabbit making mochi" in the moon's patterns.
The English word September first meant "seventh" in Latin, because long ago the calendar started in March.

months2:3.fact: Nagasaki Kunchi and Halloween. Some schools have sports day too.
months2:3.about:
Nagasaki Kunchi is held from October 7th to 9th. Dragon dances and boat shows fill the city with excitement.
October 31st is Halloween. People put out pumpkin lanterns, and children get sweets by saying "Trick or treat!"

months2:4.fact: The season when maple leaves turn red.
months2:4.about:
The season when the trees on the mountains turn red and yellow. At Shichi-Go-San, families celebrate their children growing up.
November 3rd is Culture Day, and November 23rd is Labour Thanksgiving Day.

months2:5.fact: Christmas and New Year's Eve. The last month of the year.
months2:5.about:
December 25th is Christmas. December 31st is New Year's Eve, when people eat toshikoshi soba and listen to the temple bells.
At the end of the year, people do a big clean so their homes are fresh for the new year.

#festivals-world: All over the world there are colourful festivals.

festivals-world:0.fact: New Year in China and other countries. Children get money in red envelopes.
festivals-world:0.about:
The lunar New Year celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and other countries. It falls between late January and mid-February.
Red is the colour of good luck. Families eat dumplings together and set off firecrackers. Nagasaki's Lantern Festival is a Spring Festival celebration too.

festivals-world:1.fact: A spring festival in India where people throw coloured powder at each other.
festivals-world:1.about: A festival in India that celebrates the arrival of spring. It is called the "festival of colours," and everyone, young or old, throws coloured powder and water at each other.

festivals-world:2.fact: Brazil. People dance the samba in bright costumes.
festivals-world:2.about: One of the biggest festivals in the world, held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Samba schools compete in huge parades to show the best dancing and the most beautiful costumes.

festivals-world:3.fact: Spain. The whole town throws tomatoes at each other.
festivals-world:3.about: It is held every year on the last Wednesday of August in a town in Spain called Buñol. More than 100 tonnes of tomatoes are thrown in about 1 hour.

festivals-world:4.fact: New Year in Thailand. People celebrate by splashing water on each other.
festivals-world:4.about:
Thai New Year (around April 13th to 15th). It began as an event where people poured water over Buddha statues and the hands of elders to purify them.
Now there are water fights all over town. It is a festival in the hottest time of the year.

festivals-world:5.fact: It is said to come from an old festival in Ireland.
festivals-world:5.about:
It comes from an old festival that celebrated the autumn harvest and chased away bad things.
Children dress up, visit houses in the neighbourhood and get sweets by saying "Trick or treat!" A pumpkin lantern is called a "jack-o'-lantern."

festivals-world:6.fact: December 25th. A winter celebration all over the world.
festivals-world:6.about:
December 25th. Each country celebrates differently: in Australia, at the beach in summer; in Finland, at Santa Claus Village.
Eating cake and chicken at Christmas is a custom found only in Japan.

#world-dishes: What would you like? Let's go on a food tour of famous dishes from around the world.

world-dishes:0.fact: It was born in Naples, Italy.
world-dishes:0.about: A dish born in Naples, Italy. People say the "Margherita," with tomato, mozzarella and basil, shows the red, white and green of the Italian flag.

world-dishes:1.fact: It became popular in America. Its name comes from Hamburg, a city in Germany.
world-dishes:1.about:
It is said to come from a meat dish from the port city of Hamburg in Germany. In America, the style of putting it in a bun spread.
The Sasebo burger from Nagasaki is famous too.

world-dishes:2.fact: A Mexican dish. You put fillings in a corn wrap.
world-dishes:2.about:
A Mexican dish where you put meat and vegetables in a thin wrap made of corn flour, called a "tortilla."
You hold it in your hands to eat it.

world-dishes:3.fact: A dish from India. It uses lots of spices.
world-dishes:3.about:
In India, people use many kinds of spices in their everyday cooking, and the taste is different in every home.
Japan's thick curry rice comes from a dish that came from Britain in the Meiji period.

world-dishes:4.fact: A Spanish dish. Rice and seafood are cooked in a big pan.
world-dishes:4.about:
A dish from the Valencia area of Spain. Rice is cooked with seafood or meat in a big, flat pan.
The yellow colour comes from a spice called "saffron."

world-dishes:5.fact: A Vietnamese noodle dish made with rice-flour noodles.
world-dishes:5.about:
A Vietnamese dish of rice-flour noodles in beef or chicken soup.
You add herbs and lime yourself to change the taste. Many people eat it for breakfast.

world-dishes:6.fact: A French bread. Its name means "crescent moon" in French.
world-dishes:6.about:
Bread baked with many layers of butter folded inside. Its name means "crescent moon" in French.
It is a classic French breakfast.

world-dishes:7.fact: A British dish: fried fish and potatoes.
world-dishes:7.about:
Fried white fish with fried potatoes (called "chips" in the UK).
Long ago it was sold wrapped in newspaper. People eat it with vinegar on top.

world-dishes:8.fact: A Chinese dish. In China, boiled dumplings are the classic.
world-dishes:8.about:
In China, many families eat dumplings at New Year. Their shape looks like old money, so people say they bring wealth.
In China, boiled dumplings are popular, and in Japan, fried gyōza are popular.

#sweets: I like chocolate. Here are the secrets of sweet things.

sweets:0.fact: It is made from cacao beans. In Mexico long ago, it was a bitter drink.
sweets:0.about:
It is made by roasting and grinding cacao beans and mixing them with sugar and milk. In Mexico long ago, cacao beans were even used as money.
Much of the cacao in the chocolate we eat in Japan comes from Ghana.

sweets:1.fact: It was first sold in Japan in 1869, in Yokohama.
sweets:1.about:
It is made by chilling milk, sugar, eggs and other things while mixing them. Mixing adds air and makes it smooth.
In Japan, May 9th is "Ice Cream Day."

sweets:2.fact: The machine for making cotton candy was invented by a dentist!
sweets:2.about:
In the middle of the machine, melted sugar spins around and turns into thin threads that look like cotton.
It became popular at the World's Fair in America in 1904.

sweets:3.fact: Its name comes from the Dutch word for "little cake."
sweets:3.about: A snack baked from flour, butter and sugar. In the UK, people often call them biscuits.

sweets:4.about:
Japanese purin is a "custard pudding," made by steaming eggs and milk and topping it with caramel.
Long ago, British puddings were steamed dishes that could even have meat in them.

sweets:5.fact: The hole in the middle helps the dough cook through quickly.
sweets:5.about: Sweet fried bread. It has a hole in the middle so the heat reaches the centre of the dough quickly.

sweets:6.fact: Blowing out candles on your birthday is a custom all over the world.
sweets:6.about:
Japanese Christmas cake (strawberry shortcake) is a custom found only in Japan.
Putting candles on a birthday cake and blowing them out is said to have spread from Germany.

#fruits: What fruit do you like? Let's find the secrets of fruit.

fruits:0.fact: More than half of Japan's apples are grown in Aomori.
fruits:0.about:
There are said to be more than 7,500 kinds in the world. In Japan, "Fuji" is grown the most, and Fuji is popular around the world too.
There is lots of nutrition near the skin of an apple.

fruits:1.fact: A banana plant is not a tree. It is a giant kind of grass.
fruits:1.about:
A banana plant isn't a tree but a big kind of grass. Lots of bananas grow on one "bunch."
Most bananas eaten in Japan come by ship from warm countries like the Philippines.

fruits:2.fact: The little seeds on the outside are actually the real fruits.
fruits:2.about:
The red part is a swollen part of the flower called the "receptacle." Each little dot on the outside is a real fruit with a seed inside.
Japan has many kinds, like "Amaou" (Fukuoka) and "Tochiotome" (Tochigi).

fruits:3.fact: More than 90% of it is water. It is the perfect summer fruit.
fruits:3.about:
Its home is the deserts of Africa. It is more than 90% water, so it is perfect for staying hydrated in summer.
"Suikawari," a summer game where you try to split a watermelon blindfolded, is lots of fun too.

fruits:4.fact: Lots are grown in Wakayama and Ehime.
fruits:4.about:
A classic Japanese winter fruit. Eating mikan under a kotatsu is a typical Japanese winter scene.
In English it is called a mandarin orange or a satsuma (from Satsuma in Kagoshima).

fruits:5.fact: It takes about 2 years for one fruit to grow.
fruits:5.about:
A pineapple fruit is made of lots of small flowers grown together.
In Japan they are grown in Okinawa. The English name pineapple comes from "an apple that looks like a pine cone."

fruits:6.about:
The "queen of fruits," grown in India for more than 4,000 years.
In Japan it is grown in Miyazaki and Okinawa, and the red "apple mango" is popular.

fruits:7.fact: They are also made into juice and dried grapes (raisins).
fruits:7.about:
Grapes are grown all over the world and are also made into juice and raisins.
In Japan, Yamanashi grows the most. Seedless grapes and Shine Muscat grapes, which you can eat with the skin, are popular.

#vegetables: Surprising secrets of vegetables. Maybe you'll start to like a vegetable you hate?

vegetables:0.fact: It comes from South America. In botany, it is a "fruit."
vegetables:0.about:
Its home is the Andes in South America. When it first came to Europe, people grew it just to look at.
The red colour, "lycopene," is said to be good for your body.

vegetables:1.fact: Long ago there were purple and yellow carrots too.
vegetables:1.about:
Its orange colour, "carotene," has a name like the English word carrot.
In your body, carotene turns into vitamin A, which helps keep your eyes healthy.

vegetables:2.fact: A vegetable that comes from the Andes mountains in South America.
vegetables:2.about:
Born in the Andes of South America. We eat the "stem" that swells up underground.
Fries, potato chips, curry, nikujaga… it is one of the most eaten vegetables in the world.

vegetables:3.fact: An ear of corn has the same number of silk threads as kernels.
vegetables:3.about:
People started growing corn in Mexico thousands of years ago. Along with rice and wheat, it is one of the world's three great grains.
Popcorn is made when kernels of a special kind are heated and the water inside bursts out.

vegetables:4.fact: The part we eat is the flower buds.
vegetables:4.about:
A vegetable made of lots of buds. We eat it before the flowers open.
It has lots of vitamin C, said to be even more than a lemon.

vegetables:5.fact: When you cut it, something comes out that stings your eyes and makes you cry.
vegetables:5.about:
When you cut it, a substance comes out that stings your eyes and makes tears come. If you chill it before cutting, you cry less.
It gets sweet when you fry it, and it is used in curry and hamburg steak.

vegetables:6.fact: Its Japanese name, "kabocha," is said to come from the name of a country, "Cambodia."
vegetables:6.about:
People say it got the name "kabocha" because the Portuguese brought it to Japan from Cambodia.
There is an old saying that if you eat kabocha on the winter solstice, you won't catch a cold.

vegetables:7.fact: If you let it grow until it turns red, it becomes a sweet red pepper.
vegetables:7.about:
Green peppers and paprika are the same kind of plant. A green pepper is a fruit that isn't ripe yet.
If you cut it thin or fry it in oil, it is less bitter.

#ball-sports: What sport do you like? Let's compare team sizes and rules.

ball-sports:0.fact: 11 players on a team. The World Cup is held once every 4 years.
ball-sports:0.about:
The most popular sport in the world. Only the goalkeeper can use their hands.
In the UK it is called football. Japan's men's team is "Samurai Blue," and the women's team is "Nadeshiko Japan."

ball-sports:1.fact: 9 players on a team. It was born in America and is very popular in Japan too.
ball-sports:1.about:
The batter hits the ball thrown by the pitcher and runs around the bases to score.
In Japan, the summer Kōshien tournament is hugely popular. Ohtani Shohei amazed the world as a "two-way player," great at both pitching and batting.

ball-sports:2.fact: 5 players on a team. At first, peach baskets were used as the goals.
ball-sports:2.about:
In 1891, an American teacher invented it as a sport people could play indoors in winter.
The hoop is 3.05 m high. Taking 3 or more steps while holding the ball is a foul.

ball-sports:3.fact: 6 players on a team. It was born in America in 1895.
ball-sports:3.about:
You send the ball back to the other side within 3 touches without letting it drop.
Japan's women's team won gold at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and were called the "Witches of the Orient."

ball-sports:4.fact: 15 players on a team. You must not throw the ball forwards.
ball-sports:4.about:
You run holding an oval ball, and putting it down past the other team's goal line is a "try," worth 5 points.
In 2019, the World Cup was held in Japan. After the match, both teams praise each other. This "no side" spirit is valued.

ball-sports:5.about:
A sport where you hit a ball back and forth with rackets. The scoring is strange: 0, 15, 30, 40.
Wimbledon in the UK is the oldest tournament in the world.

ball-sports:6.fact: It is also called "ping-pong." China and Japan are strong at it.
ball-sports:6.about:
A sport where you hit a small ball back and forth with paddles. The ball can go faster than 100 km per hour.
In Japan, everyone from children to older people enjoys it.

ball-sports:7.fact: A shuttlecock has been recorded going faster than 500 km per hour.
ball-sports:7.about:
A sport where you hit a feathered shuttlecock back and forth. Right after it is hit, it is the fastest of any racket sport.
Each shuttlecock uses 16 goose or duck feathers.

#olympics: Once every 4 years, athletes from all over the world gather for a festival of sport.

olympics:0.fact: The 5 rings stand for the 5 continents of the world.
olympics:0.about:
People say the 5 rings (blue, yellow, black, green and red) on a white background can show the colours of almost every flag in the world.
The modern Olympics began in Athens, Greece, in 1896.

olympics:1.fact: It began about 2,800 years ago in Olympia, Greece.
olympics:1.about:
It began in Olympia in ancient Greece as a festival to honour the gods.
The first event was just one short race of about 190 m.

olympics:2.fact: It is actually made mostly of silver, with gold on the surface.
olympics:2.about: 1st place gets gold, 2nd place silver and 3rd place bronze. The medals for the Tokyo 2020 Games were made from metal from old mobile phones and other things.

olympics:3.about: A race of 42.195 km. Its name comes from the legend of an ancient Greek soldier who ran from Marathon to Athens to tell of a victory.

olympics:4.fact: A sport born in Japan. It became an Olympic sport at the 1964 Tokyo Games.
olympics:4.about:
Kanō Jigorō created it in 1882. "Softness overcomes strength": using your opponent's power is more important than being strong.
A match "begins and ends with a bow." Now it is done all over the world, and in English it is "judo" too.

olympics:5.fact: It became an Olympic sport for the first time at the Tokyo 2020 Games.
olympics:5.about: It was held for the first time at the Tokyo 2020 Games, and Japanese teenagers winning gold medals made the news.

olympics:6.fact: Games for athletes with disabilities. They are held in the same year as the Olympics.
olympics:6.about:
World games for athletes with disabilities. There are lots of specially designed sports, like wheelchair basketball, boccia and goalball.
Tokyo hosted them in 1964 and 2021.

#winter-sports: Japan hosted the Winter Olympics in Sapporo in 1972 and in Nagano in 1998.

winter-sports:0.fact: In ski jumping, people fly more than 100 m through the air.
winter-sports:0.about:
A sport where you slide over snow on two boards. There are many events, like jumping, slalom and cross-country.
In Japan, you can enjoy it in places like Hokkaido, Nagano and Niigata.

winter-sports:1.fact: It became an Olympic sport at the 1998 Nagano Games.
winter-sports:1.about: You ride sideways on one board. In the "halfpipe," where riders spin in the air, Japanese athletes have won gold medals.

winter-sports:2.fact: In figure skating, Japanese skaters have won gold medals too.
winter-sports:2.about:
Figure skating is jumping and spinning to music. Speed skating is a race.
Hanyu Yuzuru of Japan won gold at two Olympics in a row.

winter-sports:3.fact: You slide a stone that weighs nearly 20 kg and aim for the middle of the target.
winter-sports:3.about:
You slide stones across the ice, and the one closest to the centre of the target wins. Players sweep the ice with brushes to control how the stone moves.
It is called "chess on ice" because planning is so important.

winter-sports:4.fact: The puck can go faster than 150 km per hour.
winter-sports:4.about:
A sport where you hit a disc called a "puck" with a stick into the other team's goal.
In Canada it is the national sport.

winter-sports:5.fact: You lie on your back on a sled and slide down an icy track.
winter-sports:5.about: You lie on your back and slide down an icy track feet first. There is no steering wheel and no brake: you steer by moving your body.

#jobs-town: What do you want to be? There are lots of jobs in town.

jobs-town:0.fact: A job where you cure illnesses and injuries.
jobs-town:0.about:
At a hospital, doctors find out what is causing an illness or injury and treat it. There are many kinds, like internal medicine, surgery and paediatrics (children's doctors).
To become a doctor in Japan, you study at university for 6 years.

jobs-town:1.fact: A job where you teach children school subjects and how to live well.
jobs-town:1.about:
Teachers don't just give lessons. They also watch over children as they grow. Elementary school teachers teach almost every subject.
In English lessons, there are also ALT teachers from other countries.

jobs-town:2.fact: A job where you put out fires and save people. They rush out when you call 119.
jobs-town:2.about:
Firefighters don't only put out fires. Rescuing people in accidents and disasters and driving ambulances are also their jobs.
They wait in shifts 24 hours a day so they can go out as soon as someone calls 119.

jobs-town:3.fact: A job where you keep the town safe.
jobs-town:3.about:
A job keeping the town safe. At a police box (kōban), officers give directions, look after lost property and watch over road safety.
If you call 110, you reach the police.

jobs-town:4.fact: A job where you cure animals' illnesses and injuries.
jobs-town:4.about:
An animal doctor who looks after not only dogs and cats but also farm cows and zoo animals.
Animals can't say "it hurts," so watching them carefully is important.

jobs-town:5.fact: A job where you bake bread from early in the morning.
jobs-town:5.about:
A baker's morning starts very early. They knead and bake dough before sunrise.
There are lots of kinds of bread, like anpan and melon pan, which were born in Japan.

jobs-town:6.fact: A job where you grow flowers and make bouquets.
jobs-town:6.about:
Florists buy flowers, change their water so they last longer, and make bouquets for celebrations and presents.
Flowers have meanings (the "language of flowers"), so florists help people share their feelings.

jobs-town:7.fact: A job where you grow rice and vegetables.
jobs-town:7.about:
A job growing rice, vegetables and fruit. Farmers look after their crops all year, watching the weather and the soil.
Many farmers in Japan are getting older, and new kinds of farming with drones and robots are starting.

jobs-town:8.fact: A job where you carry people around town safely.
jobs-town:8.about:
A job driving safely along a set route at set times. Drivers take extra care when older people and children get on and off.
Buses are an important way for people in town to get around.

#jobs-dream: I want to be ___. What job would you like to do in the future?

jobs-dream:0.fact: A job where you do experiments and research in space.
jobs-dream:0.about:
On the space station, astronauts do experiments, fix machines and observe the Earth.
Japanese astronauts pass JAXA's tests and train for years before going to space. English is important too.

jobs-dream:1.fact: A job where you fly planes and carry people around the world.
jobs-dream:1.about:
A job flying lots of people safely through the sky. The captain and the co-pilot fly the plane together.
Pilots all over the world use English to talk to each other in the sky.

jobs-dream:2.fact: A job where you make delicious food.
jobs-dream:2.about:
A job cooking in restaurants and hotels. Cooks can specialise in Japanese, Chinese, French, Italian food and more.
They care about how food looks and keeping it safe, not just how it tastes.

jobs-dream:3.fact: A job where you play matches for a professional team.
jobs-dream:3.about:
They practise every day with a professional team and play in matches. Many Japanese players go from the J.League to leagues overseas.
Eating and sleeping well to build their bodies is part of the job too.

jobs-dream:4.fact: A job where you cheer people up with songs.
jobs-dream:4.about:
A job sharing feelings through songs. Singers don't only practise singing but also dancing and how to talk on stage.
Some are singer-songwriters who write their own songs.

jobs-dream:5.fact: A job drawing manga. Japanese manga are read all over the world.
jobs-dream:5.about:
Manga artists think up stories, plan the panels and draw the pictures. For a weekly magazine, they may draw nearly 20 pages in a week.
Today many manga artists draw on tablets.

jobs-dream:6.about:
Programmers write instructions (programs) for computers to make games, apps and robots work.
Elementary schools have programming lessons too. Programming languages are based on English.

jobs-dream:7.about:
Zookeepers make and give food, clean the animals' rooms and check how the animals are every day.
They also raise baby animals and teach visitors about animals.

jobs-dream:8.fact: A job where you solve the world's mysteries through experiments and research.
jobs-dream:8.about:
Scientists do experiments and observations again and again to discover things no one knows yet.
They study all sorts of things, like living things, space, medicine and robots. More than 20 Japanese people have won the Nobel Prize.

#vehicles: Go straight. Turn right. Let's look at all sorts of vehicles from around the world.

vehicles:0.fact: The fastest Shinkansen runs at 320 km per hour.
vehicles:0.about:
No passenger has ever died in a Shinkansen accident, so it is one of the safest railways in the world.
In 2022, the Nishi-Kyushu Shinkansen "Kamome" opened to Nagasaki.

vehicles:1.fact: Japan's maglev set a world record of 603 km per hour in 2015.
vehicles:1.about: A train that floats above the track using the power of magnets. In the 2030s it is planned to link Tokyo and Nagoya in about 40 minutes.

vehicles:2.fact: In 1903, the Wright brothers flew a plane for the first time.
vehicles:2.about: Air flowing over the big wings makes "lift," which lets even a heavy plane float in the sky.

vehicles:3.fact: It can stay perfectly still in the air.
vehicles:3.about: It flies by spinning the big blades on top (the rotor). "Doctor helicopters" that carry people to hospital do important work too.

vehicles:4.fact: The biggest ships in the world are about 400 m long.
vehicles:4.about: Nagasaki is a shipbuilding city. Many of the world's big ships have been built at Nagasaki's shipyards.

vehicles:5.fact: It started about 200 years ago as a bicycle with no pedals.
vehicles:5.about: There are said to be more than 60 million bicycles in Japan. Wear a helmet when you ride.

vehicles:6.fact: When its ladder is stretched out, it can reach tall buildings.
vehicles:6.about: A ladder truck can stretch its ladder more than 40 m. Fire engines are red so that they stand out.

vehicles:7.fact: A vehicle that can carry lots of people at once.
vehicles:7.about: Nagasaki has lots of hills, so buses are an important way for everyone to get around.

#instruments: Can you play the piano? Let's look at all kinds of instruments from around the world.

instruments:0.fact: It has 88 keys, white ones and black ones.
instruments:0.about: Cristofori of Italy made it around 1700. It can play both loud (forte) and soft (piano), so its first name was "pianoforte."

instruments:1.about: An acoustic guitar makes its sound ring through its wooden body, and an electric guitar makes its sound louder with electricity.

instruments:2.fact: You make sounds by rubbing its 4 strings with a bow.
instruments:2.about: Violins made more than 300 years ago by Stradivari of Italy are still said to be the best instruments in the world.

instruments:3.fact: You press 3 valves to change the pitch.
instruments:3.about: Trumpets were even found in the tomb of the Egyptian king Tutankhamun, from more than 3,300 years ago.

instruments:4.fact: A recorder you learn at elementary school. People in Europe have played it for hundreds of years.
instruments:4.about: Japanese elementary school students start learning it around 3rd grade. You cover the holes with your fingers to change the pitch.

instruments:5.fact: One of the oldest instruments, found all over the world.
instruments:5.about: Drums are found all over the world and are one of the oldest instruments. Japanese taiko drums are stars at festivals.

instruments:6.fact: A Japanese instrument where you pluck 3 strings with a plectrum.
instruments:6.about: A Japanese instrument with 3 strings. It is said to come from the Okinawan sanshin. Tsugaru shamisen is famous for its powerful sound.

#school-subjects: What do you study on Monday? Can you say the names of school subjects in English?

school-subjects:0.fact: A subject where you learn to read and write Japanese and enjoy stories.
school-subjects:0.about:
You learn hiragana, katakana and kanji, read stories and explanations, and write compositions.
Elementary school students in Japan learn 1,026 kanji.

school-subjects:1.fact: A subject where you think about numbers and shapes.
school-subjects:1.about:
You learn ways of thinking that are useful in daily life, like calculating, shapes, graphs and units.
In English it is called math (USA) or maths (UK).

school-subjects:2.fact: A subject where you investigate living things and how nature works.
school-subjects:2.about: You investigate the wonders of nature, like plants and animals, electricity and magnets, weather and stars, through experiments and observation.

school-subjects:3.fact: A subject where you learn about life in your area, in Japan and around the world.
school-subjects:3.about: You learn about the jobs and lives of people in your area, the geography and history of Japan, and the countries of the world.

school-subjects:4.fact: A subject where you learn a language for talking with people around the world.
school-subjects:4.about:
More than 1.5 billion people in the world are said to use English. In Japan, children study it as a school subject from 5th grade.
The secret to getting better is to try speaking without being afraid of mistakes.

school-subjects:5.fact: A subject where you sing and play instruments.
school-subjects:5.about: You sing, play the recorder and keyboard harmonica, and listen to all sorts of music.

school-subjects:6.fact: A subject where you draw pictures and make things.
school-subjects:6.about: You draw pictures and make works from clay, paper and wood. It is a subject where you turn your ideas into shapes.

school-subjects:7.fact: A subject where you move your body and enjoy sports.
school-subjects:7.about: Short for Physical Education. You make your body stronger with vaulting boxes, skipping, swimming, ball games and more.

school-subjects:8.fact: A subject where you learn life skills like cooking and sewing.
school-subjects:8.about: A subject you start in 5th grade. You learn useful things for daily life, like cooking rice and miso soup and sewing on buttons.

#school-events: What's your best memory? Let's look back on our school memories.

school-events:0.fact: The start of a new school life. It is cherry blossom season.
school-events:0.about:
A ceremony to welcome new first-graders. In Japan the school year starts in April, but in America and many European countries it starts in September.
First-graders carrying their randoseru school bags are a typical spring scene in Japan.

school-events:1.fact: Everyone goes out together and eats their packed lunches.
school-events:1.about: The class goes out to a park, a zoo or a museum. Packed lunches and snacks are part of the fun.

school-events:2.fact: Relays and tug-of-war. The school splits into a red team and a white team.
school-events:2.about: Japanese sports days are unusual in other countries. Everyone splits into a red team and a white team and works together in tug-of-war, relays, dances and more.

school-events:3.fact: A big memory for 6th graders. You stay overnight with your friends.
school-events:3.about: The last big event of elementary school: you stay overnight with your friends and visit famous places in another prefecture.

school-events:4.fact: Classes perform songs and play music together.
school-events:4.about: Each class or grade performs a choir song or plays instruments together. Practising together brings everyone closer.

school-events:5.fact: With six years of memories in your heart, you move on to junior high school.
school-events:5.about:
The end of six years at elementary school. You receive your diploma and go on to junior high school.
If someone asks you, "What do you want to do in junior high school?", what will you say?

#inventions: Even things we use every day started with someone's invention.

inventions:0.fact: About 1,900 years ago, a way of making it spread in China.
inventions:0.about:
Cai Lun of China is said to have made paper that was easy to write on from tree bark and old cloth, and spread the idea.
Before paper, people wrote on strips of bamboo, animal skins, stone and other things.

inventions:1.fact: Around 1450, Gutenberg in Germany made a printing press.
inventions:1.about:
Gutenberg made "movable type printing" practical: each letter was made as a metal piece, and the pieces were lined up.
Books could be made quickly and in large numbers, so knowledge spread around the world.

inventions:2.fact: In 1876, Bell got the patent for the telephone.
inventions:2.about:
Alexander Graham Bell of America got the patent for the telephone. The first words spoken on it were "Mr. Watson, come here."
Telephones started in Japan in 1890.

inventions:3.fact: Edison made a light bulb that shone for a long time and spread it around the world.
inventions:3.about:
Edison tried thousands of materials, and a bulb using bamboo from Kyoto, Japan, kept shining for more than 1,000 hours.
Today, energy-saving LEDs are the most common.

inventions:4.fact: In 1886, Benz in Germany made a car that ran on petrol.
inventions:4.about:
In 1888, Benz's wife Bertha drove more than 100 km with their children and showed the world how great cars were.
Today, people are developing electric cars and self-driving cars.

inventions:5.fact: The first computers were as big as a whole room.
inventions:5.about:
"ENIAC," a computer made in 1946, weighed about 30 tonnes. Today's smartphones can calculate much faster.
Computers do all their calculations with just two numbers, 0 and 1.

inventions:6.fact: Galileo found Jupiter's moons with a telescope.
inventions:6.about: The telescope is said to have been invented by a Dutch glasses maker. Galileo improved it and studied the night sky, discovering the bumps on the Moon and four moons of Jupiter.

#town: Where is the station? Go straight. Let's say the names of buildings in town in English.

town:0.fact: Shinjuku Station, the busiest in Japan, is used by millions of people a day.
town:0.about: A place to get on and off trains. Nagasaki Station was rebuilt in 2022, and the Nishi-Kyushu Shinkansen runs from it.

town:1.fact: A place that cures injuries and illnesses. An ambulance comes when you call 119.
town:1.about: A place you go when you are hurt or ill. Big hospitals have many different departments.

town:2.fact: A place where you can borrow books for free. Japan has more than 3,000 public libraries.
town:2.about: A place where you can borrow books for free. You can use it to look things up and study too.

town:3.fact: A place for sending letters and parcels. Postboxes in Japan are red.
town:3.about: You can send letters and parcels and buy stamps. Japan's postal service started in 1871.

town:4.fact: Japan's "KOBAN" system has been copied in other countries too.
town:4.about: Japan's police boxes keep people safe right in their neighbourhoods, and they are known in other countries as "KOBAN."

town:5.fact: A place where you can play and rest.
town:5.about: A place where you can play, exercise and rest. Big parks also become shelters in a disaster.

town:6.fact: A shop where you can buy food and everyday things all in one place.
town:6.about: A shop where you can buy food and everyday things all at once. Taking your own bag is a good way to cut down on plastic bags.

town:7.fact: Many are open 24 hours. There are more than 50,000 in Japan.
town:7.about: Open 24 hours, they sell food, and you can also send parcels, take out money and do lots of other things. They are Japanese shops that surprise visitors from other countries.

town:8.fact: Fire engines and firefighters wait here, ready to go out at any time.
town:8.about: A place where fire engines and ambulances wait. Firefighters work in shifts 24 hours a day.

#stationery: Do you have a pencil? Even the stationery we use every day has secrets.

stationery:0.fact: One pencil is said to be able to draw a line nearly 50 km long.
stationery:0.about:
The lead is graphite and clay mixed together and baked. In HB, H means hard and B means black.
People say many pencils around the world are yellow because long ago the best graphite came from China, and pencils were painted yellow, the colour of the Chinese emperor.

stationery:1.fact: Long ago, people even used bread to rub out writing.
stationery:1.about: In English it is called an eraser (USA) or a rubber (UK). An eraser removes writing because the black bits from the pencil stick to the eraser instead.

stationery:2.fact: You use it to measure length and draw straight lines.
stationery:2.about: A 30 cm ruler is about the same length as "1 foot" (about 30 cm), an old British unit of length.

stationery:3.fact: Two blades rub together to cut things.
stationery:3.about: In English it is always "scissors" (plural), because there are two blades. You say "a pair of scissors."

stationery:4.fact: The glue stick is said to have been invented after someone saw a lipstick.
stationery:4.about: A German company made it in 1969. When the glue dries, the papers stick together firmly.

stationery:5.fact: Japanese notebooks are popular around the world because they are so easy to use.
stationery:5.about: Japanese school notebooks come with lots of different grids and lines, and they are a popular souvenir with visitors from other countries.

stationery:6.fact: Crayons are made by mixing wax with coloured powder.
stationery:6.about: The word comes from "crayon," the French word for pencil. They are made of wax, so you can even draw on shiny paper.

stationery:7.fact: In Japan it is called a "hotchkiss," after a company name. In English it is a stapler.
stationery:7.about: The metal pieces that hold paper together are called staples. The Japanese name "hotchkiss" is said to come from an American company called Hotchkiss.

stationery:8.fact: In English it is a pencil case. You keep all kinds of stationery in it.
stationery:8.about: Japanese pencil cases come in many styles, like boxes that open with a magnet and soft pouches.

#clothes: What's this? It's a T-shirt. Here are the names and secrets of clothes.

clothes:0.fact: It's called a T-shirt because it looks like the letter T when you spread it out.
clothes:0.about: It was first underwear, but from around the 1950s it spread as everyday clothing.

clothes:1.fact: They were born in America in 1873 as strong trousers for workers.
clothes:1.about:
A cloth from the French town of Nîmes ("serge de Nîmes") gave denim its name.
Kojima in Kurashiki, Okayama, is the home of Japanese jeans.

clothes:2.fact: A cap has a brim at the front, and a hat has a brim all the way around.
clothes:2.about: The yellow hats of Japanese elementary school children are a road safety idea: they make children easy to see from cars.

clothes:3.fact: Their rubber soles make no sound, so the name comes from "sneak" (to walk quietly).
clothes:3.about: In the UK they are called trainers. Choosing shoes that fit your feet is important for avoiding injuries.

clothes:4.fact: It is knitted from yarn. In English it is also called a jumper.
clothes:4.about: Sweaters made of sheep's wool are warm because air is trapped between the fibres.

clothes:5.fact: A coat that keeps out water, worn on rainy days.
clothes:5.about: In the 1820s, Mr. Macintosh of Britain invented a waterproof cloth using rubber.

clothes:6.fact: In English you always say "a pair of socks."
clothes:6.about: Socks come in twos, so in English you say "a pair of socks."

clothes:7.fact: Gloves without separate fingers are called mittens.
clothes:7.about: Gloves have 5 separate fingers, and mittens have only the thumb separate. Gloves come in twos too: "a pair of gloves."

#feelings: How are you? I'm happy! Let's say our feelings in English.

feelings:0.fact: People say that when you smile, the people around you smile more easily too.
feelings:0.about: The feeling you get when you are glad or having fun. A smile is a greeting understood all over the world.

feelings:1.fact: People say tears can also help calm your feelings.
feelings:1.about: Everyone feels sad sometimes. Talking to friends or family can make you feel lighter.

feelings:2.fact: People say that when you're angry, waiting 6 seconds helps you calm down.
feelings:2.about: Anger is a sign from your heart that you want to protect something important to you. Take a deep breath and try to share your feelings with words.

feelings:3.fact: Elementary school children should sleep 9 to 12 hours a day.
feelings:3.about: People say that looking at smartphone or game screens before bed makes it harder to fall asleep.

feelings:4.fact: When you're hungry, your tummy sometimes rumbles.
feelings:4.about: When you are hungry, your brain sends a signal saying "I want energy!"

feelings:5.fact: When you rest your body, you get your energy back.
feelings:5.about: After lots of exercise or study, it is important to rest well too.

feelings:6.fact: There are lots of answers to "How are you?" besides "I'm fine."
feelings:6.about: There are many answers to "How are you?": I'm fine. I'm good. I'm great! I'm OK. and more.

feelings:7.fact: When you're nervous, your heart beats faster than usual.
feelings:7.about: It is natural to feel your heart pounding before a presentation or a match. Everyone gets nervous.

#colors-shapes: What color do you like? Let's look at the wonders of colours and shapes.

colors-shapes:0.fact: The colour of Japanese postboxes and fire engines. It stands out, so it catches your attention.
colors-shapes:0.about: Red stands out even from far away. It is used as a warning colour, like on "stop" signs and red traffic lights.

colors-shapes:1.fact: The sky and sea look blue because blue light spreads out easily.
colors-shapes:1.about: The colour of the sky and sea. There are few blue foods in nature, so blue is said to be a colour that makes you less hungry.

colors-shapes:2.fact: It is easy to see from far away, so it is used for school hats and traffic lights.
colors-shapes:2.about: It can be seen well from far away, so it is used for safety, like on school hats and yellow lines.

colors-shapes:3.fact: In Japanese, a green traffic light is called "blue," but its real colour is green.
colors-shapes:3.about: In Japanese, some green things are called "blue (ao)," like "ao-shingō" (green light) and "ao-ringo" (green apple).

colors-shapes:4.fact: Manhole covers are round so they can't fall into the hole.
colors-shapes:4.about: A shape that is the same width from every direction. Tyres and coins are circles too.

colors-shapes:5.fact: Triangles hold their shape well, so they are used in bridges and steel towers.
colors-shapes:5.about: A triangle is a strong shape that doesn't change shape easily when pushed. Tokyo Tower and other structures are built with "trusses," groups of triangles.

colors-shapes:6.fact: In English, a 正方形 is a square and a 長方形 is a rectangle.
colors-shapes:6.about: In English, a 正方形 is a square and a 長方形 is a rectangle. Japanese tatami mats are rectangles.

colors-shapes:7.fact: A honeybee's nest is made of hexagons, a strong shape that fits together with no gaps.
colors-shapes:7.about: A beehive uses hexagons because they fit together with no gaps, so the bees can make lots of rooms with little wax. A soccer ball has hexagons on it too.

colors-shapes:8.fact: You can draw a star with just 5 lines.
colors-shapes:8.about: Stars are used on flags all over the world. The flag of the USA has 50 stars.

#human-body: It's your own body, but there's so much you don't know. Let's peek at its secrets.

human-body:0.fact: It beats about 100,000 times a day, sending blood all around your body.
human-body:0.about:
Your heart is a bag of muscle about the size of your fist. It beats about 3 billion times in a lifetime.
Blood goes all the way around your body in about 1 minute. When you exercise, your heart beats faster.

human-body:1.fact: An adult's body has about 206 bones. Babies have even more.
human-body:1.about:
The biggest bone is in your thigh, and the smallest is in your ear, about the size of a grain of rice.
Bones are alive, and they can join back together when they break. The calcium in milk and small fish makes them strong.

human-body:2.fact: It thinks, remembers and gives the orders that move your body.
human-body:2.about:
Your brain weighs about 1.3 kg. That's only about 2% of your body weight, but it uses about 20% of your body's energy.
While you sleep, it sorts out and stores what you learned that day.

human-body:3.fact: You blink about 15 to 20 times a minute.
human-body:3.about:
Light that enters your eye makes a picture at the back of your eye, like a camera, and it is sent to your brain so you can "see."
After looking at things close up for a long time, look far away to rest your eyes.

human-body:4.fact: It is amazingly good at telling smells apart. It can tell lots of different smells apart.
human-body:4.about:
Some say the human nose can tell apart a trillion different smells.
Food is harder to taste when you hold your nose, because much of what we taste is really smell.

human-body:5.fact: It senses sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami.
human-body:5.about:
The surface of your tongue has thousands of "taste buds" that sense flavour.
"Umami" is the fifth taste, discovered by Ikeda Kikunae of Japan.

human-body:6.fact: The biggest organ in your body. It protects your body.
human-body:6.about:
Your skin is a barrier that protects your body. An adult's skin spread out would be about as big as one tatami mat.
Old skin slowly comes off and is replaced by new skin.

human-body:7.fact: Your body has more than 600 muscles.
human-body:7.about:
Muscles stretch and shrink to move your bones. Lots of tiny muscles make the expressions on your face too.
When you exercise, your muscles get stronger.

human-body:8.fact: Children have 20 teeth, and adults have 28 to 32.
human-body:8.about:
From about age 6, children's teeth fall out and adult teeth grow in. Adult teeth are precious, because you use them for the rest of your life.
Enamel, on the surface of your teeth, is the hardest part of your body.

#earth-science: What is inside the Earth? Let's learn how volcanoes and earthquakes work.

earth-science:0.fact: The Earth is like a boiled egg: under the shell is the mantle, and in the middle is the "core."
earth-science:0.about:
It is about 6,400 km to the centre of the Earth. The "core" at the centre is said to be about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Even the deepest hole people have ever dug is only about 12 km. There are still lots of mysteries inside the Earth.

earth-science:1.fact: Volcanoes form when melted rock (magma) bursts out from underground. Japan has 111 active volcanoes.
earth-science:1.about:
When magma comes out onto the surface, it becomes "lava." Volcanoes are scary, but they also give us hot springs, rich soil and beautiful views.
Mt. Unzen in Nagasaki is a volcano too.

earth-science:2.fact: Mt. Fuji is a volcano too. It last erupted in 1707.
earth-science:2.about:
It is 3,776 m tall. It sits across Yamanashi and Shizuoka and became a World Cultural Heritage site in 2013.
You can only climb it for about 2 months in summer. The sunrise seen from the top is called "goraikō."

earth-science:3.fact: They happen when huge plates of rock under the ground move. Being prepared every day is important.
earth-science:3.about:
Japan is where 4 plates meet, so it has lots of earthquakes.
In Japan, new buildings are made to stand up to earthquakes. Check your emergency kit and evacuation place with your family.

earth-science:4.fact: Underground water heated by volcanoes. Japan has very many hot springs.
earth-science:4.about:
Japan has more than 27,000 hot spring sources. The hot spring symbol ♨️ is said to have started at Isobe Onsen in Gunma.
Hot spring water has many minerals dissolved in it, so the colours and smells are all different.

earth-science:5.fact: Traces of living things from long, long ago, left in stone.
earth-science:5.about:
Fossils form when living things from long ago get buried and slowly turn to stone over a long time. There are even fossils of footprints and poop.
Studying fossils tells us what the Earth was like long ago.

earth-science:6.fact: The Earth's surface is made of many plates, like a jigsaw puzzle.
earth-science:6.about:
The plates move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Long ago, the continents were all joined together, and that supercontinent is called "Pangaea."

#rocks-gems: Even sparkling gems started out as stones made inside the Earth.

rocks-gems:0.fact: The hardest natural stone on Earth. It is made of carbon, the same as charcoal.
rocks-gems:0.about:
It forms deep underground, more than 150 km down, under great heat and pressure.
It is so hard that diamond powder is used to polish diamonds. It is the birthstone for April.

rocks-gems:1.fact: Red rubies and blue sapphires are actually the same mineral.
rocks-gems:1.about:
Its red colour comes from a tiny bit of something called "chromium." It is the birthstone for July.
Rubies were also used in research on lasers.

rocks-gems:2.fact: It is the same mineral as ruby. When it is any colour except red, it is called sapphire.
rocks-gems:2.about:
Sapphires are famous for being blue, but there are yellow and pink ones too. It is the birthstone for September.
It is very hard, so it is used for the glass of expensive watches.

rocks-gems:3.fact: It stretches very easily: 1 g can be made into a thin thread nearly 3 km long.
rocks-gems:3.about:
Gold doesn't rust, so it stays shiny for thousands of years. Tutankhamun's mask is made of gold.
It is used in electronic parts too, and some gold is recycled from old smartphones.

rocks-gems:4.fact: A gem made inside a shellfish. Japan was the first country in the world to farm pearls.
rocks-gems:4.about:
It forms when something small gets inside a shellfish and the shellfish covers it with many layers of "nacre."
Mikimoto Kōkichi of Mie succeeded in farming pearls in 1893. Nagasaki produces lots of pearls too. It is the birthstone for June.

rocks-gems:5.fact: Jade from Itoigawa in Niigata is Japan's "national stone."
rocks-gems:5.about:
People in the Jōmon period polished jade to make jewellery. Jade from Itoigawa in Niigata has been found in faraway areas too.
It has also been treasured in China since ancient times.

rocks-gems:6.fact: A clear stone. It is used in clocks and watches too.
rocks-gems:6.about:
A stone that grows into six-sided columns. It vibrates very evenly when electricity passes through it, and this is used to make quartz watches.
Yamanashi has long been famous for quartz crystal.

rocks-gems:7.fact: Purple quartz. It is the birthstone for February.
rocks-gems:7.about: When quartz has a little iron in it, it turns purple. When it is heated, it can turn yellow.

#science-fun: Let's use science to solve the mysteries all around us!

science-fun:0.fact: It has an N pole and an S pole, and opposite poles pull towards each other. The Earth is a giant magnet too.
science-fun:0.about:
A compass needle's N pole points north because the area near the Earth's North Pole acts like an S pole.
Magnets are used in fridge doors and even in maglev trains.

science-fun:1.fact: When white light goes through it, it splits into the 7 colours of the rainbow.
science-fun:1.about:
Newton used a prism to discover that sunlight splits into many colours.
Rainbows form when raindrops act like prisms.

science-fun:2.fact: Sound is shaking air. In space there is no air, so sound can't travel.
science-fun:2.about:
Sound travels about 340 m per second through air. In water it travels about 4 times faster.
A string telephone works because your voice travels along the shaking string.

science-fun:3.fact: That zap you get from a doorknob in winter is static electricity.
science-fun:3.about:
When things rub together, tiny bits of electricity (electrons) move from one to the other, making static electricity.
When you rub your hair with a plastic sheet and it stands up, that's static electricity too.

science-fun:4.fact: When water freezes, it gets bigger and lighter, so ice floats on water.
science-fun:4.about:
If ice sank, ponds and seas would freeze from the bottom up, and fish couldn't survive the winter. Ice floating is important for living things.
Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

science-fun:5.fact: Newton is said to have thought about gravity after watching an apple fall.
science-fun:5.about:
Gravity is the force that pulls things towards each other. The Earth pulls on us, so when we jump, we come back down.
The Moon's gravity is about one sixth of the Earth's. On the Moon you could jump 6 times higher.

science-fun:6.fact: A magnifying glass lens gathers light and makes things look bigger.
science-fun:6.about:
If you focus sunlight to one spot with a magnifying glass, it gets hot enough to burn paper (never look at the Sun through one, because it hurts your eyes).
Lenses are used in glasses, cameras, microscopes and telescopes too.

science-fun:7.fact: Shadows form when light is blocked. Shadows are long in the morning and evening.
science-fun:7.about:
Shadows form on the opposite side from the light. At noon, when the Sun is high, they are short, and in the morning and evening, when it is low, they are long.
Long ago, people told the time by how shadows moved (sundials).

#heroes: Who is your hero? Here are people who changed the world.

heroes:0.fact: An American inventor who got more than 1,000 patents, for things like the light bulb and movie machines.
heroes:0.about:
He left elementary school after 3 months and was taught by his mother.
He is famous for saying, "Genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration." He also invented the phonograph (records) and movie machines.

heroes:1.fact: A scientist who won the Nobel Prize twice. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
heroes:1.about:
She was born in Poland and did her research in France. She discovered substances called "radium" and "polonium."
She is the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry.

heroes:2.fact: A scientist who thought about the mysteries of time and space. He won the Nobel Prize in 1921.
heroes:2.about:
A German-born physicist. He came up with the theory of relativity, which says that time and space can stretch and shrink.
He visited Japan in 1922 and is said to have liked Japanese culture.

heroes:3.fact: He spent his life researching infectious diseases. He used to be on the 1,000-yen note.
heroes:3.about:
Born in Fukushima. As a child, he badly burned his hand, and after an operation healed it, he decided to become a doctor.
He worked hard researching diseases in America and Africa.

heroes:4.fact: "The father of Japanese bacteriology." He has been on the 1,000-yen note since 2024.
heroes:4.about:
Born in Kumamoto. In Germany, he discovered a treatment for tetanus and was recognised around the world.
He came back to Japan, started a research institute and trained many researchers.

heroes:5.fact: She went to study in America at age 6 and worked hard for girls' education. She is on the 5,000-yen note.
heroes:5.about:
In the Meiji period, she was one of Japan's first girls to study abroad, and she studied in America for 11 years.
She came back to Japan and started a school where women could learn (today's Tsuda University).

heroes:6.fact: He walked all over Japan measuring it and made an accurate map of Japan.
heroes:6.about:
He started studying astronomy and surveying at age 50, and from age 55 he spent 17 years walking all over Japan. He walked about 40,000 km, the distance around the Earth.
His map is very accurate, even compared with today's maps.

heroes:7.fact: A British nurse who saved many lives by making hospitals clean.
heroes:7.about:
During the Crimean War, she made hospitals clean and saved the lives of many soldiers.
She used graphs to show data clearly, so she was also a pioneer of statistics. Nurses' Day (May 12th) is her birthday.

heroes:8.fact: The painter of the "Mona Lisa," who was also an inventor and a scientist.
heroes:8.about:
Painter, scientist, inventor, musician… he had many talents.
His notebooks have sketches of helicopters, flying machines, how the human body works and more, written in mirror writing.

#money: How much is it? Different countries have different names for money.

money:0.fact: Japanese money. The 5-yen and 50-yen coins have holes in them.
money:0.about:
The "yen" became Japan's unit of money in 1871. There are 6 coins: 1, 5, 10, 50, 100 and 500 yen.
A 1-yen coin weighs 1 g, and if you place it gently on water, it can even float.

money:1.fact: American money. Other countries, like Canada and Australia, use dollars too.
money:1.about:
The American 1-dollar bill shows President Washington's face. All the bills are the same size, whatever their value.
1 dollar = 100 cents.

money:2.fact: Many countries in Europe use the same money, the euro.
money:2.about:
Euro notes and coins started being used in 2002. The design on the back of the coins is different in each country.
The euro symbol is "€."

money:3.fact: British money. It has a very long history.
money:3.about:
British money is the "pound (£)." 1 pound = 100 pence.
It is one of the oldest currencies in the world still being used.

money:4.about: The symbol for Korean money is "₩." 1,000 won is about 100 yen (it changes from year to year).

money:5.about:
Chinese money is called "renminbi," and its symbol, "¥," looks like the symbol for the Japanese yen.
In China, very many people pay with their smartphones.

money:6.fact: In 2024, Japan got new banknotes. When you tilt one, the face seems to move like 3D.
money:6.about:
On the new notes issued in July 2024, the 10,000-yen note has Shibusawa Eiichi, the 5,000-yen note Tsuda Umeko, and the 1,000-yen note Kitasato Shibasaburō.
To stop fake notes, they use a 3D hologram, the first in the world.

money:7.fact: More and more people pay with cards and smartphones.
money:7.about:
You can pay just by holding up a card or smartphone.
It's handy, but be careful not to spend too much. It's important to think about the value of money too.

#games-world: Let's play! What games do children around the world play?

games-world:0.fact: A Japanese board game. You can use the pieces you capture as your own.
games-world:0.about:
On a 9×9 board, you win by capturing the king. Using the pieces you capture as your own is a rare rule among the world's chess-like games.
Thanks to Fujii Sōta's success, it has become more popular with children too.

games-world:1.fact: A board game played all over the world. It is a relative of shogi.
games-world:1.about:
It comes from an old game in India and spread to Persia and then Europe.
There are 6 kinds of pieces: king, queen, rook, bishop, knight and pawn.

games-world:2.fact: A game born in China where you use white and black stones to win territory.
games-world:2.about:
You place stones where the 19×19 lines cross, and whoever makes the bigger territory wins.
The rules are simple, but people say there are more possible games than there are atoms in the universe.

games-world:3.fact: In English it's rock, paper, scissors. It is played all over the world.
games-world:3.about:
Janken in Japan is said to have spread around the Edo period.
"Gū, choki, pā" are rock, scissors and paper in English. The chant and the hand shapes are different in each country.

games-world:4.fact: In English it's jump rope. There are team competitions too.
games-world:4.about:
Double Dutch is a sport where you jump over two turning ropes. Japanese teams are strong in world competitions.
Jumping rope is great for getting fit.

games-world:5.fact: A very old toy. There were yo-yos in Greece more than 2,000 years ago.
games-world:5.about:
A toy that has long been played with in the Philippines. "Yo-yo" is said to mean "come back" in a language of the Philippines.
Like kendama, there are world championships for tricks.

games-world:6.fact: Besides lining them up and knocking them down, there are games played with the numbers of dots.
games-world:6.about:
A game played with tiles that have dots like the faces of dice. It is said to have been born in China.
The world record for knocking down dominoes is several million.

games-world:7.fact: In English they're called cards. "Trump" means "trump card."
games-world:7.about:
The 4 suits of playing cards are spades, hearts, diamonds and clubs.
There are picture cards (king, queen and jack) and jokers. There are lots of games to play, like Old Maid, Memory and Page One.

#toys-tales: Once upon a time… stories passed down in Japan since long ago.

toys-tales:0.fact: A boy born from a peach goes to defeat ogres with a dog, a monkey and a pheasant.
toys-tales:0.about:
Momotarō, raised by an old man and an old woman, shares his kibi dango to make friends with the animals, and they work together.
Okayama is said to be the home of the story, and there is a statue of Momotarō in front of Okayama Station.

toys-tales:1.fact: A turtle he saved takes him to Ryūgū-jō, the palace under the sea.
toys-tales:1.about:
He has a wonderful time at the palace, but when he goes home, hundreds of years have passed in his village. When he opens the treasure box, white smoke turns him into an old man.
It is a very old story that makes you wonder about time.

toys-tales:2.fact: A princess born inside a bamboo stalk who goes back to the Moon in the end. One of the oldest stories in Japan.
toys-tales:2.about:
"The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter," written more than 1,000 years ago, is said to be the oldest story in Japan.
The part where she makes 5 men who want to marry her search for impossible treasures is famous too.

toys-tales:3.fact: A tiny boy travels to the capital in a bowl boat.
toys-tales:3.about:
"Issun" is about 3 cm. He uses a bowl as a boat, chopsticks as oars and a needle as a sword, and heads for the capital.
The climax is when he grows big with a magic mallet.

toys-tales:4.fact: A story about a strong boy who grew up with animals in the mountains.
toys-tales:4.about:
A strong boy who grew up wrestling with bears on Mt. Ashigara. People say he later became a samurai named Sakata no Kintoki.
He is also made into dolls for Children's Day in May.

toys-tales:5.fact: A kind old man puts hats on stone Jizō statues standing in the snow.
toys-tales:5.about:
An old man puts the hats he couldn't sell on snowy Jizō statues. When he has one hat too few, he gives his own towel.
It is a story about kindness bringing happiness.

toys-tales:6.fact: A crab and its friends work together against a mean monkey.
toys-tales:6.about:
A crab, a chestnut, a bee, a mortar and a cow pat team up.
It teaches us that even small things can stand up to a big opponent if they work together.

#world-tales: Around the world there are stories that have been told for hundreds of years.

world-tales:0.fact: One of Aesop's fables from Greece. It teaches us the value of keeping going steadily.
world-tales:0.about:
The fast hare takes a nap halfway, and the tortoise, who keeps walking slowly, wins.
Aesop is said to have lived in Greece about 2,600 years ago. "The Ant and the Grasshopper" is one of Aesop's fables too.

world-tales:1.fact: A very old story, with similar stories all over the world.
world-tales:1.about:
The version Perrault of France wrote in 1697 is famous, but China had a similar story more than 1,000 years ago.
The glass slipper comes from Perrault's version.

world-tales:2.fact: One of the folk tales collected by the Brothers Grimm in Germany.
world-tales:2.about:
The Brothers Grimm collected folk tales from all over Germany and made them into a book in 1812. "Little Red Riding Hood" and "Snow White" are Grimms' fairy tales too.
The part where they use breadcrumbs to mark the path is famous.

world-tales:3.fact: A strange and wonderful story written in Britain in 1865.
world-tales:3.about:
Its author, Lewis Carroll, was a mathematician. It started as a story he told on a boat trip to Alice and the other daughters of a friend.
Lots of strange characters appear, like the Queen of Hearts and the Cheshire Cat.

world-tales:4.fact: A story written in Italy in 1883 about a puppet whose nose grows when he tells a lie.
world-tales:4.about:
A story written by Collodi of Italy. A wooden puppet, Pinocchio, makes mistakes as he tries to become a real boy.
It is famous for "your nose grows when you lie."

world-tales:5.fact: It spread around the world as a story in "The Thousand and One Nights (Arabian Nights)."
world-tales:5.about:
"The Thousand and One Nights" is a collection of stories from the Middle East, India and other places. A woman called Scheherazade tells a story every night.
The story of Aladdin was added to the collection in the 18th century by Galland of France.

world-tales:6.fact: A British folk tale. Jack climbs a beanstalk that grows up to the sky.
world-tales:6.about:
Magic beans, traded for a cow, grow above the clouds in one night.
It is a British folk tale, and it is also popular as a Christmas play for children (a pantomime).

#robots: Robots do important work everywhere, from factories to space.

robots:0.fact: Wind-up dolls made in Japan in the Edo period. They are the ancestors of robots.
robots:0.about:
When you put tea on a "tea-serving doll," it walks to the guest. When the guest takes the cup it stops, and when the cup is put back, it turns around and goes back.
Their springs and gears are one of the roots of today's robot technology.

robots:1.fact: A robot that walks on two legs, announced by a Japanese company in 2000.
robots:1.about:
A humanoid robot made by Honda that walked on two legs. It could climb stairs and run.
ASIMO's technology is used in today's robots and cars.

robots:2.fact: It drives on Mars, taking photos and studying rocks.
robots:2.about:
NASA's "Perseverance" looks for signs of life on Mars, and it flew a small helicopter, "Ingenuity," in the Martian sky.
Messages take from a few minutes to 20 minutes to travel between Earth and Mars.

robots:3.fact: It learns the shape of your room and cleans by itself.
robots:3.about:
It uses sensors to find walls and steps, so it cleans without bumping into things.
It makes a map of the house, and when it finishes cleaning, it goes back to its charger by itself.

robots:4.fact: Robots with big arms that build cars and other things. Japan is a robot superpower.
robots:4.about:
Factory robots carry heavy things and tighten screws precisely, working without breaks.
Japan is one of the top countries in the world for making industrial robots.

robots:5.fact: A flying robot. It is used for taking photos and carrying packages.
robots:5.about:
Most have 4 or more propellers and can take photos and videos from the sky with a camera.
They do more and more jobs, like spraying crops, checking disaster areas and delivering packages.

robots:6.fact: Technology that lets computers understand language and recognise pictures.
robots:6.about:
AI learns patterns from lots of data so it can translate languages and recognise pictures.
It is a useful tool, but it can make mistakes. It is important to think for yourself and check.

#environment: What can we do for the earth? Let's think about what we can do.

environment:0.fact: Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again) and Recycle (turn back into materials).
environment:0.about:
The most important is "Reduce." Finding ways not to make rubbish comes first.
Japan sorts its rubbish very carefully. Plastic bottles are reborn as new bottles and clothes.

environment:1.fact: Plastic that ends up in the sea is sometimes eaten by fish and sea turtles.
environment:1.about:
Millions of tonnes of plastic flow into the sea every year. Some say that if nothing changes, by 2050 the plastic in the sea will weigh more than the fish.
Tiny broken bits, called "microplastics," are very hard to collect.

environment:2.about:
Solar panels are made of "semiconductors," which make electricity when light shines on them.
In Japan too, more and more homes and schools have solar panels on their roofs.

environment:3.fact: It makes electricity by turning big windmills with the wind.
environment:3.about:
Some wind turbine blades are more than 50 m long.
"Offshore wind power," with turbines built in the sea, is being developed in the sea near Gotō City in Nagasaki too.

environment:4.fact: Trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.
environment:4.about:
About two thirds of Japan is forest, so it is a "land of forests."
Forests don't just take in carbon dioxide. They also store rainwater to prevent floods and give homes to animals.

environment:5.fact: Using your own bag helps cut down on rubbish.
environment:5.about:
Since July 2020, shops in Japan have charged for plastic bags.
Using an eco bag cuts down on plastic rubbish.

environment:6.fact: Just turning off the tap while you brush your teeth saves lots of water.
environment:6.about:
More than 97% of the Earth's water is sea water. Only a tiny amount is fresh water that people can use.
One person in Japan uses about 200 litres of water a day, about a bathtub full.

environment:7.fact: Food that gets thrown away even though it could be eaten. Eating everything on your plate is kind to the Earth too.
environment:7.about:
In Japan, more than 4 million tonnes of food that could still be eaten is thrown away every year.
It's important not to buy too much, to make only as much as you can eat, and to finish your food.

#endangered-japan: Japan also has living things whose numbers have fallen and need protecting.

endangered-japan:0.fact: It once disappeared from the wild in Japan, but on Sado Island in Niigata, people are raising more and returning them to the sky.
endangered-japan:0.about:
Its scientific name is "Nipponia nippon." In 2003, the last Japanese-born crested ibis died, and people raised more from ibises given by China.
Now many crested ibises fly in the skies over Sado Island.

endangered-japan:1.fact: Carefully raised in Toyooka, Hyōgo, it flies in Japan's skies again.
endangered-japan:1.about:
It disappeared from the wild in Japan in 1971, but it was carefully raised in Toyooka, Hyōgo, and returned to the sky in 2005.
Farmers are also using fewer pesticides in their rice fields so the storks can live there.

endangered-japan:2.fact: A wild cat that lives only on Iriomote Island in Okinawa.
endangered-japan:2.about:
A wild cat found in 1965 that lives only on Iriomote Island. There are said to be only about 100.
It is a good swimmer and eats frogs and fish too.

endangered-japan:3.fact: A bird that lives on high mountains. It turns pure white in winter and brown in summer.
endangered-japan:3.about:
In Japan it lives only on high mountains in Honshu, and it is a special national natural monument.
It changes the colour of its feathers with the seasons: white like the snow in winter and brown like the rocks in summer.

endangered-japan:4.fact: A travelling fish that is born in the sea and swims up rivers.
endangered-japan:4.about:
It is born in the sea near the Mariana Islands and travels more than 2,000 km to rivers in Japan.
Its numbers have fallen, and it is in danger of dying out.

endangered-japan:5.fact: A water insect that lives in rice fields and ponds. Its numbers are falling.
endangered-japan:5.about:
A great swimmer that lives in rice fields and ponds. It dives with a bubble of air stored at the tip of its bottom.
Because of pesticides and ponds being filled in, its numbers have fallen, and it can't be seen in many areas any more.
