#japan-islands: Japan has more than 14,000 islands. The prefecture with the most islands is… Nagasaki!

japan-islands:0.fact: The biggest island in Japan, and the seventh biggest in the world.
japan-islands:0.about:
The biggest island in Japan, where about 80% of Japan's people live.
Big cities like Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya are here.

japan-islands:1.fact: Nagasaki has more than 1,400 islands, the most of any prefecture in Japan.
japan-islands:1.about:
Nagasaki's coastline is also the second longest in Japan, after Hokkaido. It is a prefecture with lots of twisting coasts and islands.
The Gotō Islands, Iki, Tsushima, Kujūku-shima and others each have their own culture and nature.

japan-islands:2.fact: A chain of islands west of Nagasaki. They are famous for their beautiful sea.
japan-islands:2.about:
About 100 km west of Nagasaki Harbour, about 140 big and small islands are lined up.
They are famous for Gotō udon, camellia oil and beautiful beaches. The islands' churches are part of a World Cultural Heritage site.

japan-islands:3.fact: An island in Kagoshima with forests of Yakusugi cedars that live for thousands of years.
japan-islands:3.about:
It rains so much that people say "it rains 35 days a month." Thanks to the rain, there are mossy forests.
The coast is warm and tropical, and the mountaintops get snow in winter, so Japan's climates are all packed into one island.

japan-islands:4.fact: An island in Niigata known as the home of the crested ibis.
japan-islands:4.about:
A big island in Niigata, in the Sea of Japan.
People there have a tradition of fishing from "tub boats." It is the home of the crested ibis.

japan-islands:5.fact: A southern island surrounded by seas with coral reefs.
japan-islands:5.about:
The biggest island in Okinawa. In Naha there is Shuri Castle, the castle of the Ryūkyū Kingdom.
Coral reefs spread through the seas around it, and you can meet sea turtles and whale sharks.

japan-islands:6.fact: Islands that are part of Tokyo. It takes about 24 hours to get there by ship from Tokyo. You can see whales.
japan-islands:6.about:
Islands about 1,000 km south of Tokyo. They have never been joined to a continent, so many living things are found only there, and they are called "the Galápagos of the East."
They became a World Natural Heritage site in 2011.

japan-islands:7.fact: The second biggest island in Japan. It gets lots of snow in winter.
japan-islands:7.about:
Hokkaido is the second biggest island in Japan, a little smaller than Honshu. In winter, drift ice comes to the Sea of Okhotsk.
Animals different from Honshu's live there, like brown bears, Ezo red foxes and Ezo deer.

#reptiles: Scaly reptiles, and amphibians that live both in water and on land. They're all amazing creatures!

reptiles:0.fact: An animal that has hardly changed since the time of the dinosaurs.
reptiles:0.about:
Crocodiles have lived for more than 200 million years without changing their shape much.
Their eyes and nostrils are on top of their heads, so they can look around while their bodies stay hidden in the water.

reptiles:1.fact: The longest venomous snake in the world. It can be more than 5 m long.
reptiles:1.about:
A snake that eats other snakes. When it is startled, it lifts the front of its body up high and spreads its hood.
It lives in the forests of India and Southeast Asia.

reptiles:2.fact: It can move its left and right eyes separately. It can change the colour of its body too.
reptiles:2.about:
It changes colour not just to hide but also to show its mood and control its body temperature.
It quickly shoots out its tongue, which is as long as its body, to catch insects. Many kinds live in Madagascar.

reptiles:3.fact: The biggest lizard in the world. It lives on islands in Indonesia.
reptiles:3.about:
A lizard that can grow to 3 m long. It lives on Komodo Island and other islands in Indonesia.
It smells with its tongue and can notice prey several kilometres away.

reptiles:4.fact: The tiny hairs on the soles of its feet let it walk on walls and ceilings.
reptiles:4.about:
The soles of its feet have millions of hairs too small to see, so it can stick to walls and even glass. This idea is being used to research new kinds of tape.
In Japan it is called "yamori" (house guard) because it eats insects around the house.

reptiles:5.fact: A big tortoise that can live for more than 100 years.
reptiles:5.about:
A big tortoise that lives on the Galápagos Islands of Ecuador in South America. It can weigh more than 200 kg.
The shape of its shell is different on each island, which gave Darwin clues for his ideas about evolution.

reptiles:6.fact: A kind of salamander that lives in a lake in Mexico. It can regrow parts of its body when they are hurt.
reptiles:6.about:
An amazing animal that grows up while still looking like a baby. The fluffy parts on the sides of its neck are its gills.
In the wild it lives only in a lake in Mexico City, and there are very few left.

reptiles:7.fact: Frogs take in water through their skin too.
reptiles:7.about:
Frogs are amphibians. As tadpoles they breathe with gills, and as adults they breathe with lungs and through their skin.
Japanese tree frogs and dark-spotted frogs are often seen in Japan's rice fields.

#aquarium: Sea creatures you can meet at the aquarium. They all have amazing secrets.

aquarium:0.fact: It lives safely among the tentacles of a sea anemone.
aquarium:0.about:
It lives among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone, which protect it. A slimy coating on the clownfish's body protects it from the stings.
It's an amazing fish: the biggest one in a group becomes the female.

aquarium:1.fact: A very fast fish that can swim at more than 70 km per hour.
aquarium:1.about:
A fish that can't breathe unless it keeps swimming all its life. It is unusual because it can keep its body warmer than the sea water.
It is famous as "toro" sushi. Kindai University was the first in the world to fully farm bluefin tuna.

aquarium:2.fact: The heaviest bony fish in the world. It lays hundreds of millions of eggs at once.
aquarium:2.about:
A huge fish that can weigh 2 tonnes. The part that looks like a tail is actually a "rudder fin."
It sometimes lies on the surface of the sea as if it is sunbathing, so in English it is called a sunfish.

aquarium:3.fact: An unusual fish whose babies grow in a pouch on the father's tummy.
aquarium:3.about:
Seahorses are fish too. They rest by wrapping their tails around seaweed.
The female lays her eggs in the pouch on the male's tummy, and the male gives birth to the babies.

aquarium:4.fact: It has 3 hearts, and its blood is blue.
aquarium:4.about:
Octopuses are very clever. They can open jar lids and solve mazes.
Their 8 arms have lots of suckers that can even sense smell and taste. When an enemy attacks, they squirt ink and escape.

aquarium:5.fact: If one of its arms is cut off, it grows back.
aquarium:5.about:
A starfish has no brain and no blood. It has eye-like spots at the tips of its arms that sense light.
It can push its stomach outside its body to eat shellfish.

aquarium:6.fact: When it is surprised, it sucks in water and puffs its body up big.
aquarium:6.about:
Many pufferfish have strong poison in their bodies. Cooks need a special licence to prepare them.
Male white-spotted pufferfish from Amami make nests with beautiful patterns on the sea floor.

aquarium:7.fact: It can't fly in the sky, but it swims through the water as if it is flying.
aquarium:7.about:
At Nagasaki Penguin Aquarium, you can see many kinds of penguins.
Penguins are black and white because from above they look dark like the sea, and from below they look white like the sky, so enemies have trouble seeing them.

aquarium:8.fact: They swim in a big school to protect themselves from big fish.
aquarium:8.about:
Thousands and thousands of sardines swim together like one living thing.
They feel the movements of the fish next to them with the "lateral line" on their sides, so they can swim without bumping into each other.

#dog-breeds: I have a dog. There are many kinds of dogs, including some from Japan!

dog-breeds:0.fact: A dog that has lived in Japan since long ago. "Shiba" is popular around the world too.
dog-breeds:0.about:
One of the oldest dog breeds in Japan, and a national natural monument.
It has a small body but is lively and very independent. Abroad it is hugely popular as the "Shiba."

dog-breeds:1.fact: "Hachikō" in Shibuya, Tokyo, was an Akita. He is famous for waiting for his owner.
dog-breeds:1.about:
A large dog from Akita, and a national natural monument.
Hachikō waited at Shibuya Station for about 10 years for his owner, Professor Ueno, who had died. He is known all over the world.

dog-breeds:2.fact: The smallest dog breed in the world. Its name comes from a place in Mexico.
dog-breeds:2.about:
Its name comes from the state of Chihuahua in Mexico. It weighs about 1 to 3 kg.
It is small but very brave and sometimes barks even at dogs bigger than itself.

dog-breeds:3.fact: A very tall dog. When it stands up, it can be taller than a person.
dog-breeds:3.about:
A large dog from Germany. When it stands on its back legs, it can be more than 2 m tall.
It is big, but it is calm and gentle.

dog-breeds:4.fact: A white dog with black spots. It is pure white when it is born.
dog-breeds:4.about:
Puppies are pure white, and black spots appear after about 2 weeks.
In America long ago, they ran alongside horse-drawn fire engines, so they are still mascots of fire stations today.

dog-breeds:5.fact: It is gentle and clever, so it also works as a guide dog.
dog-breeds:5.about:
A dog from Scotland in the UK. It was first used to fetch birds that fell into water.
Because it is gentle and clever, it also works as a guide dog and a therapy dog.

dog-breeds:6.fact: It is tough in the cold and has pulled sleds over snow.
dog-breeds:6.about:
From Siberia in Russia. It is a sled dog that can run a long way through cold snow.
Some huskies have blue eyes, or eyes of two different colours.

dog-breeds:7.fact: A very clever dog that doesn't shed much hair.
dog-breeds:7.about:
It is sometimes called the national dog of France, but it started as a dog in Germany that fetched water birds.
Its curly coat doesn't shed much, so people say it is easier to keep for people who are bothered by animal hair.

#art: Paintings, sculptures, pottery… people all over the world have made beautiful things in many ways.

art:0.fact: A painting by Leonardo da Vinci. It is in the Louvre Museum in France.
art:0.about:
A painting da Vinci worked on for years. It is full of mysteries: she has no eyebrows, and her eyes seem to look at you wherever you stand.
It was stolen in 1911, which made it even more famous around the world. Now it is protected inside a glass case.

art:1.fact: Paintings of sunflowers by the Dutch painter Van Gogh. He painted several.
art:1.about:
Van Gogh painted sunflowers to decorate the room for his painter friend Gauguin.
The bright yellow shows the sunlight of southern France. One of them is in a museum in Japan.

art:2.fact: A ukiyo-e print by Katsushika Hokusai. It shows a huge wave and Mt. Fuji.
art:2.about:
Beyond the huge wave, you can see a tiny Mt. Fuji. Hokusai made it when he was over 70.
As "The Great Wave," it is said to be the most famous Japanese picture in the world.

art:3.fact: Pottery from Hasami in Nagasaki. It has more than 400 years of history.
art:3.about:
Hasami in Nagasaki makes lots of Japan's everyday tableware. In the Edo period, its strong, cheap "kurawanka" bowls spread among ordinary people.
Its simple, easy-to-use designs are popular today.

art:4.fact: Pottery from Saga. Long ago, lots of it was shipped to Europe too.
art:4.about:
One of the first places in Japan to make porcelain. In the 17th century, lots of it was exported to Europe from the port of Nagasaki and loved by kings and nobles.
It was shipped from the port of Imari, so it is also called "Imari ware."

art:5.fact: Art where you carve stone or wood to make shapes.
art:5.about:
There is carving, where you cut away stone or wood, and modelling, where you build up clay.
In Japan, many old wooden statues are National Treasures.

art:6.fact: A picture made by fitting together pieces of coloured glass.
art:6.about:
It is made by joining pieces of coloured glass with lead frames. When light shines through, coloured shadows appear on the floor.
You can see it in the big windows of old buildings in Europe.

art:7.fact: A picture made by arranging small stones or tiles. Mosaics have existed for more than 2,000 years.
art:7.about:
People in ancient Rome decorated the floors of their houses with mosaic pictures.
Today you can make them with tiles, beads or even paper. Put lots of small pieces together and they become a big picture.

#numbers: How many? Numbers are full of interesting secrets!

numbers:0.fact: The idea of using "0" as a number is said to have started in India.
numbers:0.about:
Because we have "0," a number meaning "nothing," we can easily write places like 10, 100 and 1,000.
Roman numerals had no zero.

numbers:1.fact: Numbers are shown with letters like Ⅰ, Ⅴ and Ⅹ. You sometimes see them on clocks.
numbers:1.about:
Ⅰ=1, Ⅴ=5, Ⅹ=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1,000. When a smaller number is written on the left, as in Ⅳ and Ⅸ, it means "take away."
They are still used on clocks and for numbering movie series.

numbers:2.fact: A tool for calculating by moving beads. It has been used in Japan for a long time.
numbers:2.about:
The soroban came from China and was improved in Japan to make it easier to use.
If you learn the soroban, you can do "anzan": calculating by imagining a soroban in your head.

numbers:3.fact: The numbers on opposite faces always add up to 7.
numbers:3.about:
Dice have been used all over the world for thousands of years.
On Japanese dice, the 1 is often red. One idea is that this is because of the Japanese flag.

numbers:4.fact: 一, 十, 百, 千, 万, 億, 兆, 京… Japanese has names for even bigger numbers.
numbers:4.about:
1 man (10,000) is 10 to the 4th power, and 1 oku is 10 to the 8th power. Japanese gets a new name every 4 digits, but English gets one every 3 (thousand, million, billion).
1 oku = one hundred million.

numbers:5.fact: The distance around a circle is about 3.14 times its width. It's a number that goes on forever.
numbers:5.about:
Pi is 3.14159… and it goes on forever without repeating. Computers have calculated it to tens of trillions of digits.
March 14th is "Pi Day."

numbers:6.fact: After eleven and twelve, -teen is added, starting with thirteen.
numbers:6.about:
The English words eleven and twelve come from old words meaning "one left over after ten" and "two left over."
13 to 19 end in -teen, and 20, 30… end in -ty.

#time: What time is it? Let's look at the mysteries of time.

time:0.fact: A very old clock that tells the time by the direction of a shadow.
time:0.about:
The shadow works like the hand of a clock. Sundials were used in ancient Egypt too.
People say clock hands go "clockwise" because they follow the direction a sundial's shadow moves.

time:1.fact: When it's daytime in Japan, it's still early morning in the UK. The time is different in each country.
time:1.about:
The Earth turns once every 24 hours, so for every 15 degrees, the time shifts by 1 hour.
When it is 12 noon in Japan, it is 3 a.m. in the UK (in winter) and 10 p.m. the day before in New York (in winter).

time:2.fact: Once every 4 years, there is a year when February has 29 days.
time:2.about:
The Earth takes not exactly 365 days but about 365.24 days to go around the Sun. To fix the difference, February 29th is added once every 4 years.
People born on February 29th only have their real birthday once every 4 years.

time:3.fact: The name of the bell in London's big clock.
time:3.about:
"Big Ben" is the name of the big bell inside the clock tower in London. The tower's official name is the "Elizabeth Tower."
The bell weighs about 13 tonnes. The tune of the school chime in Japan comes from this clock's sound.

time:4.fact: One turn of the Earth is 1 day. A day is 24 hours.
time:4.about:
1 day = 24 hours = 1,440 minutes = 86,400 seconds.
The Earth's spin is very slowly getting slower, so scientists think days long, long ago were shorter than today.

time:5.fact: One trip of the Earth around the Sun is 1 year, about 365 days.
time:5.about:
1 year = 365 days. The Earth travels around the Sun at about 100,000 km per hour (300 times faster than the Shinkansen).
We have seasons because the Earth's axis is tilted.

time:6.fact: Sunday comes from "the Sun's day," and Monday from "the Moon's day."
time:6.about:
The Japanese days of the week come from 7 objects in the sky: the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn.
The English Saturday comes from Saturn, and Thursday comes from Thor, the Norse god of thunder.

#daily-life: What time do you get up? Let's compare our day with children's days around the world.

daily-life:0.fact: I get up at 6:30. Let's say the time we get up in English.
daily-life:0.about: Many Japanese elementary school children get up around 6:30 to 7:00. People say that getting morning sunlight resets your body clock.

daily-life:1.about: When you eat breakfast, your body warms up and your brain works well.

daily-life:2.fact: In Japan, many children walk to school, but some countries have school buses.
daily-life:2.about: In Japan, children often walk to school by themselves, but in many other countries parents drive their children to school.

daily-life:3.fact: I do my homework. Some countries give little homework, and some give lots.
daily-life:3.about: Homework helps you remember and really learn what you studied at school.

daily-life:4.fact: Soaking in a bathtub is one special feature of Japanese life.
daily-life:4.about: Japanese people have the custom of soaking in the bathtub, but in many countries people just take a shower.

daily-life:5.fact: I go to bed at 9:00. Sleeping well keeps your body and brain healthy.
daily-life:5.about: While you sleep, your body grows, and what you learned that day is sorted into memories.

#breakfast-world: What do you eat for breakfast? Breakfast is different in every country.

breakfast-world:0.fact: Rice, miso soup, grilled fish and natto. Many homes have bread too.
breakfast-world:0.about:
"One soup, three dishes" (rice, soup and three side dishes) is the basic shape of a Japanese meal.
Today many families have bread or cereal, so breakfasts are more varied.

breakfast-world:1.fact: The "full breakfast": eggs, bacon, sausages, grilled tomatoes and beans.
breakfast-world:1.about:
A "full English breakfast" is a weekend treat. Beans cooked in tomato sauce (baked beans) are what make it so British.
On normal days, many families have toast or cereal.

breakfast-world:2.fact: Pancakes with maple syrup. Cereal is popular too.
breakfast-world:2.about:
Pancakes, waffles, bacon and cereal, with lots of maple syrup on top.
On busy mornings, some people grab a bagel or a cereal bar and head out.

breakfast-world:3.fact: Croissants or baguettes with café au lait.
breakfast-world:3.about: French breakfast is simple. People spread butter or jam on bread, and sometimes dip it into a big cup of café au lait.

breakfast-world:4.fact: Rice porridge, or youtiao (fried dough sticks) with soy milk.
breakfast-world:4.about:
Rice porridge, or youtiao (long fried dough sticks) with hot soy milk.
Many people buy steamed buns or dumplings from street stalls in the morning.

breakfast-world:5.fact: Tortillas topped with eggs or beans are a classic.
breakfast-world:5.about:
"Huevos rancheros" are tortillas topped with fried eggs and spicy tomato sauce.
"Frijoles," mashed cooked beans, are a classic too.

breakfast-world:6.fact: Lots of little plates: cheese, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, bread and more.
breakfast-world:6.about:
Cheese, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, bread, eggs, honey… little plates fill the whole table.
The Turkish word for breakfast, "kahvaltı," means "before coffee."

breakfast-world:7.fact: People eat rice and soup with side dishes like kimchi.
breakfast-world:7.about:
Many families have a meal like dinner in the morning, with rice, soup and kimchi.
On busy mornings, "gimbap" seaweed rice rolls are popular too.

#houses-world: People around the world live in all kinds of homes that suit their climate and way of life.

houses-world:0.fact: A house made of snow blocks. Inside, it is warmer than you'd think.
houses-world:0.about:
A snow house that Inuit people of northern Canada and other areas built while travelling to hunt.
The air in the snow keeps heat in, so even when it's minus 40 °C outside, it stays much warmer inside.

houses-world:1.fact: A Mongolian house you can put up and take down. It can be put up in a few hours.
houses-world:1.about:
A round house made of a wooden frame and felt (cloth made of sheep's wool). It can be put up in 2 or 3 hours.
Nomads move with their animals each season, carrying their gers with them.

houses-world:2.fact: A house raised up on posts. It protects the house from water and animals.
houses-world:2.about:
In rainy areas like Southeast Asia, raising the floor protects houses from floods and damp.
Raised storehouses in Japan's Yayoi period were also a way to protect rice from mice and damp.

houses-world:3.fact: Tatami, shōji screens and taking off your shoes at the genkan are its special features.
houses-world:3.about:
Tatami are floor mats made of rush grass. They are a natural way to stay cool in summer and warm in winter.
Taking off your shoes at the genkan keeps the inside of the house clean.

houses-world:4.fact: "Gasshō-zukuri" houses in Gifu. Their steep roofs let snow slide off easily.
houses-world:4.about:
"Gasshō-zukuri" houses have steep thatched roofs like hands put together in prayer. Snow doesn't pile up on them, and people raised silkworms in the attic.
The villagers work together to rethatch the roofs (this is called "yui"). It became a World Heritage site in 1995.

houses-world:5.fact: A house made of mud bricks dried in the sun. You can find them in hot areas.
houses-world:5.about:
Mud is mixed with straw, put in moulds and dried in the sun to make bricks.
The thick walls store the daytime heat and release it at night, softening the desert's heat and cold.

houses-world:6.fact: Some people live in houses floating on lakes and rivers.
houses-world:6.about:
On Lake Titicaca in Peru, some people live in houses built on "floating islands" made of layers of a reed called totora.
The Netherlands has "floating houses" that rise and fall with the water level.

houses-world:7.fact: A house built up in a tree. Some people live in the forest.
houses-world:7.about:
The Korowai people, who live on the island of New Guinea in Indonesia, have long built their homes high up in trees.
Tree houses are loved all over the world as places for children to play too.

#foods-health: Food builds your body. Let's eat a good balance!

foods-health:0.fact: Meat, fish, eggs and milk. They build your body.
foods-health:0.about:
They have lots of protein, which builds your muscles, bones and blood.
Soybeans and tofu are in the red group too. School lunch menus in Japan sort foods into these 3 colours.

foods-health:1.fact: Rice, bread and noodles. They give you energy to move your body.
foods-health:1.about:
They have lots of carbohydrates and fats, which give you energy to move.
If you skip breakfast, you run out of energy in the morning.

foods-health:2.fact: Vegetables and fruit. They keep your body working well.
foods-health:2.about:
They have lots of vitamins, minerals and fibre, which keep your body working well.
People say about 350 g of vegetables a day is a good target.

foods-health:3.fact: There is lots of it in milk and small fish. It makes your bones and teeth strong.
foods-health:3.about:
Japanese people are said to often not get enough calcium. One glass of milk gives you about a third of what you need in a day.
Your body takes in calcium better with vitamin D, which your body makes when you get sunlight.

foods-health:4.fact: More than half of your body is made of water.
foods-health:4.about:
About 70% of a child's body is water. About 2 litres of water leave your body every day through sweat and breathing.
Drink water often, before you get thirsty.

foods-health:5.fact: People say chewing well helps digestion and wakes up your brain too.
foods-health:5.about:
Try to chew each bite about 30 times. Chewing well makes saliva, which helps digestion and prevents tooth decay.
It also stops you eating too much and helps you taste your food better.

#sports-world: Besides soccer and baseball, the world has lots of interesting sports!

sports-world:0.fact: Hugely popular in the UK and India. A match can last several days.
sports-world:0.about:
A sport where you hit a ball with a bat and run to score points. It is said to be a relative of baseball.
In India it is the national sport, and when there is a match the whole town goes wild.

sports-world:1.fact: A sport from Southeast Asia, like volleyball played with your feet.
sports-world:1.about:
Players kick a ball made of rattan over the net with their feet and heads.
The acrobatic kicks are amazing to watch. It is popular in Thailand and Malaysia.

sports-world:2.fact: A sport from India. The attacking player keeps saying "kabaddi."
sports-world:2.about:
The attacker holds their breath, keeps saying "kabaddi, kabaddi," touches the other team's players and comes back.
It is said to have more than 4,000 years of history in India.

sports-world:3.fact: It became an Olympic sport for the first time at the Tokyo 2020 Games.
sports-world:3.about:
A sport of riding waves, enjoyed by the people of Hawaii since long ago.
The beach at Ichinomiya in Chiba was the venue for the Tokyo 2020 Games.

sports-world:4.fact: A sport where you climb a wall by holding on to holds.
sports-world:4.about:
You climb walls about 4 m high without a rope.
Japan is strong at climbing and has won Olympic medals.

sports-world:5.fact: A sport that grew out of sword fighting in Europe.
sports-world:5.about:
There are 3 events, foil, épée and sabre, each with different rules and target areas.
Fencers wear white uniforms and masks, and an electric scoring machine judges whether a hit landed.

sports-world:6.fact: A boat race that is popular in Nagasaki. Rowers row to the beat of a gong.
sports-world:6.about:
In Nagasaki's peiron, nearly 30 people row as one to the rhythm of a gong and drum.
Every July, a championship is held in Nagasaki Harbour.

sports-world:7.fact: A game played by Japanese nobles more than 1,000 years ago. They kick a ball to each other without letting it drop.
sports-world:7.about:
A game of the nobles in the Heian period. They stood in a circle and kicked a deerskin ball to each other so it wouldn't fall.
More than winning, it was important to send back a ball that was easy for the other person to kick.

#art-timeline: From cave paintings to today's art. Walk through in order from the entrance and travel through the history of art.

art-timeline:0.fact: Horses and cattle are painted in a cave in France.
art-timeline:0.about:
In 1940, some boys chasing a dog found it by chance. There are more than 600 pictures of animals.
Scientists think the paints were made by mixing coloured earth and charcoal with animal fat.

art-timeline:1.fact: Pottery made in Japan, some of the oldest in the world.
art-timeline:1.about:
"Flame-style pottery" found in Niigata has strange decorations that look like flames.
The Jōmon people cooked nuts and fish in their pottery.

art-timeline:2.fact: The gold mask of a boy king of ancient Egypt. It is in Cairo, Egypt.
art-timeline:2.about:
In 1922, Carter from Britain discovered the king's tomb. The mask is made of about 10 kg of gold.
Tutankhamun was a boy king who became king at age 9.

art-timeline:3.fact: Pictures of stories and sports scenes in black and orange.
art-timeline:3.about:
Myths and athletes are painted in black on red clay (black-figure) or in red on a black background (red-figure).
The pots were used to hold wine and olive oil.

art-timeline:4.fact: Nearly 8,000 clay soldier statues made for an emperor of China.
art-timeline:4.about:
In 1974, farmers digging a well found them. Each of the nearly 8,000 soldiers has a different face and hairstyle.
They were made to guard the tomb of the First Emperor, who united China.

art-timeline:5.fact: Japanese pictures that beautifully show a story from the Heian period on scrolls.
art-timeline:5.about:
"The Tale of Genji," written by Murasaki Shikibu, is said to be one of the oldest novels in the world.
The scrolls use a way of drawing called "fukinuki yatai," where the roof is taken away so you look down into the rooms.

art-timeline:6.fact: A painting by Leonardo da Vinci, famous for its mysterious smile.
art-timeline:6.about:
It uses "aerial perspective": faraway scenery is painted pale and blurry to show distance.
Da Vinci never gave this painting away and kept working on it until the end.

art-timeline:7.fact: The wind god and the thunder god, painted by Tawaraya Sōtatsu. A folding screen with a beautiful gold background.
art-timeline:7.about:
The green wind god holds a bag of wind, and the white thunder god holds drums. The gold background shows how wide the sky is.
Later painters, like Ogata Kōrin, copied this painting too.

art-timeline:8.fact: A painting by the Dutch painter Vermeer. The way he painted light is very beautiful.
art-timeline:8.about:
A painting called the "Mona Lisa of the North." It shows the moment a girl looks back over her shoulder.
The blue of her turban was made from an expensive gemstone, lapis lazuli.

art-timeline:9.fact: A ukiyo-e print by Katsushika Hokusai. It had a big influence on European painters too.
art-timeline:9.about:
The tips of the wave are drawn like claws. The people in the boats face the giant wave.
The blue used is a paint from Europe called "Prussian blue."

art-timeline:10.fact: Van Gogh's painting of a swirling night sky.
art-timeline:10.about:
Van Gogh painted the night sky he saw from the window of a hospital in southern France, mixing in his memories.
The swirling sky and cypress tree make you feel strong emotions. It is now in a museum in New York.

art-timeline:11.fact: Monet painted the pond in his own garden hundreds of times. He is the leading Impressionist.
art-timeline:11.about:
In his later years, Monet painted nearly 250 pictures of the water lilies floating on his garden pond.
They show how the same pond looks different as the light changes in the morning, at noon and in the evening.

art-timeline:12.fact: A painting by Picasso. It is a "Cubist" work, where shapes are split into squares and triangles.
art-timeline:12.about:
Picasso was very good at drawing even as a child, but he invented a new way of painting that broke shapes apart on purpose.
The three musicians are painted with flat shapes that look like cut paper stuck together.

art-timeline:13.fact: A painting by Dalí. It is a "Surrealist" work famous for its melting clocks.
art-timeline:13.about:
People say Dalí got the idea for the melting clocks when he saw some melted Camembert cheese.
It is smaller than you might think, about 24 cm tall and 33 cm wide, the size of a notebook.

art-timeline:14.fact: Warhol's "Pop Art." He turned things we see every day into art.
art-timeline:14.about:
He painted 32 kinds of soup cans, one on each of 32 canvases.
He showed the idea that "art can be found in everyday life too."

art-timeline:15.fact: Kusama Yayoi's polka-dot pumpkin. It sits by the sea on Naoshima in Kagawa.
art-timeline:15.about:
Kusama Yayoi has painted polka dots and pumpkins since she was a child.
The yellow pumpkin on Naoshima is a work to enjoy along with the view of the sea and sky.

#art-movements: Painters from the same time sometimes paint with similar ideas. These are called "movements."

art-movements:0.fact: It started in Italy in the 1400s and 1500s. Artists painted people and landscapes as if they were real.
art-movements:0.about:
It means "rebirth." It was a movement to study the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome again.
"Perspective," drawing faraway things smaller, developed at this time.

art-movements:1.fact: Dramatic paintings with strong contrasts of light and shadow.
art-movements:1.about:
Light like a spotlight shines on a dark background to make dramatic pictures.
In music, the time of Bach and Vivaldi is also called "Baroque music."

art-movements:2.fact: Woodblock prints from Edo. They influenced painters all over the world.
art-movements:2.about:
"Ukiyo" means "the world of today." Popular actors, beautiful landscapes and seasonal events were drawn.
One print cost about the same as a bowl of soba, so townspeople could easily buy them.

art-movements:3.fact: Artists went outside and quickly painted how light and air change.
art-movements:3.about:
A big reason it started was the invention of paint in tubes, which let artists paint outdoors.
They used quick brushstrokes that you can still see to show the sparkle of light.

art-movements:4.fact: A way of painting with lots and lots of tiny dots.
art-movements:4.about:
Instead of mixing colours, dots of colour are placed side by side so they mix in your eyes.
TV and smartphone screens also show pictures with lots of tiny dots (pixels).

art-movements:5.fact: Artists put the shapes of things seen from many directions into one picture.
art-movements:5.about:
A new way of seeing that combines the shapes seen from the front, side and top in one picture.
"Cubism" gets its name from "cube."

art-movements:6.fact: Paintings where you enjoy the beauty of shapes and colours themselves.
art-movements:6.about:
Even if you can't tell what is painted, you enjoy the feelings that the colours, shapes and lines give you.
Kandinsky felt he could see colours when he heard music, so he painted pictures like music.

art-movements:7.about:
It means "beyond reality." Artists painted strange images from dreams and the mind.
Magritte's paintings have things like rocks floating in the sky and an apple floating in front of a face.

art-movements:8.fact: Artists turned everyday things, like adverts and comics, into art.
art-movements:8.about:
Artists used things made in large numbers, like adverts, comics and product packaging, as subjects for art.
Bright colours and the same picture repeated are its special features.

art-movements:9.fact: Some are bright, huge paintings using town walls as their canvas.
art-movements:9.about:
"Murals," painted on walls with permission, are popular all over the world as art that brightens up towns.
Art in the streets can be seen by anyone for free.

#art-japan-history: From the Jōmon period to today. Let's follow the story of Japanese art.

art-japan-history:0.fact: Pottery with patterns made by rolling rope over it. That's where the name "Jōmon" (rope pattern) comes from.
art-japan-history:0.about:
The Jōmon period lasted more than 10,000 years. Pottery was used to cook and store food.
It was named "Jōmon" after the patterns made by rolling rope.

art-japan-history:1.fact: Clay figures placed around kofun burial mounds. Some are shaped like people, animals and even houses.
art-japan-history:1.about:
Unglazed clay figures placed around kofun (huge tombs).
There are many shapes, like people, horses, houses and boats, and they show us the clothes and life of the time. Some haniwa even have smiling faces.

art-japan-history:2.fact: A scroll of rabbits and frogs playing. It is said to be "Japan's oldest manga."
art-japan-history:2.about:
A scroll kept at Kōzan-ji temple in Kyoto. It is full of fun scenes, like rabbits and frogs doing sumo and playing in the water.
Showing movement with just lines connects to today's manga.

art-japan-history:3.fact: Pictures painted by changing how dark the ink is. Sesshū is famous.
art-japan-history:3.about:
Using dark and light ink, blurring and dry-brush strokes, artists show mountains and water without any colour.
Sesshū's "View of Amanohashidate" and "Winter and Autumn Landscapes" are National Treasures.

art-japan-history:4.fact: The gods of wind and thunder painted on golden folding screens.
art-japan-history:4.about:
The thunder god and the wind god are painted on the left and right of the screens, and the empty gold space in the middle makes you feel how wide the sky is.
It is at Kennin-ji temple in Kyoto and is a National Treasure.

art-japan-history:5.fact: Itō Jakuchū painted roosters in fine detail and bright colours.
art-japan-history:5.about:
Jakuchū was the eldest son of a greengrocer in Kyoto. He is said to have kept chickens in his garden and watched them for years before painting them.
Every tiny feather is carefully painted.

art-japan-history:6.fact: Katsushika Hokusai painted Mt. Fuji as seen from many different places.
art-japan-history:6.about:
There are actually 46 prints. They became so popular that 10 more were added.
"Red Fuji" (Fine Wind, Clear Morning), showing Mt. Fuji turned red by the morning sun, is famous too.

art-japan-history:7.fact: Ukiyo-e prints by Utagawa Hiroshige. They show the scenery of the journey from Edo to Kyoto.
art-japan-history:7.about:
He drew the 53 post towns along the Tōkaidō road, plus the starting point, Nihonbashi in Edo, and the end, Sanjō Ōhashi in Kyoto.
He was very good at showing falling rain and snow, and Van Gogh copied his prints.

art-japan-history:8.fact: Pottery from Hasami in Nagasaki. It is popular as tableware for everyday use.
art-japan-history:8.about:
For more than 400 years, Hasami has made dishes for everyday life.
Today it has fans all over Japan for its stylish mugs and stackable plates.

art-japan-history:9.fact: An artist known all over the world for polka dots.
art-japan-history:9.about:
Kusama Yayoi was born in Matsumoto, Nagano. She is still making art even after turning 90.
In her mirror "Infinity Rooms," the lights seem to go on forever.

#art-world-crafts: Every country and region has its own traditional patterns and crafts.

art-world-crafts:0.fact: Paintings by Australia's First Peoples. Dots show the land and stories.
art-world-crafts:0.about:
Aboriginal people in Australia have painted on rocks for tens of thousands of years.
The dot patterns show things like waterholes, travel routes and stories passed down from long ago.

art-world-crafts:1.fact: A brightly coloured woven cloth from Ghana. Each colour has a meaning.
art-world-crafts:1.about:
It is made by joining lots of narrow strips of cloth. Gold means wealth, green means growth, blue means peace, and so on.
It is a special cloth worn on days of celebration.

art-world-crafts:2.fact: Carvings with spiral patterns by the Māori, the first people of New Zealand.
art-world-crafts:2.about:
The Māori didn't use writing. They passed on family history and stories through wood carvings and patterns.
The posts and walls of their meeting places (marae) have beautiful carvings.

art-world-crafts:3.fact: Tiles with geometric patterns that decorate the walls of a palace in Spain.
art-world-crafts:3.about:
The Alhambra in Granada, Spain, was built during the time of Islamic kings.
Its patterns, repeating with no gaps, had a big influence on the Dutch artist Escher.

art-world-crafts:4.fact: Hand-woven carpets from Iran. One carpet takes months to make.
art-world-crafts:4.about:
One carpet has millions of knots.
Many have patterns of flowers and gardens. People say the idea is to "bring the garden into the home."

art-world-crafts:5.fact: Blue patterns on white dishes. Born in China, it was loved all over the world.
art-world-crafts:5.about:
Patterns are painted on white porcelain with a blue paint called cobalt, then fired.
Japanese Arita ware and Dutch Delftware were both influenced by Chinese blue-and-white.

art-world-crafts:6.fact: Mexican cut-paper decorations. People hang them up at festivals.
art-world-crafts:6.about:
Many sheets of thin, colourful paper are stacked and patterns are cut out.
At festivals, lots of them are hung on strings above the streets.

art-world-crafts:7.fact: Nesting dolls, where smaller and smaller dolls come out one after another.
art-world-crafts:7.about:
They were made in the 1890s. One idea is that they were inspired by nesting kokeshi dolls from Hakone in Japan.
The smallest doll can be as small as a grain of rice.

art-world-crafts:8.fact: Blue pottery from the Netherlands. It was influenced by Japan's Arita ware too.
art-world-crafts:8.about:
In the 17th century, Chinese and Japanese porcelain became hugely popular, so craftspeople in Delft in the Netherlands started making copies.
Dutch designs like windmills and ships are painted on it too.

art-world-crafts:9.fact: Korean pottery with a beautiful pale green colour.
art-world-crafts:9.about:
Celadon flourished in the Goryeo period (about 900 years ago). Its clear green colour is called "bisaek."
A technique called "sanggam," where patterns are carved and filled with white or black clay, is famous.

art-world-crafts:10.fact: Patterns drawn with coloured powder on the ground in front of homes in India.
art-world-crafts:10.about:
Patterns drawn on the floor at the entrance of a home with rice flour, coloured sand or flower petals. They mean welcoming guests and good luck.
At festivals, big, colourful rangoli are drawn.

art-world-crafts:11.fact: Stone carvings by the Inuit of northern Canada. They often show animals.
art-world-crafts:11.about:
Inuit people in northern Canada carve bears, seals, owls and other animals from soft stone and bone.
"Inuksuk," human-shaped stacks of stones used as landmarks, are famous too.

#art-mediums: Paint, clay, paper, glass… art is made from all sorts of materials.

art-mediums:0.fact: Paint mixed with oil. You can paint layer after layer.
art-mediums:0.about:
Oil paint takes a long time to dry, so you can add layers and make changes over many days.
The Mona Lisa is an oil painting. Artists often paint on a cloth called canvas.

art-mediums:1.fact: Paint you thin with water. Its clear, see-through colours are its special feature.
art-mediums:1.about:
The trick of watercolour is using the white of the paper to show the bright parts.
It is the paint used in school art classes too. You can enjoy blending and blurring.

art-mediums:2.fact: Using only ink and a brush, you show dark and light.
art-mediums:2.about:
You grind an ink stick on an inkstone and change the darkness with the amount of water.
You can't fix a line once it's drawn, so you concentrate and paint in one go.

art-mediums:3.fact: You carve wood, put ink on it and press it onto paper to make many copies.
art-mediums:3.about:
A block is carved for each colour, and the colours are printed on top of each other to make a colour picture.
The prints you carve in elementary school art class work the same way.

art-mediums:4.fact: Pictures painted on wet plaster walls. The colours last for hundreds of years.
art-mediums:4.about:
You have to paint before the plaster dries, so artists decide how much to paint each day and go bit by bit.
The ceiling of the Sistine Chapel was painted in fresco too.

art-mediums:5.fact: Small stones or pieces of glass are arranged to make a picture.
art-mediums:5.about:
Each small piece is one colour, but from far away they make a picture.
The "pixels" in digital photos work in a similar way to mosaics.

art-mediums:6.fact: It is made by carving stone or pouring metal into moulds.
art-mediums:6.about:
Besides carving, there are "bronze statues," made by using a clay shape to make a mould and pouring in metal.
Unlike a painting, you can enjoy walking all the way around it.

art-mediums:7.fact: You shape clay and fire it at a high temperature.
art-mediums:7.about:
There is pottery, made from clay, and porcelain, made from stone powder.
Firing it at more than 1,000 °C makes it hard and strong.

art-mediums:8.fact: A technique where you cut out paper or photos and stick them together.
art-mediums:8.about:
The word comes from the French "coller" (to stick). It started when Picasso and Braque stuck things like newspaper onto their paintings.
You can make one with magazine cut-outs, cloth or even leaves.

art-mediums:9.fact: New art made with computers and tablets.
art-mediums:9.about:
When you draw with a tablet and pen, you can change colours and undo as many times as you like.
Most game characters and anime are made digitally too.

#philosophy-questions: Philosophy means thinking deeply about "Why?" and "Really?" There isn't always just one answer. Talk about it with your friends!

philosophy-questions:0.fact: You replace the old planks one by one with new ones. When they've all been replaced, is it the same ship or a different one?
philosophy-questions:0.about:
A puzzle that comes from the story of the ship of Theseus, a hero of ancient Greece.
Actually, the cells in our bodies are slowly being replaced by new ones too. Even so, are you still the same "you"?

philosophy-questions:1.fact: Chickens hatch from eggs, and eggs are laid by chickens. Which came first?
philosophy-questions:1.about:
A puzzle that even Aristotle in ancient Greece thought about.
Thinking scientifically, maybe the first chicken hatched from an egg laid by a bird that wasn't quite a chicken. What do you think?

philosophy-questions:2.fact: A puzzle by Zeno of ancient Greece. Can fast Achilles never catch a tortoise that started ahead of him? What's wrong with the idea?
philosophy-questions:2.about:
When Achilles reaches where the tortoise was, the tortoise has moved a little further. This repeats forever, so he can never catch up…?
Of course he really can catch up. The key to finding where the thinking went wrong is the maths idea of "infinity."

philosophy-questions:3.fact: If you take grains of sand from a sand pile one at a time, when does it stop being a "pile"?
philosophy-questions:3.about:
One grain of sand is not a pile. Take one grain from a pile and it's still a pile. But if you keep going, at some point it isn't a pile any more.
It's a puzzle about the mystery of words with no clear line, like "lots" and "big."

philosophy-questions:4.fact: Zhuangzi of China dreamed he was a butterfly. "Did I dream I was a butterfly, or is a butterfly dreaming it is me?"
philosophy-questions:4.about:
Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, happily flying around. When he woke up, a thought came to him.
How can we tell the difference between "me in a dream" and "me now"?

philosophy-questions:5.fact: If a tree falls in a forest with no one around, does it make a sound? What is "sound," anyway?
philosophy-questions:5.about:
When a tree falls, the air vibrates. But it's living things with ears and brains that hear it as "sound."
When no one is listening, is there a sound or not? Once you decide what the words mean, the answer starts to appear.

philosophy-questions:6.fact: Is it different for everyone? Is some of it the same for all of us? When do you feel happy?
philosophy-questions:6.about:
Aristotle in ancient Greece thought happiness was "living well."
Eating something delicious, playing with friends, helping someone… happiness comes in many shapes.

philosophy-questions:7.fact: How many do you need? Are you still friends after a fight? Is it OK to think differently from your friends?
philosophy-questions:7.about:
Aristotle thought there were 3 kinds of friendship: "because it's fun," "because it's useful" and "because you value the good in each other."
What does a friend mean to you?

philosophy-questions:8.fact: How can you share a cake fairly? One way is "one person cuts, and the other person chooses first."
philosophy-questions:8.about:
Is it fair for everyone to get the same amount? Or is it fair to give more to someone who is hungry?
"Making things the same" and "making things just right" can be different.

#philosophers: For a very long time, people have asked, "How can we live well?" Let's follow the words of thinkers from around the world.

philosophers:0.fact: "Don't do to others what you wouldn't want done to you." A thinker from China.
philosophers:0.about:
Confucius's sayings were collected by his students in a book called "The Analects."
"Isn't it a joy to learn something and practise it from time to time?" It means reviewing what you've learned is fun.

philosophers:1.fact: "The best thing is like water." Soft water can even wear away rock.
philosophers:1.about:
"Know when you have enough": he taught that being happy with what you already have is happiness.
His ideas are in a short book called the "Laozi" (Tao Te Ching).

philosophers:2.fact: He asked people in town questions and thought things through with them. He believed it was important to "know that you don't know."
philosophers:2.about:
Socrates never wrote a single book. His student Plato wrote down Socrates's conversations.
His way of asking question after question to think more deeply is called the "Socratic method."

philosophers:3.fact: A student of Socrates. He started a school called the "Academy."
philosophers:3.about:
"Academy" became the root of the English word academy.
With a story about people in a cave who only see shadows, he taught how important it is to know "what things are really like."

philosophers:4.fact: "If you keep doing good things, you become a good person." He thought about the importance of habits.
philosophers:4.about:
He studied everything: animals, plants, weather, politics, poetry… so he is called "the father of all learning."
He was also the teacher of Alexander the Great.

philosophers:5.fact: Famous for the butterfly dream story. He taught people to think freely and happily.
philosophers:5.about:
Zhuangzi also wrote a story about a big tree that people thought was "useless," and because of that, it was never cut down and lived a long time.
He teaches that when you change how you look at things, you can see different good points.

philosophers:6.fact: "I think, therefore I am." He thought that even if you doubt everything, there is still you, doing the thinking.
philosophers:6.about:
He was also a mathematician who came up with the "x-axis and y-axis" (coordinates) used in graphs.
He thought hard about "what is truly certain," and he is called the father of modern philosophy.

philosophers:7.fact: "Man is a thinking reed." He said people are weak, but their power to think is wonderful.
philosophers:7.about:
A genius who invented a calculator as a teenager. The unit of pressure, the "pascal," is named after him.
The "hectopascals" in weather forecasts come from his name too.

philosophers:8.fact: He thought we must never treat people only as tools for ourselves.
philosophers:8.about:
People say he went for a walk at exactly the same time every day, so the townspeople set their clocks by him.
He said, "Have the courage to think for yourself."

philosophers:9.fact: "Pile up small things and you can do big things." He is the person in the Ninomiya Kinjirō statues at schools.
philosophers:9.about:
As a child, he studied by reading a book while carrying firewood on his back, and that pose became a statue.
As an adult, he worked hard to help more than 600 villages get back on their feet.

philosophers:10.fact: In "An Encouragement of Learning," he wrote, "Heaven does not create one person above another," and taught the importance of learning.
philosophers:10.about:
From Nakatsu in Ōita, he started Keio Gijuku. He was on the 10,000-yen note until 2024.
He travelled around America and Europe and introduced the world to Japan in his book "Conditions in the West."

philosophers:11.fact: A Japanese philosopher. The "Philosopher's Path" in Kyoto is the path Nishida walked while thinking.
philosophers:11.about:
From Ishikawa. With "An Inquiry into the Good," he is said to have created Japan's first original philosophy.
The "Philosopher's Path" runs along a canal near Ginkaku-ji in Kyoto, and its cherry blossoms are beautiful in spring.

#japanese-values: Japanese has words for important ideas that are hard to translate into one word in other languages.

japanese-values:0.fact: A feeling of treasuring things. Wangari Maathai from Kenya spread it around the world.
japanese-values:0.about:
Wangari Maathai, an environmental activist from Kenya, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004. When she visited Japan in 2005, she was moved by this word.
"MOTTAINAI" is one word that holds the ideas of reduce, reuse, recycle and respect.

japanese-values:1.fact: A word of thanks for the life of the food and for the people who made it.
japanese-values:1.about:
There is no perfect English word for it, so it is explained as "Let's eat" or "Thank you for the food."
When you finish, you say "gochisōsama," to thank the people who rushed around to prepare the meal.

japanese-values:2.fact: Thinking about the other person and welcoming them with your whole heart.
japanese-values:2.about:
The word is said to come from the spirit of the tea ceremony.
In 2013, it was introduced in a speech for Tokyo's Olympic bid and became known around the world.

japanese-values:3.fact: Treasuring each meeting, thinking "this happens only once in a lifetime." The phrase comes from the tea ceremony.
japanese-values:3.about:
Ii Naosuke spread this phrase as the spirit of the tea ceremony. It means that the same tea gathering will never happen again, so welcome your guests with all your heart.
Your everyday time with friends is precious and happens only once too.

japanese-values:4.fact: Finding beauty in old things and simple things.
japanese-values:4.about:
"Kintsugi," fixing a broken bowl with gold, shares the spirit of wabi-sabi. It turns the breakage into part of the bowl's history and beauty.
It is the spirit of finding the good in things that aren't perfect.

japanese-values:5.fact: A purpose or joy that makes every day worth living. In English it is called "ikigai" too.
japanese-values:5.about:
It is sometimes explained as the place where "what you love," "what you're good at" and "what helps others" overlap.
In Okinawa, where many people live long lives, people say many live with a strong ikigai.

japanese-values:6.fact: Everyone getting along and working together. Prince Shōtoku's "Harmony is to be valued" is famous.
japanese-values:6.about:
These are the words of Article 1 of the "Seventeen-Article Constitution," set by Prince Shōtoku in 604.
"Wa" is also used for Japanese things, like "washoku" (Japanese food) and "washitsu" (Japanese-style room).

japanese-values:7.fact: "When you're in trouble, we're in it together." The spirit of helping each other.
japanese-values:7.about:
If you help someone, someday someone will help you. It is a word for everyone supporting each other.
In times of disaster, the way people in Japan help each other has drawn attention from around the world.

japanese-values:8.fact: The idea of making things a little better step by step. Companies around the world use the word "kaizen."
japanese-values:8.about:
An idea born in Japanese factories like Toyota's. All the workers share ideas to make things a little better every day.
In study and sport too, small improvements every day lead to big growth.

#proverbs: Let's compare Japanese proverbs with English proverbs that mean something similar.

proverbs:0.fact: In English, "The early bird catches the worm." Good things come to people who get up early.
proverbs:0.about:
The bird that gets up early gets the worm. It means people who act early get the chances.
In the Japanese version, "sanmon" was a little bit of money in the Edo period.

proverbs:1.fact: However many times you fail, stand up again. It's the spirit of the daruma doll.
proverbs:1.about:
A daruma doll gets back up when you knock it over, so it became the symbol of this proverb.
This Japanese proverb is used just as it is in English too.

proverbs:2.fact: Seeing something once with your own eyes is better than hearing about it a hundred times.
proverbs:2.about:
A proverb that comes from an old Chinese history book.
The English "Seeing is believing" means that seeing something makes you believe it.

proverbs:3.fact: The more of a hurry you're in, the more you should choose the safe, sure way.
proverbs:3.about: It is said to come from an old poem: the boat across Lake Biwa was a shortcut, but sometimes sank in the wind, so it was better to take the long, safe road on land.

proverbs:4.fact: Even experts sometimes fail. It has become an English proverb too.
proverbs:4.about:
Even a monkey that is good at climbing trees sometimes falls. In English people also say "Even Homer sometimes nods" (even the great poet Homer dozes off).
It's important not to worry too much when you make a mistake.

proverbs:5.fact: If you try to do two things at the same time, neither goes well.
proverbs:5.about:
This proverb is said to have come to Japan from Europe in the Meiji period.
The Japanese "abu hachi torazu" (catching neither the horsefly nor the bee) means the same.

proverbs:6.fact: Even small things become big when they're gathered together.
proverbs:6.about:
If you keep making small efforts every day, they add up to great strength.
Even 10 minutes of English study a day adds up to more than 60 hours in a year.

proverbs:7.fact: After a quarrel, people sometimes become better friends than before.
proverbs:7.about:
After rain, the ground dries harder than it was before.
After a fight, if you talk it over and make up, you can sometimes become better friends than before.

proverbs:8.fact: Choose useful things over things that just look nice.
proverbs:8.about:
The Japanese saying comes from people at cherry-blossom viewing who care more about dumplings than the flowers. It means valuing what's useful over looks.
The English proverb, "Bread is better than the songs of birds," means something similar.

proverbs:9.fact: If you keep trying even when it's hard, one day it will pay off.
proverbs:9.about:
Even a cold stone gets warm if you sit on it for three years. It teaches the importance of patiently keeping going.
The English "Rome wasn't built in a day" also means that big things take time.

#living-together: How can we all live together happily? Let's think about it.

living-together:0.fact: "Do to others what you'd be happy to have done to you." Many cultures around the world have a similar teaching.
living-together:0.about:
In English, people say "Treat others the way you want to be treated."
The other way round, Confucius said, "Don't do what you wouldn't want done to you." Compare the two ways of saying it.

living-together:1.fact: If you listen to the other person until the end, you start to understand different ideas.
living-together:1.about:
People can think much faster than they talk, so while listening we often think about other things.
Nodding and asking questions shows the other person that you are really listening.

living-together:2.fact: Take turns to speak, don't laugh at other people's opinions, and give reasons. These are tips for a good discussion.
living-together:2.about: When you disagree, first say what's good about the other person's opinion, then give yours. This helps the discussion move forward.

living-together:3.fact: Majority voting is a quick way to decide. But we want to value the opinions of the few too.
living-together:3.about:
Even when something is decided by a vote, listening to the feelings of people with a minority opinion can lead to a better answer.
Looking for an answer that everyone thinks is "OK" is called "consensus."

living-together:4.fact: So that everyone can be safe and treated fairly. Rules can also be changed by talking things over.
living-together:4.about:
If you could use your hands in soccer, the game would be a mess. Rules are promises so everyone can have fun.
Try making your own class rules together.

living-together:5.fact: Things we like, things we're good at, languages… the world is interesting because people are different.
living-together:5.about:
There are more than 7,000 languages and many cultures in the world.
Learning about differences lets you meet new ways of thinking.

living-together:6.fact: People say that when you share your thanks, you feel happy too.
living-together:6.about:
One study found that when people wrote thank-you letters, the writers felt happier for weeks.
"Thank you" is a word treasured all over the world.

living-together:7.fact: Saying sorry when you make a mistake, and forgiving. Both take courage.
living-together:7.about:
When you say sorry, putting into words what you did wrong helps your feelings come across.
Forgiving also makes your own heart feel lighter.

#hello-world: There are said to be more than 7,000 languages in the world. How many can you say hello in?

hello-world:0.fact: "Hello." It is used in many countries, like the UK, the USA and Australia.
hello-world:0.about: About 400 million people speak English as their first language, but with people who learn it as a second language, it's more than 1.5 billion. It is the most studied language in the world.

hello-world:1.fact: "Nǐ hǎo." One of the languages with the most speakers in the world.
hello-world:1.about: Chinese has 4 tones (voice pitches), so the same "ma" can mean "mother," "horse" and other things.

hello-world:2.about: Korean puts words in an order very similar to Japanese. Some words are similar to Japanese too, like "gabang" (bag), "kaban" in Japanese.

hello-world:3.fact: "Hola." The language of Spain and many countries in Central and South America.
hello-world:3.about:
An official language in more than 20 countries. More than 40 million people speak it in the USA too.
Like "¡Hola!", it has an upside-down "¡" at the start of a sentence.

hello-world:4.fact: "Bonjour." It is spoken in France, Canada and countries in Africa too.
hello-world:4.about:
About 30% of English words are said to come from French.
Restaurant, menu and ballet come from French too.

hello-world:5.fact: "Hallo." It is spoken in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
hello-world:5.about:
In German, every noun starts with a capital letter.
The Japanese words "arubaito" (part-time job, from Arbeit = work) and "karute" (medical chart) come from German.

hello-world:6.fact: "Ciao." You can use it for both "hello" and "bye-bye."
hello-world:6.about:
Many music words are Italian, like piano, forte, tempo and soprano.
Spaghetti and pizza are Italian words too.

hello-world:7.fact: "Olá." The language of Portugal and Brazil. The Japanese word "pan" (bread) comes from Portuguese!
hello-world:7.about: The Japanese words "pan" (bread), "botan" (button), "kappa" (raincoat) and "tempura" are said to come from Portuguese. Portuguese people who came to Nagasaki in the 16th century brought them.

hello-world:8.fact: "Privet." It is written in Cyrillic letters.
hello-world:8.about:
Russian is the language of Russia, the biggest country in the world. It is written in Cyrillic letters.
"Ikra" means "fish eggs" in Russian, and that's where the Japanese word "ikura" comes from.

hello-world:9.fact: "Marhaba." A language written from right to left.
hello-world:9.about:
A language spoken in more than 20 countries. The numbers 0 to 9 spread around the world through Arabia.
The English words sugar and coffee come from Arabic too.

hello-world:10.fact: "Namaste." In India, people put their hands together when they greet each other.
hello-world:10.about:
One of the official languages of India. Hundreds of languages are spoken in India, and English is widely used too.
The English words shampoo and pyjamas come from Hindi.

hello-world:11.fact: "Sawasdee." You say it with a "wai," putting your hands together.
hello-world:11.about:
Thai has 5 tones.
To speak politely, men add "khrap" and women add "kha" at the end of a sentence.

hello-world:12.fact: "Jambo." It is spoken in Kenya and Tanzania.
hello-world:12.about:
More than 100 million people in East Africa use it. "Safari" means "journey" in Swahili.
"Hakuna matata" means "no worries."

hello-world:13.fact: "Aloha." It has many meanings, like "hello," "goodbye" and "love."
hello-world:13.about:
The Hawaiian alphabet has only 13 letters (5 vowels and 8 consonants).
"Mahalo" means "thank you." "Aloha" carries feelings of love and kindness.

hello-world:14.fact: "Kia ora." The language of the first people of New Zealand.
hello-world:14.about:
Māori is an official language of New Zealand, along with English and sign language.
New Zealand's Māori name is "Aotearoa" (land of the long white cloud).

hello-world:15.fact: "Irankarapte." The language of the Ainu of Hokkaido. It means "Let me gently touch your heart."
hello-world:15.about:
The language of the Ainu people, who live in Hokkaido and other places. It has no writing and has been passed down through songs and stories.
Many place names in Hokkaido come from Ainu, like "Sapporo" and "Shiretoko."

#school-lunch-world: What's for lunch? What do children around the world eat for lunch at school?

school-lunch-world:0.fact: It is said to have started in Yamagata in 1889. Children on lunch duty serve it themselves.
school-lunch-world:0.about:
Japanese school lunches are balanced menus planned by nutritionists. Children serving and clearing up by themselves is said to be rare in the world.
Nagasaki school lunches sometimes have champon or sara udon.

school-lunch-world:1.fact: Rice, soup and side dishes like kimchi on a metal tray. Children eat with chopsticks and a spoon.
school-lunch-world:1.about: In South Korea, school lunch is free at many schools. It comes with rice, soup and 3 or 4 side dishes like kimchi.

school-lunch-world:2.fact: It is sometimes served like a full meal: starter, main course, cheese and dessert.
school-lunch-world:2.about:
French school lunch is a course meal: starter, main, cheese and dessert. Some schools have a lunch break of nearly an hour and a half.
Eating is thought of as part of education.

school-lunch-world:3.fact: In 1948, it became the first country in the world to give free school lunch to every child.
school-lunch-world:3.about: It is a buffet, and children take as much as they will eat. They can drink as much milk or water as they like.

school-lunch-world:4.fact: Pizza, chicken and milk cartons. Many schools let children choose in the cafeteria.
school-lunch-world:4.about: In the school cafeteria, children choose from the menu and put it on their trays. Many children also bring a lunch box from home.

school-lunch-world:5.fact: Rice and stewed black beans (feijão) are the classic.
school-lunch-world:5.about: In Brazil, a law says school lunches must use food grown by local farmers.

school-lunch-world:6.fact: India's school lunch, eaten by tens of millions of children every day, is one of the biggest in the world.
school-lunch-world:6.about: Schools serve a hot lunch so that children come to school and study. Bean curry (dal) and rice are the classic.

school-lunch-world:7.fact: Pasta and dishes made with local vegetables are served.
school-lunch-world:7.about: Using fresh local food, schools serve pasta, a main dish, salad and fruit. Many schools use organic food.

school-lunch-world:8.fact: There are days with jacket potatoes (baked potatoes with the skin on) or fish and chips.
school-lunch-world:8.about:
Lunch staff called "dinner ladies" serve the food. Lunch is free for younger elementary school children.
At some schools, Friday is fish and chips day.

#orchestra: An orchestra is made of 4 groups: strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion.

orchestra:0.fact: The instrument with the most players in an orchestra. It plays high notes.
orchestra:0.about:
Inside the body there is a little post called the "sound post," which helps the sound ring.
The hair of the bow is made from horse tail hair.

orchestra:1.fact: A little bigger than a violin, with a softer sound.
orchestra:1.about: A bit bigger than a violin, with a slightly lower sound. It has the important job of supporting the harmony.

orchestra:2.fact: You sit and play it held between your knees. Its sound is said to be like a human voice.
orchestra:2.about: You stand its endpin on the floor and play it sitting down. It has a wide range, so it can "sing" from low notes to high notes.

orchestra:3.fact: The biggest string instrument. It is usually played standing up.
orchestra:3.about: It is about 1.8 m tall, sometimes taller than a person. In jazz, it is usually played by plucking the strings with your fingers.

orchestra:4.fact: You pluck its 47 strings with your fingers.
orchestra:4.about:
It has 7 pedals at the bottom, and pressing them changes the pitch.
People playing harps are even painted on the walls of ancient Egypt.

orchestra:5.fact: It is made of metal, but it belongs to the woodwind family.
orchestra:5.about: It used to be made of wood, so it is still a "woodwind." It doesn't use a reed. You blow across it like blowing across the top of a bottle.

orchestra:6.fact: Before a concert, everyone tunes to the oboe's "A" note.
orchestra:6.about:
It makes sound by vibrating 2 thin reeds. Players often make their own reeds by hand.
Its high, clear sound carries a long way.

orchestra:7.fact: It makes sound by vibrating one "reed."
orchestra:7.about: An instrument with a very wide range, from low notes to high notes. It is a central instrument in wind bands too.

orchestra:8.fact: A low-sounding woodwind. If you stretched out its tube, it would be 2.5 m long.
orchestra:8.about: A woodwind with a long tube folded up. With its funny low sound, it can show things like an animal walking.

orchestra:9.fact: A coiled-up tube. Stretched out, it would be about 4 m long.
orchestra:9.about: It started as a hunting horn used for signals. The player puts their right hand inside the bell to adjust the pitch and sound.

orchestra:10.fact: A bright, loud sound. It often plays the melody.
orchestra:10.about:
It makes notes of different pitches with combinations of its 3 valves and the buzzing of the lips.
Fanfares are what trumpets do best.

orchestra:11.fact: You slide the "slide" in and out to change the pitch.
orchestra:11.about: Moving the slide changes the length of the tube, so the sound slides smoothly up and down.

orchestra:12.fact: A big instrument that plays the lowest notes in the brass family.
orchestra:12.about: Stretched out straight, its tube would be more than 5 m long. It supports the very bottom of the orchestra's sound.

orchestra:13.fact: Drums that look like big pots. You can change their pitch.
orchestra:13.about:
Drums whose pitch can be changed by using a pedal to tighten or loosen the skin. Players use 2 to 5 of them in a row.
They can make powerful sounds like thunder or a heartbeat.

orchestra:14.fact: With a baton, the conductor shows the tempo and feeling and brings everyone's sound together.
orchestra:14.about:
The conductor doesn't play an instrument but shows the tempo, the volume and the feeling of the music.
Before the concert, they study the score and learn every part of the piece.

#composers: The composers on the music room wall. What kind of music did they write?

composers:0.fact: "The Four Seasons" shows spring, summer, autumn and winter with violins.
composers:0.about:
A musician from Venice. He taught music at a home for girls and wrote lots of pieces for his students.
You may have heard "Spring" from "The Four Seasons" at school or on TV.

composers:1.fact: A composer called "the father of music." He wrote more than 1,000 pieces.
composers:1.about:
Bach's family were all musicians, and he had more than 20 children.
Pieces like "Air on the G String" and "Minuet" are still played all over the world.

composers:2.fact: A genius who started composing at age 5. He also wrote variations on "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star."
composers:2.about:
In his short life of 35 years, he wrote more than 600 pieces.
As a child, he toured all over Europe giving concerts, and he amazed people by playing the piano blindfolded.

composers:3.fact: He kept composing even after he lost his hearing. In Japan, his "Ninth" is a classic at the end of the year.
composers:3.about:
Even after he could no longer hear, he heard the music in his mind and kept writing great pieces.
The "Ode to Joy" from his Ninth Symphony is sung by choirs all over Japan at the end of every year.

composers:4.fact: "The poet of the piano." He was born in Poland and wrote lots of piano music.
composers:4.about:
A Polish composer who worked in Paris. Almost all the music he wrote was for piano.
Every 5 years, the "International Chopin Piano Competition" is held in Poland.

composers:5.fact: He wrote the ballets "The Nutcracker" and "Swan Lake."
composers:5.about:
A Russian composer. "The Nutcracker" is a ballet about a magical Christmas night.
In the "Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy," the celesta makes a twinkling, magical sound.

composers:6.fact: A Japanese composer who wrote "Kōjō no Tsuki" and "Hana."
composers:6.about:
He was born in Tokyo and spent his childhood in Taketa, Ōita.
He went to Germany as the second Japanese person to study music abroad, but he died young, at 23. He also wrote "Oshōgatsu."

composers:7.fact: Famous for "Clair de Lune." He even used a Hokusai print on the cover of his music.
composers:7.about:
A French composer. He loved Hokusai's "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" and used it on the cover of his music "La Mer" (The Sea).
His dreamy sounds, like light or water, have a lot in common with Impressionist paintings.

composers:8.fact: The suite "The Planets." He showed Jupiter, Mars and other planets through music.
composers:8.about:
An English composer. He wrote music about 7 planets (the Earth is not included).
The melody of "Jupiter" became a big hit in Japan as a song too.

composers:9.fact: A Japanese composer who wrote "Akatombo" and "Kono Michi."
composers:9.about:
One of the first people to create a real orchestra in Japan.
Besides "Akatombo," he wrote many children's songs, like "Kono Michi" and "Pechka."

#world-instruments: Around the world there are all kinds of instruments made from local wood, bamboo, animal horns and more.

world-instruments:0.fact: A Japanese instrument where you pluck 13 strings with picks on your fingers.
world-instruments:0.about:
It came from China about 1,300 years ago. You move the "ji," bridges that hold up the strings, to tune it.
"Haru no Umi," often played at New Year, is a piece for koto and shakuhachi.

world-instruments:1.fact: A Japanese bamboo flute. Its name comes from its length: 1 shaku 8 sun (about 54 cm).
world-instruments:1.about:
It has only 4 holes on the front and 1 on the back. Players make many different sounds by changing the angle and strength of their breath.
Its sound is used in movie music around the world too.

world-instruments:2.fact: An Okinawan instrument with 3 strings. It is one of the ancestors of the shamisen.
world-instruments:2.about:
An Okinawan instrument with snakeskin on its body. It came from China around the 15th century.
It is essential for Okinawan folk songs and Eisā music.

world-instruments:3.fact: A Chinese instrument with 2 strings. The bow goes between the strings.
world-instruments:3.about:
A Chinese instrument with snakeskin on its body. You play it with the bow held between its 2 strings.
Its sound is sad and sweet, like a singing voice.

world-instruments:4.fact: A Korean instrument with 12 strings. It looks like the Japanese koto.
world-instruments:4.about:
A traditional Korean instrument with more than 1,500 years of history. You play it by plucking silk strings with your fingers.
Today some players even play K-pop songs on the gayageum.

world-instruments:5.fact: A string instrument from India with a mysterious sound.
world-instruments:5.about:
It has nearly 20 strings. Besides the strings you play, there are "sympathetic strings" that ring along with them.
It became known around the world when the British band the Beatles used it in their songs.

world-instruments:6.fact: An instrument of Australia's First Peoples. It is made from a tree hollowed out by termites.
world-instruments:6.about:
Players buzz their lips to make a long, low droning sound.
They use a skill called "circular breathing": breathing in through the nose while still blowing out through the mouth.

world-instruments:7.fact: An instrument from Scotland. It stores air in a bag so it can keep playing without stopping.
world-instruments:7.about:
With the air stored in the bag, it can keep sounding without a break.
Players wearing the Scottish "kilt" are a famous sight.

world-instruments:8.fact: An instrument from Trinidad and Tobago, made from an oil drum.
world-instruments:8.about:
Oil drums are hammered and dented so that different parts play different notes.
It is one of the newest acoustic instruments, born in the 20th century.

world-instruments:9.fact: A small Hawaiian instrument with 4 strings. It comes from a Portuguese instrument.
world-instruments:9.about:
Its name is said to mean "jumping flea" in Hawaiian, from the way players' fingers hop around.
It's small and easy to play, so it is sometimes used in school music lessons.

world-instruments:10.fact: A drum from West Africa. You play it with your hands.
world-instruments:10.about:
A drum with goatskin stretched over a hollowed-out wooden body. Depending on how you hit it with your hand, it can make low or high sounds.
It is popular in "drum circles," where everyone plays together in a ring.

world-instruments:11.fact: A "thumb piano" from Africa. You pluck metal strips with your thumbs.
world-instruments:11.about:
In Africa it is called names like "mbira," and it has been played for hundreds of years.
It is small enough to hold in your hands and has a gentle sound like a music box.

world-instruments:12.fact: A long wooden horn used in the mountains of Switzerland. Some are more than 3 m long.
world-instruments:12.about:
It was first used in the mountains to call cows and send signals to faraway villages.
Its sound echoes off the mountains and is said to carry 10 km.

world-instruments:13.fact: A flute made of tubes of different lengths in a row. It is famous in Andean music.
world-instruments:13.about:
A flute made of bamboo or reed tubes lined up from longest to shortest. The longer the tube, the lower the note.
It is often used in "folklore" music from Peru and Bolivia.

#world-dance: Let's dance! There are all kinds of dances around the world.

world-dance:0.fact: Dancers dance on their toes. It developed in France and Russia.
world-dance:0.about:
It was born in the royal courts of Italy, and King Louis XIV of France loved it and helped it grow.
Ballet words are still French. Dancers stand on their toes in pointe shoes.

world-dance:1.fact: A Spanish dance. Dancers make rhythms with clapping and the sound of their shoes.
world-dance:1.about:
An art of singing, guitar and dance born in Andalusia in southern Spain.
Dancers make strong rhythms with hand clapping ("palmas") and by striking the floor with their shoes ("zapateado").

world-dance:2.fact: A dance from Hawaii. Dancers tell stories with their hand movements.
world-dance:2.about:
In old Hawaii, which had no writing, it was an important way to pass on history and myths.
Each hand movement has a meaning, like "sea," "flower" or "rain."

world-dance:3.fact: A traditional Māori dance. New Zealand's rugby team performs it before matches too.
world-dance:3.about:
A traditional Māori dance that shows strength with stamping feet, wide eyes and tongues stuck out.
It is also performed at celebrations and to show welcome and respect.

world-dance:4.fact: A lively dance danced at Brazil's carnival.
world-dance:4.about:
It grew out of the music and dances of Afro-Brazilian people.
Dancers move their feet very quickly to the fast rhythm of the drums.

world-dance:5.fact: A dance for two people, born in Argentina.
world-dance:5.about:
It was born at the end of the 19th century in the port of Buenos Aires, Argentina.
