club-origins-culture:2.fact: Painting, clay, design. You make art with whatever you like.
club-origins-culture:2.about:
In the art club, you paint pictures, make things from clay and wood, and design posters.
You might show your work at the school festival or enter contests. More and more art clubs are drawing digital illustrations too.

club-origins-culture:3.fact: You do experiments and observations and present your research.
club-origins-culture:3.about:
In the science club, you do experiments, observe living things and stars, and make rockets and robots.
There are contests where junior high students present their research, like the Japan Students Science Awards, held since 1957. It's like carrying on your elementary school summer projects.

club-origins-culture:4.fact: You make games and apps with programming.
club-origins-culture:4.about:
In the computer club, you make games and apps with programming and edit videos.
There are contests where junior high and high school students compete in programming. The ways of thinking about programming you learned in elementary school will help.

club-origins-culture:5.fact: They do the lunchtime broadcasts and host school events.
club-origins-culture:5.about:
The broadcasting club does the lunchtime broadcasts, the announcements at events and makes the school news programme.
Members practise speaking clearly and writing scripts. Many TV announcers were in the broadcasting club when they were students.

club-origins-culture:6.fact: You learn how to make tea and the spirit of hospitality.
club-origins-culture:6.about:
In the tea ceremony club, you learn how to whisk matcha, how to bow and how to eat the sweets.
"Ichigo ichie," which is important in the tea ceremony, means "This meeting happens only once in a lifetime, so welcome your guest with all your heart."

club-origins-culture:7.fact: There's even "calligraphy performance," where you write on huge paper to music.
club-origins-culture:7.about:
In the calligraphy club, you practise writing characters beautifully with a brush and ink.
"Calligraphy performance," where a team writes on huge paper to music, is popular too. The national high school championship is held in Ehime.

club-origins-culture:8.fact: Some teams build robots and aim for world championships.
club-origins-culture:8.about:
In the robotics club, you build robots and make them move with programs. There are contests where robots complete set tasks, and even contests for robots that play football.
Japanese teams do well at world contests like the WRO (World Robot Olympiad), where children from around the world take part.

club-origins-culture:9.fact: Traditional Japanese games that train your thinking.
club-origins-culture:9.about:
Shogi and go are both board games where you think many moves ahead. Shogi has a rule that is unusual in the world: you can use the pieces you capture as your own.
Go was born in China, and now it's played all over the world. Some people become professionals while they're in junior high school.

#secondary-schools-world: What kind of schools do junior high students around the world go to? Uniforms, timetables, holidays… they're all different.

secondary-schools-world:0.fact: Everyone has their own locker. Students ride yellow school buses.
secondary-schools-world:0.about:
In many parts of America, students in grades 6 to 8 go to "middle school." Each student has a locker in the hallway, and they move to a different classroom for each subject.
Yellow school buses are a symbol of American schools. When students finish, they make a "yearbook" full of photos.

secondary-schools-world:1.fact: Many schools have uniforms with ties, and students are split into teams called "houses."
secondary-schools-world:1.about:
In the UK, children go to "secondary school" from age 11. Many have a uniform with a blazer and tie.
At some schools, students are split into teams called "houses" and compete for points in sports and events. At 16, they take important exams called "GCSEs."

secondary-schools-world:2.fact: Lessons are fairly short, and school lunch is free.
secondary-schools-world:2.about:
In Finland, the school day has fairly short lessons, and time to rest outside between lessons is valued.
School lunch has been free for everyone since 1948. Because students do so well, teachers from all over the world come to visit.

secondary-schools-world:3.fact: A country where studying is very important. Some students study until night.
secondary-schools-world:3.about:
South Korea is a country where studying is very important, and many students go to "hagwon" (cram schools) after school.
On the day of the university entrance exam, companies start work later so students aren't late, and planes are stopped during the listening test.

secondary-schools-world:4.fact: At around 10, children decide which type of school to go to next.
secondary-schools-world:4.about:
In Germany, elementary school lasts 4 years (until about age 10). Then children choose from several types of school, like ones for going to university and ones for learning job skills.
On the first day of school, there is a custom of getting a big cone called a "Schultüte," filled with sweets and stationery.

secondary-schools-world:5.fact: Junior high school is called "collège." Many schools have Wednesday afternoons off.
secondary-schools-world:5.about:
In France, children aged 11 to 15 go to "collège." Grades are given out of 20.
Many schools have no lessons on Wednesday afternoons, so children do sports or other activities. Lunchtime is long, so they can take their time eating school lunch.

secondary-schools-world:6.fact: Children on faraway farms go to the "School of the Air" and learn from a distance.
secondary-schools-world:6.about:
In the middle of Australia, there are farms hundreds of kilometres from any town. So in 1951, the "School of the Air," which taught lessons by radio, began.
Now children study with teachers far away over the internet, through a screen.

secondary-schools-world:7.fact: It has the world's biggest school, with more than 50,000 students.
secondary-schools-world:7.about:
India is a country with a huge number of children. In Lucknow in northern India, there is the world's biggest school, with more than 50,000 students.
In many areas, children learn two or more languages, such as English and their local language.

secondary-schools-world:8.fact: Japan starts in April. But many countries start in September.
secondary-schools-world:8.about:
Japanese schools start in April, in cherry blossom season. But in many countries, like America, the UK, France and China, the new school year starts in September.
In Australia and Brazil, in the Southern Hemisphere, the summer holidays end in January or February, and the new school year starts then.

#summer-japan: "I went to the summer festival. I enjoyed fireworks." The fun of summer in Japan has a long history.

summer-japan:0.fact: The colours of fireworks change depending on the kind of metal mixed in.
summer-japan:0.about:
The colours of fireworks are decided by the metals mixed into the gunpowder. Strontium makes red, sodium makes yellow, barium makes green and copper makes blue. It's the "flame test" from science class.
Tokyo's Sumida River Fireworks are said to come from a river festival in Ryōgoku that began in 1733. Ōmagari in Akita and Nagaoka in Niigata are famous too.

summer-japan:1.fact: Food stalls, bon dancing and portable shrines. The whole town gets lively.
summer-japan:1.about:
At summer festivals, food stalls line the streets, people do bon dancing, and portable shrines and floats move through the town. Many festivals are to drive away summer heat and illness and to wish for a good harvest.
Summer in Nagasaki has Shōrō Nagashi and peiron boat races. Going out in a yukata is part of the fun of summer.

summer-japan:2.fact: A summer event where families gather to welcome their ancestors.
summer-japan:2.about:
Obon is an event in August (July in some areas) when people have long believed their ancestors come back home. Many people return to their home towns, and families get together.
Each area has its own customs, like welcoming and farewell fires, bon dancing and Nagasaki's Shōrō Nagashi.

summer-japan:3.fact: It started in 1928 and became a classic summer holiday morning activity.
summer-japan:3.about:
Radio exercises began on radio broadcasts in 1928. They are exercises anyone can do, moving lots of different parts of the body.
Gathering in the park on summer holiday mornings to exercise and get a stamp on your card is a classic scene of summer in Japan.

summer-japan:4.fact: A big summer holiday homework where you choose your own topic and research it.
summer-japan:4.about:
A "free research project" is summer holiday homework where you choose your own topic and research it, do experiments or make something.
Finding out about things you wonder "why?" about is a scientist's first step. Sometimes new discoveries have come from elementary school students' projects.

summer-japan:5.fact: It opens in the morning and closes by noon. A classic for observation diaries.
summer-japan:5.about:
Morning glories open their flowers around dawn and close by noon. The vines wind around their poles in one particular direction as they grow.
They came from China as medicine around the Nara period, and in the Edo period there was a boom in growing morning glories with rare colours and shapes.

summer-japan:6.fact: It even appears in "The Pillow Book," written more than 1,000 years ago.
summer-japan:6.about:
Shaved ice appears in "The Pillow Book," written by Sei Shōnagon more than 1,000 years ago, as ice with sweet syrup. Back then it was a real luxury, made with winter ice stored in an "ice house."
Today there are lots of flavours, like strawberry, melon and Uji kintoki (green tea and sweet beans).

summer-japan:7.fact: Wearing a blindfold, you split a watermelon by following people's voices.
summer-japan:7.about:
Watermelon splitting is a game where you wear a blindfold, hold a stick, and split a watermelon by following the people around you shouting "Right!" and "Forward!"
Watermelons come from Africa and are about 90% water. They're the perfect fruit for hot summers.

summer-japan:8.fact: A clever Japanese way to feel cool through a tinkling sound.
summer-japan:8.about:
Wind chimes came from bells hung under the eaves of temples in China. Glass wind chimes spread in the Edo period.
Feeling cool from a sound is part of Japanese summer wisdom. Nanbu wind chimes (iron) from Iwate and Edo wind chimes (glass) from Tokyo are famous.

summer-japan:9.fact: You catch sōmen noodles flowing down a bamboo chute with your chopsticks.
summer-japan:9.about:
Water and sōmen noodles are sent down a chute made from split bamboo, and you scoop them up with chopsticks and eat them. Takachiho in Miyazaki is said to be one of the places where it started.
Shimabara in Nagasaki is known for hand-stretched sōmen. Sōmen must be less than 1.3 mm thick.

#summer-world: Summer holidays in Japan last about 6 weeks. Some countries have 3 months off, and in some, Christmas comes in summer!

summer-world:0.fact: The summer holidays last from June to September, about 3 months!
summer-world:0.about:
In Italy, the summer holidays last from mid-June to mid-September, about 3 months. Summers are very hot, so schools began closing then.
Families go to the sea or the mountains, and on summer evenings they enjoy strolling and eating gelato in the town square.

summer-world:1.fact: The summer holidays are about 6 weeks, about the same as in Japan.
summer-world:1.about:
In the UK, the summer holidays last from late July to early September, about 6 weeks. Many schools give almost no summer homework.
Eating ice cream and fish and chips in seaside towns is a classic summer treat.

summer-world:2.fact: Children spend weeks with friends by lakes and in forests.
summer-world:2.about:
American summer holidays last about 2 to 3 months. Many children go to "summer camp" by lakes or in forests for days, or sometimes weeks.
Away from their families, they try canoeing, campfires, hiking and crafts with friends. Toasting marshmallows over the campfire is a classic.

summer-world:3.fact: People wear flower crowns and dance around a pole.
summer-world:3.about:
In Sweden, "Midsummer" is celebrated around the summer solstice, when the days are longest. People dance around a pole decorated with flowers (a maypole), and there's even a song where they dance like frogs.
They wear flower crowns and eat new potatoes and strawberries. It stays light outside even at night.

summer-world:4.fact: December is summer! People spend Christmas at the beach.
summer-world:4.about:
In Australia, in the Southern Hemisphere, December is the middle of summer. People spend Christmas having barbecues and surfing at the beach.
There are even decorations of Santa Claus on a surfboard. The seasons are the opposite of Japan's.

summer-world:5.fact: Spending time in a cottage by a lake, with a sun that never sets.
summer-world:5.about:
Finland is said to have more than 500,000 summer cottages called "mökki." Having a sauna by the lake and then jumping into the water is a summer treat.
In the north, there's the "midnight sun," when the sun doesn't set all day in summer.

summer-world:6.fact: For two months, July and August, many people take a long break.
summer-world:6.about:
In France, the school summer holidays, "les grandes vacances," last about 2 months, July and August. Grown-ups often take several weeks off in a row too.
In August in Paris, some shops close for the holidays. Lots of people head to the beaches in the south or to the mountains.

summer-world:7.fact: A summer treat of milk ice topped with fruit and red beans.
summer-world:7.about:
Bingsu is a Korean summer treat of finely shaved ice or milk ice topped with red beans, fruit, rice cakes, kinako (roasted soybean flour) and more.
"Patbingsu," topped with red beans, is the traditional flavour. It's served on a big plate and shared by everyone.

summer-world:8.fact: A custom of resting on hot afternoons. Shops sometimes close too.
summer-world:8.about:
In hot countries like Spain, there was a custom of taking a long lunch break and resting in the hottest part of the afternoon. This is called a "siesta."
Instead, dinner is very late, around 9 p.m. Now town life has changed, and more and more people don't take a siesta.

#seaside-science: "I went to the sea. I saw a crab." The seaside is full of science mysteries!

seaside-science:0.fact: The Moon pulls on the sea, so the tide comes in and goes out about twice a day.
seaside-science:0.about:
The Moon's pull (gravity) makes the sea bulge out towards the Moon and on the opposite side. Because the Earth turns once a day, most seashores get high tide and low tide about twice a day.
Around the new moon and the full moon, the Sun's pull adds to it, making "spring tides" with a big difference. The Ariake Sea has the biggest tides in Japan.

seaside-science:1.fact: Most waves are made by wind blowing over the sea.
seaside-science:1.about:
Most waves are made when wind blowing over the sea pushes the water. Waves made by a faraway typhoon can travel thousands of kilometres to reach the shore.
The water itself doesn't move forward; it moves round in circles in the same place. What a wave carries is "energy."

seaside-science:2.fact: Salt dissolved from rocks was carried to the sea by rivers.
seaside-science:2.about:
When rain soaks into rocks and soil, tiny amounts of salt and other things dissolve, and rivers carry them to the sea. Sea water evaporates in the sun, but the salt stays behind.
After this happened over a very, very long time, the sea became salty. About 3.5% of sea water is salt.

seaside-science:3.fact: Okinawa's star-shaped sand is the shells of tiny creatures.
seaside-science:3.about:
"Star sand," found on islands in Okinawa like Taketomi and Iriomote, is the shells of tiny creatures called "foraminifera."
Sand is usually made from broken-up rock, but some white beaches are made from bits of coral and shells. Look at beach sand with a magnifying glass!

seaside-science:4.fact: Their spiral shapes follow a beautiful number pattern.
seaside-science:4.about:
A snail shell has a spiral shape that widens little by little as it grows. Similar shapes can be seen in the way sunflower seeds are arranged and in the swirl of a typhoon.
Shells are mostly made of calcium carbonate, the same as chalk and marble.

seaside-science:5.fact: Bits of glass are polished by waves for decades.
seaside-science:5.about:
When bits of glass from things like bottles are polished by waves and sand for decades, their corners wear away and they look like frosted glass. This is sea glass.
White, brown and green are common, and blue and red are rare. When you pick it up, check that the edges aren't sharp.

seaside-science:6.fact: When the tide goes out, you can meet crabs, hermit crabs and sea anemones.
seaside-science:6.about:
When the tide goes out, water is left in hollows in the rocks, making "tide pools." Crabs, hermit crabs, sea anemones, starfish and small fish live there.
After looking at creatures, gently put them back where they were. Go rock-pooling with a grown-up, and check the tide times first.

seaside-science:7.fact: The beaches of Yakushima get more loggerhead turtles than anywhere else in Japan.
seaside-science:7.about:
The beaches of Yakushima in Kagoshima are among the places in the North Pacific where the most loggerhead turtles come to lay eggs. At night, the mother turtle digs a hole in the sand and lays about 100 eggs.
About 2 months later, the baby turtles all head for the sea together at night. Bright lights can make the baby turtles lose their way.

seaside-science:8.fact: Even when plastic breaks into tiny pieces, it doesn't go away.
seaside-science:8.about:
Most rubbish on beaches is plastic. Even when ultraviolet light and waves break plastic into tiny pieces, it doesn't break down naturally, and it stays in the sea as "microplastics."
On islands like Tsushima in Nagasaki, lots of rubbish washes up from other countries too. A beach clean is something anyone can do.

seaside-science:9.fact: If you get pulled out to sea, swim parallel to the shore to escape.
seaside-science:9.about:
A "rip current" is a strong current flowing from the shore out to sea. Even good swimmers find it hard to swim against it back to the shore.
If you get pulled out, stay calm and swim parallel to the shore to get out of the current, or float and wave for help. At the sea, a life jacket and a grown-up keep you safe.

#camping-outdoors: "I went camping. I saw many stars." Let's learn the skills for spending time in nature.

camping-outdoors:0.fact: A Mongolian ger is a round home you can put up and carry.
camping-outdoors:0.about:
The "ger," the home of Mongolian nomads, is a round house made of a wooden frame covered with felt, and it can be put up in 1 to 2 hours. It suits a life of moving with the animals each season.
People all over the world have come up with homes they can carry. Today's tents carry on that wisdom.

camping-outdoors:1.fact: Fire needs three things: fuel, air and heat.
camping-outdoors:1.about:
For something to burn, it needs three things: fuel (wood), air (oxygen) and heat. This is called the "fire triangle."
To put out a campfire, pour water on it to take away the heat and cut off the air. Always use fire with a grown-up, and have water ready.

camping-outdoors:2.fact: Vega, Altair and Deneb. It includes the Tanabata stars too.
camping-outdoors:2.about:
In the summer night sky, if you join Vega in Lyra, Altair in Aquila and Deneb in Cygnus, you get a big triangle.
Vega is Orihime and Altair is Hikoboshi, the two people in the Tanabata story. At campsites with few town lights, you can see the Milky Way too.

camping-outdoors:3.fact: The red end of the needle always points north.
camping-outdoors:3.about:
A compass needle is a magnet. The Earth is like a giant magnet, so the needle always points north and south.
It was invented in China, and sailors long ago used it to find their way at sea. Using it with a map makes it harder to get lost.

camping-outdoors:4.fact: The bowline is called the "king of knots."
camping-outdoors:4.about:
A bowline makes a loop that stays the same size and is easy to untie even after being pulled hard. It's used on boats and in rescues, and it's called the "king of knots."
There are lots of knots for different jobs, like the reef knot and the round turn and two half hitches. Knowing how to tie rope helps when camping and in disasters.

camping-outdoors:5.fact: Curry and rice at camp is a Japanese classic!
camping-outdoors:5.about:
A "hangō" is a pot for cooking rice outdoors. At Japanese camps, cooking rice in a hangō and making curry is a classic.
Just like with a kamado, the trick to tasty rice is the fire: "First a small flame, then a big flame in the middle."

camping-outdoors:6.fact: Only female mosquitoes, which lay eggs, bite people.
camping-outdoors:6.about:
Only female mosquitoes bite people. They need blood for the nutrients to make eggs. Males drink things like flower nectar.
Mosquitoes find people by following the carbon dioxide we breathe out, our body heat and our smell. Long sleeves and insect repellent keep them away.

camping-outdoors:7.fact: Take your rubbish home and leave nature as it is.
camping-outdoors:7.about:
"Leave it more beautiful than when you came" is a saying people value at camps and in the mountains. Take your rubbish home, don't trample plants, and don't feed wild animals.
Around the world, the same idea, "Leave No Trace," is spreading.

camping-outdoors:8.fact: Rain gear, water, a hat and a torch. Be ready for the weather to change.
camping-outdoors:8.about:
Weather in the mountains and by rivers changes easily, so bring rain gear, a jacket, a hat, water, a torch and plasters.
In summer, watch out for heatstroke and drink water often. Packing heavy things close to your back makes a rucksack easier to carry.

#school-trips-japan: "My best memory is the school trip. We went to Nara." Let's visit the popular places where elementary and junior high students from all over Japan go.

school-trips-japan:0.fact: A very Japanese school event that started in the Meiji period.
school-trips-japan:0.about:
A trip like an outing in 1886 by a Tokyo school (the school that later became the University of Tsukuba) is said to have been the first school trip.
As trains spread, schools all over the country began going to faraway towns. School events where friends travel together for several days are rare in the world.

school-trips-japan:1.fact: Kiyomizu-dera and Kinkaku-ji. A city that was the capital for more than 1,000 years.
school-trips-japan:1.about:
Kyoto was Japan's capital for more than 1,000 years from 794. It has lots of World Heritage Sites and famous places, like Kiyomizu-dera, Kinkaku-ji and the thousands of torii gates of Fushimi Inari Taisha.
On school trips, groups get around by taxi or bus, and buying yatsuhashi sweets as souvenirs is a classic.

school-trips-japan:2.fact: About 1,300 deer live in Nara Park.
school-trips-japan:2.about:
Nara is an old capital, where the city of Heijō-kyō was built in 710. The Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji is about 15 m tall. About 1,300 deer live in Nara Park, and if you give them deer crackers, they sometimes bow.
Hōryū-ji is said to be the oldest wooden building in the world.

school-trips-japan:3.fact: The three wise monkeys, "see no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil," are famous.
school-trips-japan:3.about:
Nikkō Tōshō-gū in Tochigi has carvings of the three wise monkeys, "see no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil," and the "sleeping cat."
Nearby Kegon Falls is 97 m high. In autumn, the mountains turn red and yellow, and lots of people visit.

school-trips-japan:4.fact: Tokyo Skytree is 634 m tall, the tallest tower in Japan.
school-trips-japan:4.about:
Tokyo, the capital of Japan, has the 634 m Tokyo Skytree, the National Diet Building, museums and more.
634 is a play on words: 6-3-4 can be read "mu-sa-shi," an old name for the area. On school trips, changing trains is an important experience too.

school-trips-japan:5.fact: A southern island with blue seas, coral reefs and Shuri Castle.
school-trips-japan:5.about:
Okinawa is a group of islands with blue seas and coral reefs. There was once a country called the "Ryūkyū Kingdom," and Shuri Castle was its castle. After a fire in 2019, it is being rebuilt.
Students try Okinawan culture, like snorkelling, playing the sanshin and making sātā andagī doughnuts.

school-trips-japan:6.fact: You can try milking cows and making butter on big farms.
school-trips-japan:6.about:
In Hokkaido, you can try milking cows and making butter and ice cream on big farms. Some schools have ski lessons in winter.
Hokkaido is about a fifth of Japan's area. There's also "Upopoy," a place where you can learn about the culture of the Ainu, an Indigenous people.

school-trips-japan:7.fact: There are towns inside one of the world's big calderas.
school-trips-japan:7.about:
Mount Aso in Kumamoto has a huge hollow called a "caldera," made by volcanic eruptions, with towns and rice fields inside it.
Kumamoto Castle was damaged in the 2016 earthquake, but its main tower has been repaired and looks as good as ever.

school-trips-japan:8.fact: Dejima, Chinatown, Glover Garden. School trip students come from all over Japan!
school-trips-japan:8.about:
Lots of school trip students come to Nagasaki from all over the country. There's so much to see: Dejima, where Japan traded with the Netherlands in the Edo period, Chinatown, Glover Garden, Megane Bridge and the night view from Mount Inasa.
They eat champon and castella and learn about lanterns and the history of ships. Your town is a "town of memories" for children all over Japan.

school-trips-japan:9.fact: Right in front of the city, Sakurajima is sending up smoke.
school-trips-japan:9.about:
Sakurajima, which sits in front of Kagoshima City, is an active volcano that still sends up smoke. You can get there by ferry in about 15 minutes.
On days when volcanic ash falls, people in the city collect it in special "ash bags." The "Sakurajima daikon," the world's biggest radish, is famous too.

#ocean-2: Ocean Animals, part 2. From sea lions to the world's biggest crab, the sea is still huge!

ocean-2:0.fact: The biggest member of the sea lion family. Males can weigh more than 1 tonne.
ocean-2:0.about:
The Steller sea lion is the biggest kind of sea lion. Males grow to about 3 m long and can weigh more than 1 tonne. In winter, they come to the seas around Hokkaido too.
Sea lions have ear flaps and can bend their back flippers forward to walk on land. That's how you can tell them apart from seals.

ocean-2:1.fact: Its Japanese name comes from spots that look like old coins ("zeni").
ocean-2:1.about:
The harbour seal lives on rocky shores in places like Cape Erimo in Hokkaido. Its body has round spots that look like old coins called "zeni."
Seals have no ear flaps, and on land they wriggle along on their bellies. When they swim, they move their back flippers from side to side.

ocean-2:2.fact: The male's nose looks like an elephant's. It dives more than 1,500 m deep.
ocean-2:2.about:
Male northern elephant seals have a big nose like an elephant's trunk and can weigh more than 2 tonnes.
They dive more than 1,500 m deep and can hold their breath for over an hour. Their numbers once fell very low, but with protection they have recovered a lot.

ocean-2:3.fact: The biggest octopus in the world. With its arms spread out, it's more than 3 m across.
ocean-2:3.about:
The giant Pacific octopus is the biggest octopus in the world. With its arms spread out it can be more than 3 m across and weigh over 50 kg. It's caught in the seas of Hokkaido and Tōhoku.
An octopus mother guards her eggs for months without eating anything, until her babies hatch.

ocean-2:4.fact: It "talks" by changing the colour and pattern of its skin in an instant.
ocean-2:4.about:
Cuttlefish skin has lots of cells that change colour and light, so they can change their patterns in an instant to "talk" to each other.
Inside their body is a light bone called a "cuttlebone," which they use to control how deep they float. They are said to be about as clever as something between a squid and an octopus.

ocean-2:5.fact: About 3 m across with its legs spread. The biggest crab in the world, and it lives in Japan's seas.
ocean-2:5.about:
The Japanese spider crab is the biggest crab in the world, about 3 m across with its legs spread out. It lives in the deep sea on Japan's Pacific side, in places like Suruga Bay in Shizuoka.
It's an old type of crab called a "living fossil," and it's said to live for 100 years.

ocean-2:6.fact: One of the heaviest bony fish in the world. It lays hundreds of millions of eggs.
ocean-2:6.about:
The ocean sunfish is one of the heaviest bony fish in the world, sometimes weighing more than 2 tonnes.
It's said to lay hundreds of millions of eggs at a time. You can sometimes see it lying on its side at the surface, sunbathing.

ocean-2:7.fact: It spreads its fins and flies hundreds of metres over the sea.
ocean-2:7.about:
A flying fish spreads its big, wing-like front fins and glides hundreds of metres over the sea. It's a trick for escaping from bigger fish.
In Nagasaki, flying fish are called "ago," and "ago dashi" broth made from grilled flying fish is used in ramen and New Year ozōni soup.

ocean-2:8.fact: More than 95% of its body is water. Look for its 4 rings.
ocean-2:8.about:
The moon jellyfish is often seen in Japanese harbours too, and its bell has a pattern of 4 rings. More than 95% of its body is water.
There's even an amazing jellyfish called the "immortal jellyfish," which can turn back into a baby when it gets old.

ocean-2:9.fact: Males sing "songs" that last for dozens of minutes.
ocean-2:9.about:
Humpback whales have long front flippers and are sometimes called "angels of the sea." In winter, they come to the seas around Okinawa and Ogasawara to raise their babies.
Males sing long "songs" with repeating parts, and males in the same sea sing the same song. The songs change a little each year.

ocean-2:10.fact: A big, fast fish that swims at about 80 km per hour. It's farmed in Nagasaki too.
ocean-2:10.about:
The Pacific bluefin tuna is a big fish that can grow to 3 m long and sometimes swims at about 80 km per hour. It can't breathe unless it keeps swimming, so it swims even while it sleeps.
Nagasaki is one of the prefectures where bluefin tuna farming is common.

ocean-2:11.fact: In schools of tens of thousands, they swim like one living thing.
ocean-2:11.about:
Sardines form schools of tens of thousands and move as if they were one big animal to protect themselves.
Sardines are important fish that hold up the ocean food chain, and they are food for lots of creatures, like whales, tuna and seabirds.

#arctic: The Arctic is a world made of frozen sea. Let's find out the secrets of bodies that beat the cold.

arctic:0.fact: With its very long fur, it's fine even at minus 40°C.
arctic:0.about:
Musk oxen survive cold of minus 40°C with very long fur and a fluffy layer underneath (qiviut). This wool is said to be several times warmer than sheep's wool.
When wolves attack, the adults form a circle with the young ones in the middle to protect them.

arctic:1.fact: It sometimes stands on its back legs and hops along. In winter it's pure white.
arctic:1.about:
Arctic hares are pure white in winter, and in summer some turn greyish, depending on where they live. Their ears are fairly short, so they don't lose body heat easily.
Sometimes they stand on just their back legs and hop like a kangaroo.

arctic:2.fact: It digs tunnels under the snow to get through the winter.
arctic:2.about:
Lemmings are small rodents that live in the Arctic tundra. In winter they dig tunnels under the snow, and the snow protects them from the cold wind.
The story that they "jump off cliffs" is a mistake spread by an old film. Every few years, their numbers go up and down a lot.

arctic:3.fact: A white wolf that survives nights lasting for months.
arctic:3.about:
Arctic wolves have white fur and live on the northern islands of Canada and in Greenland. In winter, there are months of night when the sun doesn't come up.
Because they live where there are almost no people, they are sometimes not very afraid of humans.

arctic:4.fact: It makes so many sounds that it's called the "canary of the sea."
arctic:4.about:
The beluga is a small, pure white whale. It makes all kinds of sounds, like whistles and chirps, so it's called the "canary of the sea."
Unlike other whales, it can move its neck and look back over its shoulder.

arctic:5.fact: Babies have pure white, fluffy fur.
arctic:5.about:
Baby harp seals have pure white, fluffy fur when they are born, so they are hard to see on the ice.
Adults have a pattern on their backs that looks like a harp, which is where their name comes from.

arctic:6.fact: It can carry more than 10 fish in its colourful beak.
arctic:6.about:
The Atlantic puffin is a seabird with a bright orange and yellow beak. Using its tongue and spines in its beak, it can carry more than 10 small fish at once.
Underwater, it swims with its wings. Their numbers are falling, and people are working to protect them.

arctic:7.fact: It flies between the Arctic and the Antarctic, the longest migration in the world.
arctic:7.about:
Arctic terns fly between the Arctic and the Antarctic every year. In one year they fly about 70,000 km, and in a lifetime they fly as far as going to the Moon and back several times.
They follow the summer in the north and the south, so they're said to see more sunlight in a year than any other creature.

arctic:8.fact: It lives more than 200 years, the longest-living mammal in the world.
arctic:8.about:
The bowhead whale is known to live more than 200 years, the longest of any mammal.
It has a big head and can even break through thick ice with it to breathe. It eats by filtering tiny shrimp (krill) with its baleen.

arctic:9.fact: A slow-swimming shark that is thought to live more than 250 years.
arctic:9.about:
The Greenland shark lives in the cold, deep Arctic seas and is thought to live more than 250 years. It only grows about 1 cm a year.
It swims at about 1 km per hour, making it one of the slowest-swimming sharks in the world.

arctic:10.fact: A fish that lives even in the most northern lakes in the world.
arctic:10.about:
The Arctic char is a member of the salmon family, and it lives even in the most northern lakes in the world. It loves cold water.
Some travel between the sea and rivers. In northern countries, it's an important food.

#japan-animals-2: Japan is long from north to south, and it has lots of amazing animals, from the brown bears of Hokkaido to the wildcats of Iriomote.

japan-animals-2:0.fact: The deer of Nara and Miyajima are this kind too. In summer they have white spots.
japan-animals-2:0.about:
Sika deer live all the way from Hokkaido to Kyushu. Their summer coat has white spots. Only males have antlers, and they grow new ones every spring.
The deer in Nara Park and on Miyajima in Hiroshima are sika deer too, and they have lived alongside people for a long time.

japan-animals-2:1.fact: A favourite in Japanese folk tales. It's actually a member of the dog family.
japan-animals-2:1.about:
The tanuki (raccoon dog) is a member of the dog family that lives in Japan and East Asia. It's the only member of the dog family that hibernates in winter (though only lightly).
In folk tales it's a favourite trickster that fools people. It even lives in the middle of Tokyo. In English it's called a raccoon dog, but it's a different animal from a raccoon.

japan-animals-2:2.fact: A fox that lives in Hokkaido. In winter its fur gets thick and fluffy.
japan-animals-2:2.about:
The Ezo red fox is a kind of red fox that lives in Hokkaido. In winter its fur gets thick and fluffy, and it sleeps wrapped in its tail.
It's famous for hunting by listening for mice under the snow, then jumping and diving in head first. Don't touch wild foxes.

japan-animals-2:3.fact: Its Japanese name comes from the white crescent moon pattern on its chest.
japan-animals-2:3.about:
The Asian black bear lives in Honshu and Shikoku and has a white crescent-shaped pattern on its chest. It's good at climbing trees and loves nuts like acorns.
In winter it hibernates in a den and gives birth to its babies there. When you go into the mountains, use a bell or your voice to let bears know people are there.

japan-animals-2:4.fact: A bear that lives in Hokkaido, the biggest land animal in Japan.
japan-animals-2:4.about:
The Ezo brown bear lives in Hokkaido. Males can weigh more than 300 kg, making it the biggest land animal in Japan.
In autumn it catches and eats salmon swimming up rivers, and stores fat in its body to get ready for hibernation. You can see wild brown bears in Shiretoko.

japan-animals-2:5.fact: In winter it curls up like a ball and hibernates. It's a Natural Monument.
japan-animals-2:5.about:
The Japanese dormouse is a small animal found only in Japan, and it's a national Natural Monument. It's also called a "living fossil" because it has hardly changed since very ancient times.
In winter it lowers its body temperature, curls up like a ball and hibernates for almost half a year.

japan-animals-2:6.fact: It spreads the skin between its arms and legs and glides from tree to tree.
japan-animals-2:6.about:
The Ezo flying squirrel lives in the forests of Hokkaido. It spreads the skin between its arms and legs (its gliding membrane) and glides tens of metres from tree to tree.
Its big black eyes are for being active at night. It's popular for its cute face.

japan-animals-2:7.fact: Its long, thin body makes it quick, and it's a good swimmer too.
japan-animals-2:7.about:
The Japanese weasel is an animal with a long, thin body that lives near rivers and rice fields in Japan. It catches mice, frogs and fish, and it's a good swimmer too.
Even though it's small, it's brave and will face animals bigger than itself.

japan-animals-2:8.fact: A wildcat that lives only on Iriomote in Okinawa. There are only about 100.
japan-animals-2:8.about:
The Iriomote cat is a wildcat that lives only on Iriomote Island in Okinawa, and there are said to be only about 100. It was found in 1965 and surprised researchers around the world.
It's a good swimmer and eats all kinds of things, like frogs, birds and lizards. To protect it from traffic accidents, the island has "Watch out for wildcats" road signs.

japan-animals-2:9.fact: The biggest beetle in Japan. The males have very long front legs.
japan-animals-2:9.about:
The Yanbaru long-armed beetle is the biggest beetle in Japan, and it lives only in the "Yanbaru" forests of northern Okinawa Island. It was only discovered in 1983 and is still full of mysteries.
A male's front legs can be longer than its body. It grows up in holes in big old trees, so protecting the forest is important.

japan-animals-2:10.fact: About 1.8 m across with its wings spread. A big owl that catches fish.
japan-animals-2:10.about:
Blakiston's fish owl is one of the biggest owls in the world, about 1.8 m across with its wings spread. It catches and eats fish in forests near rivers in Hokkaido.
The Ainu people called it "Kotan Kor Kamuy" (the god who protects the village) and treasured it. Today there are said to be only about 200.

japan-animals-2:11.fact: A big eagle that flies from Russia to Hokkaido in winter.
japan-animals-2:11.about:
Steller's sea eagle is a very big eagle that flies from Russia to Hokkaido in winter. Look for its thick yellow beak and its white shoulders and tail.
Lots of them perching on the drift ice is a famous winter sight in Shiretoko and Nemuro.

japan-animals-2:12.fact: It once disappeared from the wild in Japan, but its numbers are coming back on Sado.
japan-animals-2:12.about:
The crested ibis, whose scientific name is "Nipponia nippon," is a bird that represents Japan. Wild crested ibises in Japan once disappeared, but birds sent from China were bred on Sado Island in Niigata, and they have been released into the wild since 2008.
Now hundreds of crested ibises fly in the skies over Sado.

japan-animals-2:13.fact: A newt with a red belly. If it loses part of its body, it grows back.
japan-animals-2:13.about:
The Japanese fire-bellied newt has a black back and a red belly. The red colour is a signal that says "I'm poisonous!"
It can regrow its legs, its tail and even parts of its eyes, so it's used in research. Wash your hands after touching one.

japan-animals-2:14.fact: A big fruit-eating bat that lives only on the Ogasawara Islands.
japan-animals-2:14.about:
The Bonin flying fox is a bat that lives only on the Ogasawara Islands, part of Tokyo. Its wings are about 80 cm across, and it eats fruit and flower nectar.
In winter, dozens of them gather to sleep. They carry pollen, so they have an important job protecting the islands' plants.

#rainforest-2: Rainforests cover only about 6% of the Earth's land, but more than half of all kinds of living things are said to live there.

rainforest-2:0.fact: Its bright yellow colour is a sign that says "I'm poisonous."
rainforest-2:0.about:
The golden poison frog is a small frog that lives in the rainforests of Colombia, and it's one of the most poisonous frogs in the world.
Its poison comes from the ants and other things it eats, so frogs raised in zoos aren't poisonous. Long ago, people put its poison on the tips of hunting darts.

rainforest-2:1.fact: Green when it's asleep. When it gets a fright, it opens its bright red eyes.
rainforest-2:1.about:
During the day, the red-eyed tree frog sleeps with its green body and legs pressed against a leaf, hidden.
When a snake or other animal attacks, it suddenly flashes its bright red eyes and orange feet to startle the attacker, then escapes.

rainforest-2:2.fact: The king of the forest, with claws as big as a bear's.
rainforest-2:2.about:
The harpy eagle lives in the rainforests of Central and South America and is one of the most powerful eagles in the world. Its talons are about 12 cm long, as big as a bear's claws.
It flies quickly between the trees and catches sloths and monkeys. It's the national bird of Panama.

rainforest-2:3.fact: In the morning, its call can be heard several kilometres away.
rainforest-2:3.about:
Howler monkeys live in Central and South America and make loud calls with a special throat. Their calls can be heard several kilometres away, making them one of the loudest land animals.
In the morning and evening, the troop howls together to say "This is our forest!"

rainforest-2:4.fact: A "farmer" ant that carries leaves and grows fungus in its nest.
rainforest-2:4.about:
Leafcutter ants cut leaves and carry them to their nest, but they don't eat the leaves. They use them as fertiliser to grow fungus inside the nest, and they eat that.
They have been "farming" since long before humans. Millions of them live in one nest.

rainforest-2:5.fact: Its wings shine blue, but there's no blue colouring in them.
rainforest-2:5.about:
The wings of the blue morpho shine blue, but they have no blue colouring (pigment). Very tiny shapes on the surface of the wings reflect light so they look blue.
This is called "structural colour," and it's used in research on things like cloth that doesn't fade.

rainforest-2:6.fact: The biggest rodent in the world. It's a good swimmer.
rainforest-2:6.about:
The capybara is the biggest rodent in the world, weighing about 50 kg. It has small webs between its toes and is good at swimming and diving.
In Japanese zoos, capybaras are popular for bathing in hot baths with yuzu fruit in winter.

rainforest-2:7.fact: Black and white. Its babies are striped.
rainforest-2:7.about:
The Malayan tapir has an unusual pattern: its front half is black and its back half is white. In a dark forest, the pattern makes its body shape hard to see.
Babies have stripes like a watermelon. In Japan, it's also known from the legend of the "baku" that eats dreams.

rainforest-2:8.fact: The biggest flower in the world, up to 1 m across.
rainforest-2:8.about:
Rafflesia is the biggest flower in the world, sometimes 1 m across and weighing 10 kg. It has no leaves, stems or roots, and lives by taking nutrients from another plant.
It smells like rotten meat to attract flies, which carry its pollen. The flower only lasts a few days.

rainforest-2:9.fact: It dissolves insects that fall into its pitcher and uses them as food.
rainforest-2:9.about:
The pitcher plant makes a pitcher at the end of its leaves and lures insects with a sweet smell. The rim of the pitcher is slippery, and insects that fall in are dissolved by the liquid inside.
Because it grows in poor soil, it began getting nutrients from insects. Some are big enough for mice to fall into.

rainforest-2:10.fact: It spreads the skin between its ribs and glides from tree to tree.
rainforest-2:10.about:
The flying dragon spreads out its ribs so the skin on the sides of its body works like wings, and it glides several metres from tree to tree.
It's called a "dragon," but it's only about 20 cm long. It spreads the yellow flap on its throat to signal to others.

rainforest-2:11.fact: A small, hairy rhino. There are said to be fewer than 50 left.
rainforest-2:11.about:
The Sumatran rhino is the smallest rhino, and its body is covered in reddish-brown hair. Of all living rhinos, it's the closest relative of the ancient woolly rhino.
There are said to be fewer than 50 in the wild, and it's on the edge of extinction. Efforts to protect it continue, and babies have been born at a breeding centre.

#savanna-2: On the wide grasslands of the savanna live creatures with all kinds of jobs, from animals on a great migration to nature's cleaners.

savanna-2:0.fact: More than a million travel huge distances looking for grass.
savanna-2:0.about:
On the savannas of Tanzania and Kenya, more than a million wildebeest travel every year with zebras and gazelles, moving in a big circle in search of fresh grass.
This is called the "Great Migration," one of the biggest animal migrations on Earth.

savanna-2:1.fact: It runs at about 80 km per hour and escapes by zigzagging.
savanna-2:1.about:
Thomson's gazelle is a small antelope that runs at about 80 km per hour. Its top speed is slower than a cheetah's, but it escapes by zigzagging and suddenly changing direction.
When it senses danger, it jumps high on all four legs, called "stotting," to warn the others.

savanna-2:2.fact: It kneels to eat grass. When it runs away, its tail sticks straight up!
savanna-2:2.about:
The warthog has big wart-like bumps on its face and tusks that curve upwards. Its neck is short, so it kneels on its front knees to eat grass.
When it runs away, it holds its tail straight up like an antenna so its babies don't lose sight of it.

savanna-2:3.fact: The biggest bird in the world. Its egg is the biggest too!
savanna-2:3.about:
The ostrich is the biggest bird in the world, more than 2 m tall and over 100 kg. It can't fly, but it runs at about 70 km per hour.
Its egg is the biggest in the world too: one egg equals about 25 chicken eggs. Its eyes are said to be bigger than its brain.

savanna-2:4.fact: A bird of prey that catches snakes by kicking them with its long legs.
savanna-2:4.about:
The secretary bird walks across the grassland on its long legs, and when it finds a snake, it kicks it quickly to catch it. Its kicks are lightning fast and very accurate.
Its English name is said to come from its head feathers, which look like the pens that secretaries long ago tucked behind their ears.

savanna-2:5.fact: Inside a mound several metres tall, it always stays cool.
savanna-2:5.about:
A termite mound is a huge nest made of mud that can be several metres tall. It has air passages inside, so the temperature inside doesn't change much even when it's hot outside.
The "Eastgate" shopping centre in Zimbabwe copies this idea and stays cool while hardly using air conditioning.

savanna-2:6.fact: Dogs that live together as a family, and each one has a different pattern.
savanna-2:6.about:
The African wild dog is a member of the dog family in Africa, and each one has a different coat pattern. Pack members get along very well and even share food with injured members.
They hunt together as a pack, and they are said to be very successful hunters. Their numbers are falling, and they need protection.

savanna-2:7.fact: An upside-down tree that stores lots of water in its trunk.
savanna-2:7.about:
The baobab grows in Africa and Madagascar. It stores lots of water in its thick trunk to survive dry times. When it has no leaves, it looks like its roots are growing upwards, so it's called the "upside-down tree."
Some baobabs are said to live for thousands of years.

savanna-2:8.fact: With its long tongue, it eats tens of thousands of ants in one night.
savanna-2:8.about:
The aardvark is an African animal that digs into termite mounds with its strong claws and licks up ants with its sticky tongue, almost 30 cm long. It eats tens of thousands in one night.
Its name means "earth pig," but it isn't related to pigs. The holes it digs become homes for other animals too.

savanna-2:9.fact: It rides on the backs of giraffes and rhinos and eats the bugs on them.
savanna-2:9.about:
The red-billed oxpecker rides on the backs of giraffes, rhinos and buffaloes and eats ticks and other bugs on their bodies.
The animals get rid of bugs, and the oxpeckers get food. They sometimes call out to warn of danger too. They help each other out.

savanna-2:10.fact: The leader of the group is a female. Family bonds are strong.
savanna-2:10.about:
Spotted hyenas live in groups, and the leader of the group is a female. Mothers care for their young for a long time.
People often think they only steal other animals' leftovers, but they are actually skilled hunters too. They talk to each other with calls that sound like laughing.

savanna-2:11.fact: Nature's cleaners. They stop diseases from spreading.
savanna-2:11.about:
Vultures like the white-backed vulture eat the bodies of dead animals, so they are "nature's cleaners." Thanks to them, diseases are stopped from spreading.
They have few feathers on their heads so they don't get dirty while eating. Their numbers have fallen a lot, and people are working to protect them.

#desert-2: Deserts get almost no rain. The creatures that live there have amazing tricks for getting water.

desert-2:0.fact: A camel's hump isn't full of water. It's full of fat.
desert-2:0.about:
A camel's hump holds fat, not water. When there's no food, the camel turns the fat into energy to survive.
Camels can drink more than 100 litres of water at once. Long eyelashes and nostrils that can close protect them from sand.

desert-2:1.fact: A rare wild camel that can even drink salty water.
desert-2:1.about:
The wild Bactrian camel has two humps. Only about 1,000 live in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia and China, so it's a very rare animal.
It can drink very salty water that other mammals can't. It's thought to be a different species from the tame Bactrian camels people keep.

desert-2:2.fact: It stores food in its tail and can go months without eating.
desert-2:2.about:
The Gila monster is a venomous lizard that lives in the deserts of the southwestern USA and Mexico. It moves slowly and very rarely attacks people.
It stores food energy in its thick tail and can go months without eating. A medicine was even made from research on this lizard's saliva.

desert-2:3.fact: It's better at running than flying. It runs at about 30 km per hour.
desert-2:3.about:
The greater roadrunner can fly, but it's much better at running, at about 30 km per hour.
On cold desert mornings, it warms up by letting sunlight hit the black skin on its back. It's a brave bird that even catches lizards and rattlesnakes.

desert-2:4.fact: A rat that can live its whole life without drinking water.
desert-2:4.about:
Kangaroo rats can live their whole lives drinking almost no water. They make water inside their bodies from the seeds they eat, and their wee is very concentrated, so they don't waste water.
They escape from snakes by making big jumps on their long back legs, like kangaroos.

desert-2:5.fact: Shine a black light on it, and it glows blue-green.
desert-2:5.about:
Scorpions have hardly changed for hundreds of millions of years. When you shine a black light (ultraviolet light) on them, they glow blue-green, and nobody is quite sure why.
Mothers carry their babies on their backs to protect them. The stinger on the tail is venomous, so never touch one if you find it.

desert-2:6.fact: A cactus that grows more than 12 m tall. Some live 200 years.
desert-2:6.about:
The saguaro is a big cactus that grows in the Sonoran Desert of the USA and Mexico. Some grow more than 12 m tall and live more than 200 years.
When it rains, its trunk swells up to store lots of water. Holes that woodpeckers make in the trunk become homes for other birds too.

desert-2:7.fact: An insect that collects fog on its back to drink.
desert-2:7.about:
Africa's Namib Desert gets almost no rain, but fog rolls in from the sea in the morning. The fog-basking beetle does a headstand to catch the fog on its back, and the water drops that collect run down into its mouth.
Scientists are copying this to research tools that collect water from the air.

desert-2:8.fact: A jumping expert with huge ears for its size.
desert-2:8.about:
The long-eared jerboa is only about 10 cm long, but its ears are bigger than its head, about a third of its body length.
It's active at night and hops along on its long back legs to catch insects. Its big ears also help it lose body heat.

desert-2:9.fact: It spends most of the year in a hole in the ground.
desert-2:9.about:
The desert tortoise lives in places like the Mojave Desert in the USA and spends nearly 95% of the year in burrows it digs in the ground.
It stores water in its bladder, so it can go months without drinking. Its numbers are falling, and people worry it could die out.

desert-2:10.fact: The only bear in the world that lives in a desert. There are only a few dozen.
desert-2:10.about:
The Gobi bear is a kind of brown bear that lives in Mongolia's Gobi Desert, and it's the only bear in the world that lives in a desert. There are said to be only a few dozen.
It eats roots, berries and insects. In Mongolia, it's protected as a national treasure.

#mountain-animals: High mountains are cold and steep, with thin air. The animals that live there are expert climbers.

mountain-animals:0.fact: It wraps its thick, long tail around itself like a scarf.
mountain-animals:0.about:
Snow leopards live in high mountains in Asia, like the Himalayas. Even the soles of their feet are furry, so walking on snow doesn't feel cold.
Their long tails help them balance, and when they sleep they wrap their tails around their faces like a scarf. They're so rarely seen that they're called "ghosts of the mountains."

mountain-animals:1.fact: A long-haired cow that can live even above 5,000 m.
mountain-animals:1.about:
Wild yaks are members of the cattle family that live on the Tibetan Plateau, 4,000 to 6,000 m above sea level. Their long hair, which hangs down to their bellies, keeps out the cold.
Tame yaks are important working partners for Tibetan people, giving milk and wool and carrying loads.

mountain-animals:2.fact: Its hooves don't slip, so it can walk freely on cliffs.
mountain-animals:2.about:
Mountain goats live on cliffs in the Rocky Mountains. The outside of each hoof is hard and the inside is soft like rubber, so it grips rocks firmly.
It's called a "goat," but it's really closer to the serow. It's a relative of Japan's serow.

mountain-animals:3.fact: It climbs the almost vertical wall of a dam to lick salt.
mountain-animals:3.about:
The Alpine ibex is a kind of wild goat with big curved horns. At a dam in Italy, ibexes are famous for clinging to the almost vertical wall and licking salt from the stones.
Their numbers once fell to about 100, but with protection there are now tens of thousands again.

mountain-animals:4.fact: A relative of the alpaca's ancestors. It has the finest wool in the world.
mountain-animals:4.about:
The vicuña is a member of the camel family that lives about 4,000 m up in the Andes. It's thought to be the ancestor of the alpaca.
Its wool is the finest in the world and very expensive. Long ago, it's said that only the Inca kings could wear it. It even appears on the coat of arms on Peru's flag.

mountain-animals:5.fact: More than 3 m across with its wings spread. It flies for hours without flapping.
mountain-animals:5.about:
The Andean condor is one of the biggest flying birds in the world, more than 3 m across with its wings spread. One was recorded flying for more than 5 hours on rising warm air, hardly flapping at all.
It's a symbol of several South American countries.

mountain-animals:6.fact: A big, powerful eagle that lives in Japan's mountains too.
mountain-animals:6.about:
The golden eagle is a big eagle, about 2 m across with its wings spread, and it lives in Japan's mountains too. Its dives are said to reach more than 200 km per hour.
In Japan its numbers are falling, and it's a national Natural Monument. In Mongolia, there's a tradition of hunting together with golden eagles.

mountain-animals:7.fact: A round-eared relative of the rabbit that calls "pichit!"
mountain-animals:7.about:
The Ezo pika is a small, round-eared relative of the rabbit that lives on rocky slopes in Hokkaido's mountains. It calls "pichit!" to warn others of danger.
It doesn't hibernate. Instead, it collects grass in summer and stores it in gaps between rocks. It's said to be an animal that has survived since the Ice Age.

mountain-animals:8.fact: It hibernates for more than half the year. It warns others with a whistle-like call.
mountain-animals:8.about:
The Alpine marmot is a member of the squirrel family that lives in Alpine meadows. For more than 6 months a year, the family stays in its burrow and hibernates.
When it spots an eagle or another danger, it warns the others with a high, whistle-like call.

mountain-animals:9.fact: The "bird of the gods" of the Japanese Alps. In winter it turns pure white.
mountain-animals:9.about:
The rock ptarmigan lives high in the Japanese Alps and has long been treasured as the "bird of the gods." Its feathers are brown in summer and pure white in winter, so it blends into the snow.
Even its toes are covered in feathers. Its numbers are falling, and people are protecting it in zoos and in the mountains. It's a Special Natural Monument of Japan.

mountain-animals:10.fact: It lives above 6,000 m, one of the highest-living creatures in the world.
mountain-animals:10.about:
The Himalayan jumping spider is a small spider that lives on Everest above 6,000 m. It's one of the creatures that live permanently at the highest places in the world.
Where there are almost no plants, it survives by eating insects blown up by the wind.

#wetlands-mangroves: Wetlands are places between water and land. They are treasured as "cradles" for birds, fish and insects.

wetlands-mangroves:0.fact: A worldwide promise to protect important wetlands. Japan has more than 50.
wetlands-mangroves:0.about:
In 1971, in a town in Iran called Ramsar, countries made a promise to protect important wetlands where water birds gather: the "Ramsar Convention."
In Japan, Kushiro Marsh was the first to be listed, and now more than 50 places are listed. They include tidal flats on the Ariake Sea, like Higashiyoka in Saga and Arao in Kumamoto.

wetlands-mangroves:1.fact: The biggest marsh in Japan. It's the home of the red-crowned crane.
wetlands-mangroves:1.about:
Kushiro Marsh in Hokkaido is the biggest marsh in Japan. Red-crowned cranes, which people thought had disappeared, were found there, and thanks to protection their numbers grew.
Marshes also store water in heavy rain, which helps prevent floods.

wetlands-mangroves:2.fact: A fish that hops across the Ariake Sea mudflats on its fins.
wetlands-mangroves:2.about:
The mudskipper is a fish that lives on the Ariake Sea mudflats and moves over the mud by hopping with its front fins. It can even breathe air through its skin and mouth.
In summer, males jump high to show off to females. The Ariake Sea has the biggest tides in Japan, so wide mudflats appear.

wetlands-mangroves:3.fact: A "living fossil" that hasn't changed for more than 200 million years.
wetlands-mangroves:3.about:
The horseshoe crab is a "living fossil" that has hardly changed for more than 200 million years. It's called a crab, but it's closer to spiders and scorpions.
Its blood is blue and is used in tests to check whether medicines are safe. In Japan, you can see them on tidal flats in Okayama, Fukuoka and Saga.

wetlands-mangroves:4.fact: Forests that grow in sea water. Iriomote has Japan's biggest mangroves.
wetlands-mangroves:4.about:
Mangroves are forests of trees that grow by the sea where sea water and river water mix. They stand in the mud on roots like octopus legs and protect the coast from waves and typhoons.
The spaces between the roots are homes for small fish and crabs. Iriomote Island in Okinawa has the biggest mangrove forest in Japan.

wetlands-mangroves:5.fact: Its pink colour comes from the shrimp and algae it eats.
wetlands-mangroves:5.about:
Flamingos are grey when they hatch, but the colouring in the tiny shrimp and algae they eat turns them pink.
Some say they sleep standing on one leg to keep in body heat. Both fathers and mothers feed their chicks "flamingo milk" from their throats.

wetlands-mangroves:6.fact: It catches fish by sweeping its spoon-shaped beak through the water.
wetlands-mangroves:6.about:
The black-faced spoonbill sweeps its flat, spoon-shaped beak from side to side in the water to catch fish and shrimp.
It's a rare bird, with only a few thousand in the world, and in winter some come to places like the tidal flats of Kyushu.

wetlands-mangroves:7.fact: An expert swimmer with webbed feet and a long tail.
wetlands-mangroves:7.about:
Otters are expert swimmers that use their webbed feet and thick tails. Their fur is so thick that water doesn't soak through to their skin.
The Japanese river otter, which lived in Japan, was declared extinct in 2012. Now, in places like Europe, rivers have become cleaner and otters are coming back.

wetlands-mangroves:8.fact: It stands still on its long legs and catches fish in an instant.
wetlands-mangroves:8.about:
The grey heron is the biggest heron in Japan. It stands very still on its long legs in rivers and rice fields, and when a fish comes near, it shoots out its neck and catches it in an instant.
Dozens of them gather to build nests in trees. In Japanese it's called the "blue heron," but it's really a grey bird.

wetlands-mangroves:9.fact: It's born in a sea more than 2,000 km away from Japan.
wetlands-mangroves:9.about:
The Japanese eel is born in the sea near the Mariana Islands, more than 2,000 km from Japan. The see-through, leaf-shaped babies ride ocean currents to Japan's rivers.
Japanese researchers spent a long time finding this birthplace. Their numbers are falling, so protecting them is important.

wetlands-mangroves:10.fact: The biggest water insect in Japan. The father protects the eggs.
wetlands-mangroves:10.about:
The giant water bug is the biggest water insect in Japan, with strong front legs for catching frogs and fish.
The mother lays eggs on plants above the water, and the father splashes water on them so they don't dry out. Because of things like pesticides, their numbers have fallen and they've become rare.

#city-animals: Towns are full of wild animals too! They are clever animals that make good use of the way people live.

city-animals:0.fact: A very clever crow that gets cars to crack walnuts for it.
city-animals:0.about:
Carrion crows in Sendai, Miyagi became famous for putting walnuts on the road so cars would run over them and crack them open.
Crows are very clever birds that remember people's faces and use tools. Finding better ways to put out rubbish is a battle of wits with crows.

city-animals:1.fact: A relative of the "homing pigeon" that can fly home from hundreds of kilometres away.
city-animals:1.about:
Town pigeons are rock doves. They can find their way home from hundreds of kilometres away using the Earth's magnetism and the position of the sun.
In the days before phones, they were used as "homing pigeons" to carry letters.

city-animals:2.fact: The most familiar bird, which builds nests in gaps in people's houses.
city-animals:2.about:
Sparrows build nests in places like gaps under the roofs of houses, and they have always lived close to people. You hardly ever find them where there are no people.
"Fukura suzume," a puffed-up sparrow, is a winter word in haiku and is used as a lucky pattern too.

city-animals:3.fact: A nest under a shop's roof is a sign of good business.
city-animals:3.about:
Swallows fly to Japan from Southeast Asia in spring and build mud nests under the roofs of shops and stations. Places with people are safer from crows and other attackers.
In Japan, people say "a house where swallows build a nest will do well," so swallows have long been welcomed.

city-animals:4.fact: Some deer bow before they get a deer cracker.
city-animals:4.about:
The deer of Nara Park are wild deer that have been treasured for a long time, and they are a national Natural Monument. Some bow their heads to people holding deer crackers, which delights tourists from all over the world.
But they are wild animals, so they might suddenly butt with their antlers or bite. Watch them gently.

city-animals:5.fact: Wild tanuki live even in gardens in the middle of Tokyo.
city-animals:5.about:
Wild tanuki (raccoon dogs) live in Tokyo's Imperial Palace grounds, big gardens and the woods in neighbourhoods. They're active at night, so they're hard to spot.
Connecting green spaces in towns helps protect the lives of animals.

city-animals:6.fact: London is said to have about 10,000 foxes.
city-animals:6.about:
London has lots of foxes that live in the city, and they raise their cubs in gardens and parks. It's not unusual to see them walking the streets at night.
They're animals that have got used to town life by making good use of the food people leave out.

city-animals:7.fact: Experts at opening bins. They even have the nickname "trash pandas."
city-animals:7.about:
Toronto in Canada has lots of raccoons, and their clever hands can open bins. The city even made bins that raccoons can't open.
The raccoons in Japan come from escaped pets, and they aren't originally from Japan.

city-animals:8.fact: In Lopburi, Thailand, there are lots of macaques right in the middle of town.
city-animals:8.about:
In Lopburi, Thailand, lots of long-tailed macaques live in the town around old ruins. Every year, there's even a festival with a feast for the monkeys.
In the wild around the world, long-tailed macaques are decreasing, and they're said to be at high risk of extinction.

city-animals:9.fact: Nagasaki is said to have lots of cats with bent tails.
city-animals:9.about:
Nagasaki is said to have lots of cats with bent tips on their tails. One idea is that in the Edo period, cats on trading ships from the Netherlands and Southeast Asia came ashore and had kittens in Nagasaki.
People say a bent tail "hooks good luck," and these cats are a little Nagasaki speciality.

city-animals:10.fact: They use tall buildings instead of cliffs and raise their chicks in cities.
city-animals:10.about:
Peregrine falcons originally nest on cliffs. Now they use tall buildings and steel towers instead of cliffs and raise their chicks in big cities around the world.
They dive from buildings to catch pigeons. Some cities stream live video of their nests.

city-animals:11.fact: In the evening, it flutters across the town sky. It eats lots of mosquitoes in one night.
city-animals:11.about:
The Japanese house bat is the bat you see most often in Japanese towns. It rests in gaps in roof tiles and walls.
It flutters around in the evening and is said to eat about half its body weight in insects in one night. It's a town friend that cuts down on mosquitoes.

#islands-animals: On islands cut off by the sea, amazing creatures that live nowhere else are born.

islands-animals:0.fact: A huge tortoise that lives more than 100 years.
islands-animals:0.about:
The Galápagos giant tortoise is a very big tortoise that can weigh more than 200 kg and lives more than 100 years.
The shells are shaped differently on each island, and this gave Darwin a clue for thinking about evolution. "Galápago" is an old Spanish word for "tortoise."

islands-animals:1.fact: The only lizard in the world that dives in the sea to eat seaweed.
islands-animals:1.about:
The marine iguana is the only sea lizard in the world. It dives into the sea to eat seaweed on rocks.
Salt that gets into its body from sea water is blown out of its nose like a "sneeze." After swimming, it warms its black body by sunbathing on the rocks.

islands-animals:2.fact: Little birds with different beaks on each island. The stars of evolution research.
islands-animals:2.about:
Finches on the Galápagos Islands have different beak shapes on each island: thick beaks for cracking hard seeds, thin beaks for catching insects, long beaks for eating cactus fruit…
Using these birds as clues, Darwin put together the idea of "evolution": living things slowly change over a long time.

islands-animals:3.fact: The biggest lizard in the world, up to 3 m long.
islands-animals:3.about:
The Komodo dragon lives on Komodo Island and other islands in Indonesia. It can be 3 m long and weigh more than 70 kg, making it the biggest lizard in the world.
It smells with its tongue and can find prey several kilometres away. It's protected in a national park, which is also a World Heritage Site.

islands-animals:4.fact: It walks with its striped tail held up high.
islands-animals:4.about:
The ring-tailed lemur is a primate that lives only in Madagascar. It holds its black-and-white striped tail up high to signal to the rest of its group.
In the morning, it sunbathes with its arms spread wide. Nearly 90% of Madagascar's wildlife is found nowhere else.

islands-animals:5.fact: The biggest meat-eater in Madagascar. An expert tree climber.
islands-animals:5.about:
The fossa is the biggest meat-eating mammal in Madagascar. It looks like a cat, but it's more closely related to the mongoose.
It balances with its long tail and moves quickly through the trees, hunting lemurs.

islands-animals:6.fact: A bird that can't fly. Its nostrils are at the tip of its beak.
islands-animals:6.about:
The kiwi is a flightless bird from New Zealand and is the country's symbol. People from New Zealand are sometimes called "Kiwis," and the kiwifruit is named after this bird too.
Unusually for a bird, its nostrils are at the tip of its beak, so it can sniff out worms in the ground. It lays a very big egg for its size.

islands-animals:7.fact: The only parrot in the world that can't fly. It walks around at night.
islands-animals:7.about:
The kākāpō is the only flightless parrot in the world, and it's also the heaviest parrot. It walks around at night and is good at climbing trees.
At one time there were only about 50, but thanks to work to protect them, each bird with its own name, there are now more than 200.

islands-animals:8.fact: A big pigeon that couldn't fly. It disappeared about 350 years ago.
islands-animals:8.about:
The dodo was a big, flightless relative of the pigeon that lived on Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. On an island with no predators, it wasn't afraid of people.
It disappeared within about 100 years of people arriving on the island. There's an English saying, "dead as a dodo," and the dodo reminds us how important it is to protect living things.

islands-animals:9.fact: A little bird that lives only on islands like Hahajima in Ogasawara.
islands-animals:9.about:
The Bonin white-eye is a little bird that lives only on islands like Hahajima in the Ogasawara Islands, part of Tokyo. Look for the black markings around its eyes. It's a Special Natural Monument of Japan.
The Ogasawara Islands have never been joined to a continent, so they're called the "Galápagos of the Orient." They became a World Natural Heritage Site in 2011.

islands-animals:10.fact: People thought it had disappeared, but it was found again 80 years later!
islands-animals:10.about:
The Lord Howe Island stick insect is a big stick insect from Lord Howe Island in Australia. People thought it had disappeared after rats arrived on the island around 1920.
In 2001, survivors were found again on a rock sticking out of the sea nearby! Now they're being bred in zoos, and there are plans to return them to the island.

#cave-deep-earth: Caves have no light. Some creatures lose their eyes, some glow… meet the amazing creatures that live in the dark.

cave-deep-earth:0.fact: A white salamander that can't see. It lives more than 100 years.
cave-deep-earth:0.about:
The olm is a white salamander that lives in underground water in caves in places like Slovenia. Its eyes are buried under its skin, so it can't see, but it finds prey by sensing smells and electricity.
It's thought to live more than 100 years, and one was recorded living 10 years without eating anything. Long ago, people thought olms were "baby dragons."

cave-deep-earth:1.fact: A fish that lost its eyes from living in dark caves.
cave-deep-earth:1.about:
This fish lives in caves in Mexico. It's the same species as fish that live in rivers, but from living in the dark it lost its eyes and colour.
Instead, it senses movement in the water with the "lateral line" along its side. It's used in research into how evolution works.

cave-deep-earth:2.fact: Insects that glow pale blue on the cave ceiling, like a starry sky.
cave-deep-earth:2.about:
In the Waitomo Caves in New Zealand, thousands of glowworms (the larvae of fungus gnats) glow pale blue on the ceiling, just like a starry sky.
They hang down glowing threads and catch insects that are drawn to the light. To protect the light, camera flashes aren't allowed in the cave.

cave-deep-earth:3.fact: It sends out ultrasound from its nose to fly in caves.
cave-deep-earth:3.about:
The horseshoe bat has a nose shaped like a horseshoe, and it sends out ultrasound from its nose, not its mouth.
Even in pitch-dark caves, it uses the echoes to find rocks and insects and can fly without bumping into things. In winter, it hibernates in caves.

cave-deep-earth:4.fact: A wingless insect that feels its way through the dark with long antennae.
cave-deep-earth:4.about:
The cave cricket is a wingless relative of the grasshopper, with antennae longer than its body and long back legs. Its Japanese name, "kamadouma," comes from how it was often seen around old kamado stoves.
In the dark, it feels its surroundings with its antennae, and it escapes by making big jumps.

cave-deep-earth:5.fact: One of Japan's biggest limestone caves. Small creatures live inside too.
cave-deep-earth:5.about:
Akiyoshi-dō in Yamaguchi is one of the biggest limestone caves in Japan. It was made by rainwater dissolving limestone over hundreds of thousands of years.
Amazing shapes line the cave, like stalactites hanging from the ceiling, stalagmites growing up from the floor, and the "Hundred Plates," which look like terraced rice fields. Insects and shrimp-like creatures with tiny eyes live inside too.

cave-deep-earth:6.fact: The biggest cave in the world. There's a jungle and clouds inside!
cave-deep-earth:6.about:
Son Doong Cave in Vietnam is the biggest cave in the world. Its huge spaces could fit a 40-storey building, and light comes in through holes where the ceiling collapsed, so a jungle grows inside.
It's said that clouds even form inside the cave. It was found in 1990 and explored properly in 2009.

#why-seasons: "What season do you like? — I like summer." But why do we have seasons at all?

why-seasons:0.fact: The Earth goes around the Sun tilted at about 23.4 degrees.
why-seasons:0.about:
The seasons don't change because of the distance from the Sun. They change because the Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees.
When the Northern Hemisphere, where Japan is, tilts towards the Sun, the Sun climbs high, its light is stronger and the days are longer, so it's summer. In fact, the Earth is closest to the Sun in January!

why-seasons:1.fact: The day with the most daylight of the year, around June 21st.
why-seasons:1.about:
The summer solstice is the day the Sun climbs highest in the sky, so daytime is longest. In Tokyo, there are about 14 and a half hours of daylight.
But the hottest time is July and August, because the ground and the sea take time to warm up.

why-seasons:2.fact: The day with the least daylight of the year. People take a yuzu bath.
why-seasons:2.about:
The winter solstice is the day with the shortest daytime of the year. In Japan, there's a custom of taking a bath with yuzu fruit floating in it and eating pumpkin to stay healthy through the cold winter.
After the winter solstice, the days slowly get longer. People long ago treasured it as "the day the Sun comes back to life."

why-seasons:3.fact: Day and night are almost the same length. Both are national holidays.
why-seasons:3.about:
On the spring and autumn equinoxes, the Sun rises due east and sets due west, and day and night are almost the same length.
Both are national holidays in Japan, and the week around each is called "ohigan." There's a saying: "The heat and the cold last until ohigan."

why-seasons:4.fact: On the summer solstice, Sapporo has more than an hour and a half more daylight than Naha!
why-seasons:4.about:
Japan is a long country from north to south. On the summer solstice, Sapporo in the north has about 15 hours of daylight, but Naha in the south has about 13 and a half.
On the winter solstice it's the other way around: Naha has more daylight. The further north you go, the bigger the difference between summer and winter.

why-seasons:5.fact: Near the North Pole, the Sun doesn't set in summer or rise in winter.
why-seasons:5.about:
Near the North and South Poles, there's the "midnight sun" in summer, when the Sun doesn't set all day, and the "polar night" in winter, when it doesn't rise all day.
In the north of Norway and Finland, it's bright enough to read a book outside even at midnight in summer.

why-seasons:6.fact: In Singapore, near the equator, there are about 12 hours of daylight all year.
why-seasons:6.about:
Near the equator, the Sun always passes high in the sky, so it's hot all year and the days are always about 12 hours long.
In Singapore, you can wear summer clothes all year round. Instead, there are rainier times and drier times.

why-seasons:7.fact: In tropical countries, the seasons change between "rainy and dry" rather than "hot and cold."
why-seasons:7.about:
In India and Southeast Asian countries, there's a "rainy season," when wet winds (monsoons) blow in from the sea, and a "dry season," with little rain.
Rainy season rain is important for farming. Japan's "tsuyu" rainy season is part of the same Asian rainy season.

why-seasons:8.fact: When it's summer in Japan, it's winter in Australia.
why-seasons:8.about:
In the Southern Hemisphere, the seasons are the opposite of Japan's. In December, it's summer in Australia, New Zealand and Argentina.
If you want to ski in July, you can go to the Southern Hemisphere. New Year is in the middle of summer!

why-seasons:9.fact: On Uranus, which spins on its side, summer lasts about 21 years.
why-seasons:9.about:
